vets.capabilities_check:
All listed symbols exist, but the core prior code has a bug. Locations: minnesota_gibbs (puremacro/var/bvar.py:266), minnesota_optimal_lambda (bvar.py:467), simulate_var_paths (puremacro/posterior.py:14), fan_chart_quantiles (posterior.py:60), berkowitz_test (puremacro/forecast/density.py:182), crps_gaussian (density.py:41), gelman_rubin (puremacro/mcmc.py:58).

(1) Lambda2 bug, verified numerically in scratch check1.py. In _build_minnesota_dummies (bvar.py:241-253) the inner `for eq` loop keeps overwriting the same Xd cell, so the last equation's value wins. When lambda2 is not 1, the implied prior mean of the own first lag (lstsq(Xd,Yd)) becomes [0.5, 0.5, 1.0] instead of [1,1,1], and the prior variance takes the cross-lag value. Every function built on these dummies inherits this: minnesota_gibbs, _minnesota_log_marginal_likelihood and minnesota_optimal_lambda. At lambda2=0.5, minnesota_posterior (equation by equation) and the mean of minnesota_gibbs differ by up to 0.068; at lambda2=1 the gap is 0.0006. The conjugate Kronecker NIW prior cannot express lambda2≠1 anyway. The validation case at puremacro/validation/cases_var.py:112-137 only checks lambda2=1 against the library's own dummies, so it is circular.

(2) minnesota_gibbs is not a Gibbs sampler. It draws iid from the NIW posterior (bvar.py:341-346). R-hat is 1.00 and ESS/n is about 1 even with 30 draws, so the claim in examples/mcmc_diagnostics.py:10-12 ("small n_draws produces marginal R-hat") is false. The module docstring (bvar.py:14) still says Gibbs sampling is "deferred to v2". The only true Gibbs sampler is bvar_sv (bvar_sv.py:987).

(3) The marginal-likelihood formula is correct. It matches an independent basic-marginal-likelihood-identity computation up to a constant +0.0149 at four hyperparameter points; the constant comes from the 1e-8 jitter at bvar.py:432,448.

(4) Missing GLP conventions: no prior-mean option for the own lag (it is hard-coded to 1, which is wrong for growth rates), the scale comes from an AR(p) with ddof=0 instead of GLP's AR(1), the IW prior has n degrees of freedom instead of n+2, the search is grid-only, and there is no hyperprior or SOC/DIO prior.

(5) crps_ensemble (density.py:57) is the right score for BVAR draws; crps_gaussian is not. Berkowitz is valid only for h=1.
vets.oracle_check:
The proposed oracle, Gibbs draws against the closed form, is nearly tautological: minnesota_gibbs samples that closed form directly. With lambda2=1, an independent NumPy NIW posterior matches the draw mean within 1.5 MCSE; with lambda2=0.5 the check fails because of the bug.

A much stronger independent oracle exists and can be obtained. Primiceri's research page links GLPreplicationWeb.zip (downloaded to scratch/wf/bvar-feas-review). It contains bvarGLP.m, logMLVAR_formin.m (the closed-form log ML, about 20 lines) and the Stock-Watson data DataSW.mat: 200 quarters, 1959Q1-2008Q4, seven variables. I transcribed the MN-only logML to NumPy (check2.py). On GLP's small VAR (RGDP, PGDP, FedFunds; p=5) the argmax is lambda=0.426, and the posterior mode under the Gamma(mode 0.2, sd 0.4) hyperprior is 0.417. The medium VAR gives 0.172. Swapping only the scale to GLP's AR(1) residual variance moves puremacro's small-VAR value to 0.422 (check3.py).

The published tables I read are Table 2 (MSFE; e.g. small-VAR one-quarter real GDP: VAR 13.57, BVAR 9.61, RW 10.23) and Table 3 (log-score differences). They use MN+SOC+DIO priors and hyperpriors, so they can serve only as a qualitative target (BVAR beats the flat-prior VAR). The glp example's claim (glp_lambda_search.py:9,58) is false. On the default grid, lambda1 is 0.2 for T=60 to 960, together with lambda2=0.5, which is a bug artifact. On a fine grid with lambda2=lambda3=1, lambda1 falls slightly: 0.29, 0.26, 0.26, 0.22, 0.22. GLP's own finding is that lambda falls with model size, not that it rises with T.

Notebook 47 (lines 73, 265-285) builds fans with simulate_var_paths from fit_var plus coefficient jitter, which the 09-20 review flagged as not real posterior draws. This notebook would give 47 a proper posterior.

The proposal is not in PLAN.md. The 09-20 "uncertainty lab" is about DiD coverage, so the overlap is small. The five examples (bvar_fan_chart, glp_lambda_search, posterior_predictive_fan, mcmc_diagnostics, gk_robust_from_gibbs) are uncovered by any notebook, and two of them print false claims.

ideas.title: Bad luck or bad policy? Minnesota, stochastic-volatility and Primiceri (2005) TVP-VAR-SV on the Great Moderation
ideas.anchor_notebook: new; follows 47 (fit_var only) and the course SVAR module
ideas.question: Was the US Great Moderation a fall in shock volatility or a change in the transmission coefficients, and how much of the answer comes from the prior?
ideas.description: Fit a 4-variable quarterly VAR (GDP growth, inflation, unemployment, fed funds) three ways. First, a Minnesota BVAR with hyperparameters chosen by marginal likelihood (minnesota_optimal_lambda, GLP 2015). Second, bvar_sv, which gives volatility paths, rhat and log_scores. Third, tvp_var_sv_fit for drifting coefficients. Before fitting the data, show on a planted DGP (a volatility break plus a drifting coefficient) that each sampler recovers what it should and that a constant-parameter VAR does not. Compare impulse responses before and after 1984 across models, and log predictive scores across models. Use longrun.chunked so the MCMC chains can resume on a tablet, a unique Pyodide story.
ideas.paper: Primiceri (2005); Sims & Zha (2006); Giannone, Lenza & Primiceri (2015); Bańbura, Giannone & Reichlin (2010)
ideas.oracle_detail: Planted volatility paths and coefficient drift, recovered by the bvar_sv h_draws and the tvp_var_sv_fit beta_t. There is also a closed form: the minnesota_gibbs posterior mean converges to the analytical NIW mean from minnesota_posterior, which the validation gallery already pins (validation/cases_var.py:235, _bvar_minnesota_analytical_ref). Published conclusions (Primiceri, Sims-Zha) are qualitative and must be quoted from fetched sources.
ideas.data_detail: datasets.load_macro_quarterly() has real_gdp, gdp_growth_annualized and fed_funds for 1954Q3-2026Q1 (287 rows). load_macro_monthly() has cpi, core_cpi, unemployment_rate, fed_funds and nfci for 1971-01 to 2026-06, aggregated to quarterly.
ideas.library_gaps: tvp_var_sv_fit keeps the contemporaneous matrix A constant (Primiceri with the constant-A simplification, per its docstring), so it cannot replicate Primiceri's time-varying simultaneity. BVAR_SVResult.r_hat is a dict, not an array. There is no TVP impulse-response helper found at a given date. Minnesota GLP omits the sum-of-coefficients prior (docstring bvar.py:467).
ideas.plan_overlap: None in PLAN.md, which covers DSGE and VFI. Notebook 47 uses only fit_var. mcmc_diagnostics.py and bvar_fan_chart.py are examples, not notebooks.

Quote published conclusions only from fetched sources (the Primiceri abstract and Del Negro-Primiceri section 5); fetch Sims-Zha 2006 before citing it.
vets.capabilities_check:
All 7 symbols exist at the stated lines. Smoke tests ran on the real 4-variable panel and on a planted DGP; scripts are in scratchpad/wf/tvpsv-review/smoke1-6.py.

(1) minnesota_posterior (bvar.py:40) returns the posterior mean only, built from per-equation dummies.

(2) minnesota_gibbs (bvar.py:266) is not a Gibbs sampler. It draws iid from the NIW posterior built by _build_minnesota_dummies, which has a lambda2 bug at bvar.py:243-254: one stacked dummy row is overwritten in the eq loop, so Xd ends at cross_coeff for every variable except the last. At lambda2=0.5 the implied prior mean of the own first lag is [0.5,0.5,0.5,1.0] instead of 1. Consequence: |minnesota_posterior A1 - mean(minnesota_gibbs A1)| is 0.246 at lambda2=0.5 and 0.005 at lambda2=1.

(3) minnesota_optimal_lambda (bvar.py:467) is a grid search on the NIW marginal likelihood (0.01 s). Its default lambda2_grid=(0.5,1.0) (bvar.py:474) scores the buggy prior. It has no sum-of-coefficients prior and no hyperprior. On the real data it picks lambda1=0.3, lambda2=1, lambda3=1.

(4) bvar_sv (bvar_sv.py:987) works: 2.9 ms per sweep at n=4, p=2. With 2x(1000+1500) draws, max R-hat is 1.094. The structural SDs fall after 1985 in all four equations. Caveats:
- Log-volatility is a stationary AR(1), not Primiceri's random walk.
- log_scores is the in-sample lppd with smoothed h.
- The out-of-sample score, .log_score(holdout), keeps the posterior fixed and does not filter h.
- The coefficients are constant, so irf(t_idx) changes across dates only through the impact scale.

(5) tvp_var_sv_fit (tvp.py:320) runs at 19 ms per sweep (n=4, p=2). Gaps:
- A is a weighted-OLS plug-in, not a posterior draw (tvp.py:423-424).
- The Q prior is IW(Q_prior_scale*I, k+2) (tvp.py:450), not scaled by V(B_OLS).
- P0 is 4I (tvp.py:387); the log-vol start is h0=0, p0=10 (tvp.py:437).
- One chain only: no R-hat, no thin argument, no seed argument, no log score, no IRF helper.
- beta_draws take 75 KB per draw.
- The Gibbs step order matches Del Negro-Primiceri Algorithm 2 (checked against the fetched sr619.pdf).

(6) tvp_var_fit (tvp.py:124) is fine.

(7) longrun.chunked (_job.py:321) only handles independent items fn(i, rng) with rng=default_rng([seed,i]). It cannot checkpoint Markov-chain state, and neither sampler has a resume or initial-state API. The claim that MCMC chains can resume on a tablet is false.
vets.oracle_check:
Volatility recovery is a strong oracle. On the planted DGP (n=3, T=250, SDs halved at T/2), both samplers recover pre/post structural SDs of about 0.92/0.53 against truths of 1.0/0.5.

Coefficient drift is a weak oracle. Over 6 seeds the true drift is -0.225. At the default Q_prior_scale=1e-4, tvp_var_sv_fit's posterior-median drift ranges from -0.066 to +0.025, and its 90% band covers the truth in 0/6 seeds. At 1e-3 coverage is 6/6 but the estimates are attenuated (-0.045 to -0.219). On a DGP with no drift, the spurious drift is at most 0.09. So the claim that each sampler recovers what it should fails at the defaults; the answer is driven by the prior.

The proposal misstates validation/cases_var.py:235. That case pins minnesota_posterior against a stacked-dummy closed form at lambda2=1 with n=2, p=1. minnesota_gibbs is not part of it, and the two disagree whenever lambda2 is not 1.

Published conclusions exist to quote qualitatively:
- Primiceri abstract, from the fetched tvsvar_final_july_04.pdf: both systematic and non-systematic policy changed, with a "negligible effect on the rest of the economy"; non-policy shocks matter more.
- Del Negro-Primiceri 2015 section 5, from the fetched sr619.pdf: corrected results are "qualitatively similar" and "smoother".
- Sims-Zha 2006 was not fetched.

vets.capabilities_check:
All the named symbols exist at the cited lines: minnesota_posterior bvar.py:40, minnesota_gibbs bvar.py:266, minnesota_optimal_lambda bvar.py:467, bvar_sv bvar_sv.py:987, tvp_var_fit tvp.py:124, tvp_var_sv_fit tvp.py:320, longrun.chunked _job.py:321. Four of them do not do what the proposal assumes.
(1) CONFIRMED BUG in _build_minnesota_dummies (bvar.py:241-253). Each (lag, variable) dummy row is written once per equation into the same Xd cell, and the last write wins. With lambda2 != 1, the conjugate prior therefore puts a prior mean of lambda2 on the own first lag of every variable except the last. Scratch run at lambda2=0.5 on a 3-variable panel: implied own-lag prior means are [0.5, 0.5, 1.0]. That run is n=3, p=2, 1954Q3-2001Q3, 4-quarter CPI inflation, unemployment and fed funds, built from the raw bundled CSVs; call it "the 3-variable panel" below. On that panel the minnesota_gibbs mean differs from the minnesota_posterior mean by 0.284 at lambda2=0.5 and by 0.002 at lambda2=1. lambda2=0.5 is the default of both functions, and the marginal likelihood behind minnesota_optimal_lambda uses the same dummies. The only validation case pins lambda2=1 (validation/cases_var.py:119,131), which hides the bug.
(2) tvp_var_sv_fit never draws A. It sets A to the weighted-OLS point estimate (tvp.py:423-424), whereas bvar_sv draws it (bvar_sv.py:1262). Bands on structural (recursive monetary-shock) impulse responses therefore understate uncertainty.
(3) The TVP-VAR prior is not Primiceri's. beta0 comes from OLS on the first 40 or fewer observations of the same sample (tvp.py:379), so there is no separate training sample. The Q prior is Q_prior_scale*I (tvp.py:389), not scaled by the OLS variances.
(4) longrun.chunked only handles independent items, each seeded with rng([seed, i]) (_job.py:321-335). Neither sampler accepts or returns chain state, so "MCMC chains resume on a tablet" is false. Only a whole chain, or its summaries, can be one item.
(5) There is no TVP impulse-response or predictive-density helper. The pieces a notebook helper needs are there: irf.py:7, and mcmc.py has gelman_rubin and effective_sample_size. bvar_sv.log_score(holdout) exists (bvar_sv.py:599).
Runtime (native, work env, 3-variable panel): tvp_var_sv_fit takes 9.5 ms per iteration (10k iterations is about 1.6 min); the 4-variable version takes 14.2 ms; bvar_sv takes 1.5 ms per sweep. Pyodide time was not measured.
vets.oracle_check:
Simulation truth is independent of puremacro and obtainable. But the claim that "each sampler recovers what it should" is FALSE for the coefficient-drift arm. Scratch runs used tvp_var_sv_fit with p=1, T=190 and 1500+1500 draws, on two seeds:
- Volatility break with fixed coefficients (true late/early sd ratio 0.40): recovered ratios are 0.34 to 0.67, with no spurious drift in the policy coefficient (change -0.004 to -0.036).
- Break of +0.60 in the policy coefficient with constant volatility: recovered +0.06 and +0.11 at the default Q_prior_scale=1e-4 (the 90% bands exclude the truth), and +0.24 at 1e-3.
- Linear drift of +0.30: recovered +0.03 and +0.05 at 1e-4, and +0.10 and +0.12 at 1e-3.
So under the default prior the model leans toward "bad luck". That is the real teaching result: a power/prior diagnostic, not a recovery check. Apparent volatility changes when the true volatility is constant matched the realized shock variances of the sample (checked), so they are not misattribution.
The "closed form" oracle (the minnesota_gibbs mean equals the NIW/minnesota_posterior mean) is internal to puremacro. It holds only at lambda2=1 because of the dummy bug. An NIW conjugate prior cannot carry lambda2 != 1 anyway.
Published anchors are qualitative only. I read them this session in the Primiceri (2005) accepted version (faculty.wcas.northwestern.edu/~gep575/tvsvar_final_july_04.pdf, via pypdf):
- sample 1953:I-2001:III, 2 lags, GDP-deflator inflation, unemployment and the 3-month T-bill;
- 10,000 iterations with the first 2,000 discarded; kQ=0.01, kS=0.1, kW=0.01;
- Fig. 1 shows volatilities with 16th/84th percentile bands; Figs. 2-3 show impulse responses at 1975:I, 1981:III and 1996:I;
- "the Q matrix contains 231 free parameters".
The Sims-Zha abstract (ideas.repec.org/p/pri/cepsud/110, fetched): "The best fit is with a version that allows time variation in structural disturbance variances only."
Del Negro-Primiceri 2015 (newyorkfed sr619, fetched): Algorithm 2 draws s^T right before Sigma^T. The step order in tvp_var_sv_fit is consistent with it.
There are no tables to match, and the bundled data differ (CPI and fed funds instead of the deflator and T-bill). An independent software fixture is possible through R bvarsv 1.1 (CRAN, GPL; its page does not mention the DNP correction), but R is not installed here. Octave is installed, but I found no public Primiceri code: his research page lists only the errata PDFs.

ideas.title: Cointegration on real data: balanced-growth great ratios with Engle-Granger, Johansen, DOLS/FM-OLS, VECM and threshold VECM
ideas.anchor_notebook: new, or a lab in notebooks/course/01b_kaldor_capital_es.py (Kaldor facts)
ideas.question: Do log output, investment and consumption share one stochastic trend with the (1, -1) vectors that balanced growth implies, and how much do the answer and the estimated vector depend on deterministic terms and estimator?
ideas.description: Test for cointegration with engle_granger, phillips_ouliaris and johansen. Estimate the vector by OLS, dols (Stock-Watson leads and lags) and fm_ols, and compare with the theory value of -1. Fit fit_vecm and read the adjustment speeds. Let tvecm_fit show an asymmetric correction of the great ratio. Teaching point verified in scratch: on bundled log real_gdp and real_investment, johansen trace statistics equal statsmodels coint_johansen(det_order=0) exactly (34.3771, 6.0527), yet r̂ = 2 under Case III. So the deterministic-term choice (Case III versus a trend) decides the verdict, and the notebook must teach it.
ideas.paper: King, Plosser, Stock & Watson (1991); Johansen (1991); Stock & Watson (1993); Phillips & Hansen (1990); Phillips & Ouliaris (1990); Hansen & Seo (2002)
ideas.oracle_detail: statsmodels coint_johansen and VECM outputs, frozen as goldens in the validation-gallery pattern. They matched to 4 decimals in a scratch run on bundled data. The johansen docstring (var/vecm.py:160-165) declares the Case III/det_order=0 equivalence and cites the MacKinnon-Haug-Michelis critical values. A closed-form theory vector (1, -1) serves as the economic benchmark. Planted-beta recovery is already in validation/cases_cointegration.py (DOLS and FM-OLS). KPSW's published estimates may be used only after fetching the paper.
ideas.data_detail: load_macro_quarterly has real_gdp and real_investment for 1954Q3-2026Q1. Real consumption (FRED PCECC96) must be fetched with puremacro.fetch.fred or frozen as a CSV.
ideas.library_gaps: johansen supports only Case III (unrestricted constant), so there is no restricted-trend case, and that is exactly the case this application needs. fit_vecm and johansen return dicts, not result objects.
ideas.plan_overlap: None. Zero notebooks use any cointegration function; examples cointegration_johansen.py and fm_ols_dols_demo.py use only simulated data.

vets.required_changes:
1. Add a Case IV (restricted linear trend) option to johansen and fit_vecm. Validate trace statistics against statsmodels VECM(deterministic='coli') log-likelihood differences, NOT coint_johansen(det_order=1). Take Case IV 5% critical values from a fetched MacKinnon-Haug-Michelis (1999) source, or simulate and freeze them with a seed. Freeze goldens for the Case III and Case IV trace statistics on the bundled data.
2. Fix phillips_ouliaris normalisation at cointegration_modern.py:361-365 and add a golden against arch phillips_ouliaris (Za/Zt within tolerance).
3. Replace engle_granger's heuristic adf_p (vecm.py:118) with MacKinnon critical values or p-values. Align the residual-ADF specification with statsmodels coint or arch engle_granger and freeze a golden.
4. Fix fit_vecm so it returns rank-r residuals (vecm.py:318-320), a beta normalised on the first variable, Gamma, and alpha SEs. Only with those in place can weak exogeneity be taught (golden: statsmodels VECM 'co' alpha/beta/stderr_alpha). Otherwise drop weak exogeneity.
5. Drop tvecm_fit from the notebook, or keep it as an explicitly exploratory aside, until it has a Hansen-Seo threshold test and the delay convention (tvecm.py:113-114) is fixed or documented. Never claim "asymmetric correction" from point estimates.
6. Fix the example claims first: examples/cointegration_johansen.py:4-6,42 (the true rank is 2) and examples/tvecm_demo.py:7 (the planted asymmetry is not recoverable with trim=0.15 and a conditional-ECM DGP).
7. Data: freeze PCECC96 plus nominal GDP, PCEC and GPDI into puremacro/datasets/data with manifest entries and a loader. Say that real chained great ratios drift because of relative prices (link to 01b), and frame (1,-1) as a hypothesis the data partly reject: nominal i-y holds, c-y fails. Do not promise r=2.
8. Use the correct symbol puremacro.fetch.fetch_fred.
9. Trim scope. Keep EG, PO, Johansen III vs IV, OLS vs DOLS vs FM-OLS with a small (at most 500-rep) bias Monte Carlo, and a VECM. Drop money demand. Build a bilingual 69 plus _es twin, with a pointer from 01b.

ideas.title: Letting the data pick the rotation: identification through heteroskedasticity and non-Gaussianity, and what it estimates under nonlinearity
ideas.question: When can second moments across regimes, or non-Gaussian shocks, identify a structural VAR without economic zero restrictions, and how much of a sign-restricted answer comes from the Haar prior rather than the data?
ideas.description: Simulate SVARs with a known B0. Vary (i) the variance ratio across two regimes, including the proportional case where Rigobon fails; (ii) shock kurtosis, including Gaussian, where independent-component identification fails; and (iii) smooth variance change for magmav_svar. Measure recovery of B0 up to column sign and permutation, and the power of gaussian_lr_test. Then take a two-variable sign-restricted system and compare the Haar-prior posterior (sign_restrictions, as in 06) with gk_robust_bands. Its identified set has analytic endpoints in the bivariate case. Close with bundled data: pre/post-1984 as the Rigobon regime, and news_maxshare or maxshare versus the proxy route already in 17.
ideas.paper: Rigobon (2003); Lanne, Meitz & Saikkonen (2017); Magnusson & Mavroeidis (2014); Giacomini & Kitagawa (2021); Uhlig (2004) max share
ideas.oracle_detail: The planted B0 and true IRFs are the oracle; recovery is scored after sign and permutation alignment. For the bivariate sign case, the analytic identified-set bounds are compared with gk_robust_bands at n_var_draws=1 (a point-identified VAR). The validation gallery already has a Rigobon case (validation/cases_var.py, hetero/rigobon_svar references).
ideas.data_detail: The Monte Carlo is synthetic. The empirical close uses bundled load_macro_quarterly and load_macro_monthly, with regime dates as a user-defined indicator.
ideas.library_gaps: Result-field names are inconsistent: HeteroResult.B, NonGaussianSVARResult.B0, MagMavSVARResult.B. non_gaussian_svar returns no bootstrap bands. hetero needs an exogenous binary regime indicator.
ideas.plan_overlap: Not in PLAN.md. It extends notebook 17, which uses cholesky, proxy, sign_restrictions, narrative_sign_svar and identify_maxshare; none of the statistical-identification estimators appears in any notebook.

Errors are max-abs after column-normalising, then aligning sign and permutation.
- Rigobon: error 0.061 with regime variances (4,1). It rises to 0.307 in the proportional (3,3) case and 0.310 in the near-equal (1.2,1) case, so the planned failure modes show up.
- FastICA (non_gaussian_svar): error 0.053 for t(5) shocks and 0.045 for Laplace, versus 0.385 for Gaussian.
- magmav_svar (40 reps): error 0.064 with one break, 0.073 with a smooth logistic change and 0.055 with smooth sine changes (picks 3-4 breaks). The proportional case gives 0.380. Homoskedastic data selects k=0 and falls back to Cholesky with a warning.

Caveats found:
(1) The names overstate the methods. magmav_svar is sup-Wald+BIC break detection (at most 4 breaks) plus a Frobenius minimum-distance fit. It is not Magnusson-Mavroeidis 2014: the Econometrica abstract (fetched via web search) describes GMM with stability restrictions, applied to the NKPC. non_gaussian_svar is logcosh FastICA, not LMS pseudo-ML. gaussian_lr_test is a Jarque-Bera kurtosis sum, not an LR.
(2) magmav's convergence flag depends on the data scale (BFGS gtol=1e-6 absolute, magmav.py:206). At Y x100, eu=(0,0) is a false failure even though B is correct. At Y x0.01, eu=(1,1) on 30/30 reps but the median error is 0.142, against 0.048 at scale 1. On raw bundled monthly data it also returns eu=(0,0). The pipeline works around this by standardising (tools/run_uncertainty_ident_spec_curve.py:729-737).
(3) gaussian_lr_test evaluated at the ICA estimate is oversized: under a Gaussian DGP at T=200 it rejects 11.7% at the 5% level (300 reps), against 6.3% at the true B0. It is about nominal at T=500. For n>=3, rejecting 'all Gaussian' does not mean the model is identified (that needs at most one Gaussian shock).
(4) news_maxshare is just maxshare with horizon 40 (maxshare.py:98-100). It has no Barsky-Sims zero-impact TFP restriction.
(5) sign_restriction_svar (sign.py:39) fixes the OLS reduced form, so its bands are the Haar-induced distribution over the set, not a posterior.

Five problems with the capabilities as proposed:
(1) The estimators normalize column scale differently: Rigobon sets regime-0 variance to 1 (hetero.py:174-189), ICA sets unit variance (non_gaussian.py:192-196), and magmav sets the geometric-mean regime variance to 1 (magmav.py:217-223). (2) magmav_svar does not implement Magnusson-Mavroeidis (2014). The Econometrica abstract, fetched this session, describes GMM inference that exploits moment instability, applied to the NKPC. The code is a multi-break Rigobon: piecewise-constant regimes, sup-Wald/BIC break search and a Frobenius loss. It is not built for smooth variance change, although in my runs it still recovered B under logistic and linear drifts (min |cos| 0.999 and 0.994) because any split identifies B when B is constant. With k=0 it silently returns Cholesky (magmav.py:305-314): under homoskedasticity it chose k=0 in 29 of 30 reps (min |cos| 0.894).

Rigobon (n=3, T=400, planted B0 with D0=I, 40 reps): median relative error 0.164 with variance ratios (0.5, 2, 4). It rises to 0.533 with near-equal ratios and 0.540 with proportional ratios. With ratios (2, 2, 4), only the distinct column is recovered: median |cos| 0.988 against 0.926 and 0.932 for the other two.

ICA (non_gaussian_svar): median relative error 0.636 with Gaussian shocks, 0.253 with t10, 0.149 with t6 and 0.091 with Laplace. With two Gaussian shocks and one Laplace, only the Laplace column is recovered (|cos| 0.994 against 0.94).

The main refutation is the test itself. Under Gaussian shocks, at nominal 5%, 300 reps: the p-value that non_gaussian_svar reports rejects 0.093 and 0.097 of the time at n=2 (T=200 and 800), and 0.223 and 0.287 at n=3. The same statistic rejects 0.037-0.070 with the true B0 and 0.030-0.057 with the Cholesky factor. The chi2(n) calibration ignores that ICA picks the most non-Gaussian rotation. So "power of gaussian_lr_test" is not meaningful until size is fixed. The statistic is also a Jarque-Bera kurtosis test, not an LR test. And its null (all shocks Gaussian) is not the identification condition (at most one Gaussian) once n is 3 or more.

Bivariate sign-restriction oracle: the analytic set is real. The admissible impact vectors form an arc of angles, and each response is |c|cos(theta - phi), so its extremes sit at the arc ends or at an interior stationary point. I coded it. gk_robust_bands_from_gibbs, given the population (A, Sigma) as a single draw, converges to it from inside at O(1/N): maximum error 3.7e-2 at N=200, 5.9e-3 at N=2000 and 1.2e-3 at N=20000. gk_robust_bands with n_var_draws=1 is within 1.8e-3 of the analytic set at the OLS estimate. The quantiles from sign_restrictions match the analytic Haar-implied quantiles: at h=0, analytic 5%/50%/95% = -0.816/-0.509/-0.054 against Monte Carlo -0.815/-0.501/-0.050.

Baumeister-Hamilton (2015, Econometrica 83(5)) is the right reference for "inside the set, the posterior equals the prior" (confirmed by web search). The existing validation case, var.rigobon_hetero_positive_variances (validation/cases_var.py:67-74), only checks that the variance ratios are positive. It is not a recovery oracle.

ideas.title: What sign restrictions assume: Uhlig (2005), ADRR (2018) narrative restrictions and Giacomini-Kitagawa robust bands on the real monetary VAR
ideas.question: Does output fall after a contractionary monetary shock once the Volcker narrative restrictions are imposed on Uhlig's six-variable VAR?
ideas.description: Rebuild Uhlig's monthly data for 1965-2003 from FRED: IP, CPI or an interpolated deflator, commodity prices (PPIACO), FFR, nonborrowed reserves and total reserves. Impose his sign restrictions for months 0-5, then ADRR's October 1979 sign and 'overwhelming contribution' restrictions, and show Giacomini-Kitagawa robust bands. The current tests/test_replication_adrr2018.py pins synthetic output and says the Uhlig data 'cannot be fetched offline', but every series is on FRED and can be frozen.
ideas.paper: Uhlig (2005 JME); Antolín-Díaz & Rubio-Ramírez (2018 AER)
ideas.oracle_detail: Uhlig (2005) Figures 5-7 and ADRR (2018) Figures 2-3 report IRFs graphically: to transcribe from the papers. Second oracle: ADRR's MATLAB replication package (AER) run once, with median and 68% bands frozen as numbers.
ideas.data_detail: FRED INDPRO, CPIAUCSL, PPIACO, FEDFUNDS, BOGNONBR, TOTRESNS (Fed/BLS, public domain). Freeze a 1965-2003 slice into package data.

Smoke run (scratch smoke1-3.py) on the ADRR spec with FRED stand-ins: monthly 1965:01-2007:11, p=12, h=0..5 signs [IP 0, CPI -, PPIACO -, TRARR -, BOGNONBR -, FFR +], Oct-1979 shock_sign plus hd_dominance(overwhelming, FFR). It reproduces the headline. Without narrative restrictions, the IP response at h=12 has median +0.14 and a 68% band of [-0.24,+0.48] (25bp normalization). With them, the median is -0.19 and the band [-0.31,-0.06]; the band stays below zero through h=60 in OLS mode. Four problems remain. (1) Draws are too slow and too few survive: 20k rotations give 532 sign-accepted and 20 narrative-accepted draws (ESS 19), in 13.5 s (OLS) or 57 s (bayes_draws). The loop redraws one rotation at a time and recomputes the full H=60 IRF for each (narrative_sign.py:844-871). (2) The bayes_draws stability filter (|eig|<0.999, narrative_sign.py:479-490, redraw loop at 846-856) rejects 299/400 NIW draws on this levels VAR, whose OLS max root is 0.9994. It does so silently, since n_unstable only counts total failures, so the posterior is truncated. (3) gk_robust_bands builds the identified set from the min/max over accepted Haar draws, which is an inner approximation. At the OLS estimate the default n_q_per_draw=500 accepted 8 rotations and gave an IP h=0 set of [-0.112,+0.412]. SLSQP on the unit sphere found feasible rotations spanning [-0.397,+0.562]; at h=12, MC with 5000 draws gave [-0.499,+0.678] against [-0.708,+0.782]. The 'robust' bands are therefore too narrow, the opposite of what they are for. (4) estimate_var always includes a constant (puremacro/var/estimate.py:8-9), while ADRR use none.
vets.oracle_check: The oracle is better than the proposal says, because ADRR report numbers in the text, not only in figures. From the Sept-2016 ADRR working paper (ECB-hosted PDF, fetched, pages 27-32 read with pypdf and page 28 rendered): fn 8 gives monthly data, 12 lags, no constant or trend, uninformative priors, and a sample of Jan 1965-Nov 2007. Table 3 restricts GDP deflator, commodity prices, TR and NBR negative and FFR positive for horizons 0-5, with output unrestricted. Under the baseline, the probability of an expansionary Oct-1979 shock is about 11% (p.28). Under Restrictions 4+5 the shock is 2-5 s.d. and explains 100-150 bp of the roughly 225 bp unexpected FFR rise (p.31); under Alternative Restriction 5 it explains 50-115 bp (p.32). The Dec-2016 Fedea version gives the same sample, lags and numbers according to a WebFetch summary; that summary garbled Table 3, which the rendered page corrects. Analogues computed on FRED stand-ins: P(eps<0)=0.163; narrative shock 2.70-3.18 s.d.; monetary contribution 1.04-1.20 pp of a 1.99 pp FFR forecast error. These fit the published ranges, so tolerance assertions are feasible. The proposal's 'ADRR Figures 2-3' does not match the WP, where the monetary figures are Figs 7-9; the AER numbering is unverified. A second oracle, openICPSR 113168 (ADRR code), returned 403 without login: the user must download it manually, and MATLAB_R2026a.app is installed. bsvarSIGNs (R, GPL-3) is an independent implementation and ships ADRR's 'monetary' data (1965:01-2007:08 per its manual), but R is not installed here.

ideas.title: LP or VAR? Bias-variance-coverage by horizon against a DSGE-generated truth
ideas.question: When the true impulse response comes from a known New Keynesian model, how do local projections and VARs trade bias against variance across horizons and sample sizes?
ideas.description: DGP: a three-equation NK model via dsge.build, with interest-rate smoothing (rho_i=0.8) and AR(1) demand, cost-push and monetary shocks (rho 0.9/0.5/0.5, sd 0.5/0.3/0.25). Each exogenous process is written as a control plus a lagged state so its innovation hits at h=0. In build's timing, xp.v - rho*x.v - e is a one-period news shock; the first prototype showed the nominal rate falling on impact. The econometrician sees the output gap x, the rate i and the monetary innovation, which is recoverable exactly as v - rho_v*v_lag. Inflation is omitted, so the VAR is VAR(infinity). Estimators, horizons 0-16: lp_hac(n_lags=4, shock as regressor, no contemporaneous controls), la_lp, smooth_lp, and VAR(p), p in {2,4,8}, with the shock ordered first (internal instrument) using fit_var + irf. Optional: bootstrap_bands for VAR coverage. Monte Carlo: R=200, T in {100,200,400}. Prototype at T=200 (true response at h=8: -0.137 per unit shock): LP bias 0.068, sd 0.86; VAR(4) -0.016, 0.40; VAR(2) -0.043, 0.23. LP HAC 90% coverage was 0.84-0.87. Runtime per replication: lp_hac 28-110 ms native (36 ms Pyodide) for 17 horizons, la_lp about 106 ms native, smooth_lp 2.4 ms, VARs under 1 ms. That is about 40 s native for R=200 and an estimated 45-80 s in Pyodide; gate R with runtime.fit(n_sim=...) and run in longrun.chunked. Figure: (a) squared bias and variance by horizon for each estimator; (b) RMSE ratio LP/VAR(4) by horizon for three T; (c) coverage by horizon. Exercise: change T or p; assert that the MC variance of VAR(p) is below LP's at h>=8. A pitfall cell shows that passing contemporaneous observables as LP controls made X'X singular ('rank 18 of 20') with as many shocks as observables.
ideas.paper: Plagborg-Moller and Wolf (2021, Econometrica); Li, Plagborg-Moller and Wolf (2024, J. Econometrics); Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Moller (2021); Barnichon and Brownlees (2019)
ideas.oracle_detail: True IRF from LinearModel.irf of the data-generating model (exact, Klein QZ); the poor-man's invertibility matrix G-N L^-1 F had max |eig| 1.4e-8, so the observed-shock design is valid. MC s.e. reported for every bias/coverage number.
ideas.data_detail: Simulated from a build() NK model; no files.
ideas.library_gaps: (1) lp_hac always adds the controls contemporaneously (puremacro/lp/jorda.py:90-91) and has no lag-only option; users must pre-shift controls. (2) lp_hac and la_lp spend about 6 ms per horizon on pandas shifting; that dominates the Monte Carlo cost. (3) LinearModel has no accessor for the realised innovations of simulate(); the lab backs them out from the AR identity.
ideas.plan_overlap: Not in PLAN.md. 07 teaches LP on one synthetic sample and 06 the SVAR; no notebook compares them against a structural truth. dsge.build has 0 showcase call sites (PLAN.md lists 'build with a callable' as uncovered).

A stronger, noise-free bias oracle is easy to build, and I built it. I took the exact autocovariances of (m, x, i) from the model's MA coefficients (irf out to K=600) and solved Yule-Walker for the VAR(p) pseudo-true IRF. ideas.title: What does an SVAR recover from a known DSGE? Invertibility, news and foresight shocks, and external instruments
ideas.question: When structural shocks cannot be recovered from current and past observables, what does a VAR identify, and how much does adding forward-looking variables help?
ideas.description: DGP A (news, closed form): build() model with TFP growth da_t = s_t + n_{t-4} (four-state news pipeline) and an asset price p_t = beta*E_t(p_{t+1}+da_{t+1}), beta in {0.9, 0.99}. DGP B (invertible benchmark): the lab-72 NK model with observables (x, pi, i). Population part: poor-man's invertibility check on G - N L^{-1} F from LinearModel.solution. The degree of invertibility is R^2 of each shock projected on current and past observables, computed by long-simulation projection or a steady-state Kalman Riccati. Computed here: max |eig| 1.1111 at beta=0.9 and 1.0101 at 0.99 (=1/beta); the news shock's R^2 on current plus 40 lags of (da,p) was 0.671 and 0.947; the NK benchmark's eigenvalue was 1.4e-8. Monte Carlo: R=200, T=200. VAR(4) on (da,p): (i) news_maxshare(target=da); (ii) Barsky-Sims max-share restricted to columns orthogonal to the first Cholesky column, done inline; (iii) Cholesky. Information sets: da alone, (da,p), and (da,p,c) with a PIH consumption variable. Runtime: population under 1 s; Monte Carlo under 10 s natively. Figure: true vs recovered news IRFs (median and 90% MC range) for each beta and identification; R^2 bars by information set; eigenvalue plot against the unit circle. Exercise: change the news lead or beta. Assert max|eig| = 1/beta to 1e-8 and that R^2 rises with beta.
ideas.paper: Fernandez-Villaverde, Rubio-Ramirez, Sargent and Watson (2007); Leeper, Walker and Yang (2013); Barsky and Sims (2011); Forni and Gambetti (2014); Plagborg-Moller and Wolf (2022)
ideas.oracle_detail: For DGP A the MA determinant's zeros satisfy 1+w+w^2+w^3=0 with w=z/beta, so max |eig| of the inverted system is exactly 1/beta. That is verified numerically to 4 decimals. The true news IRF comes from LinearModel.irf; the R^2 comes from a 20,000-period simulation (simulation truth).
ideas.data_detail: Simulated from build() models.
ideas.library_gaps: (1) puremacro.dsge has no invertibility diagnostic, either a poor-man's ABCD eigenvalue check or a Kalman R^2 degree of invertibility; the lab writes about 10 lines of numpy. (2) news_maxshare (maxshare.py:98-100) is plain max-share at a long horizon. Its docstring cites Barsky-Sims (2011) but it does not impose their zero-impact restriction on TFP, and identify_maxshare has no such option. The lab should show the difference and file it.
ideas.plan_overlap: 45 computes news_irf and DSGE-VAR on synthetic data but never asks what an SVAR recovers. 17 compares identifications on real data without a truth. Not in PLAN.md.

vets.required_changes:
1. Oracles. Replace the simulated R^2 'truth' with the Kalman Riccati value (stacked [x;u] state, Lyapunov P0; ridge only when obs > shocks). Correct 0.947 to 0.9696 at beta=0.99. Add the exact checks: R^2(n | p alone) = beta^6 to 1e-8, R^2(n | da alone) = 0, and the population VAR(inf) Cholesky-2nd da(h=4) = sqrt(R^2).

2. Separate truncation from non-invertibility. Add a population VAR(p) section (Yule-Walker from the exact MA(4) autocovariances or first_order_moments) plotting da(h=4) against p in {1,...,200}, with sqrt(R^2) as the asymptote. Present the T=200 VAR(4) MC as the finite-sample layer on top, and say plainly that truncation dominates at beta=0.99. DGP B cannot separate these effects.

3. Max-share. Target the TFP level (a VAR in levels on a = cumsum(da), as Barsky-Sims do), not growth. Present plain news_maxshare identifying the permanent-TFP mix as the reason the zero-impact restriction is needed.

4. Zero-impact vs Cholesky. Run the zero-impact max-share only in a VAR with 3 or more variables (e.g. (a,p,z)), or drop it and say it equals Cholesky in the bivariate case.

5. Information sets. Replace PIH c with a noisy news signal z = n + sv*v. R^2 is 0.807 at beta=0.9 with sv=1, and z doubles as the external instrument. Or keep c only in the population R^2 bars as the 'no gain, same discount factor' result, never in a VAR.

6. DGP B. Write the 3-equation NK inline with build() and lagged shock states (poor-man |eig| about 1e-16, R^2=1). Lab 72 does not exist.

7. Stock-Watson test direction. Test whether lagged z Granger-causes y with granger_causality(df, source="z", target=y), citing SW 2018 Sec. 4 and 5. Optionally add the Hausman LP-IV vs SVAR-IV contrast.

8. LP-IV normalisation. Normalise on p (x="p"), since the news shock has zero impact on da. Call proxy_svar with n_boot=1 in the MC, and file the n_boot=0 bug.

9. Symbols. Add proxy_svar (var/identify/proxy.py:74), lp_iv (lp/iv.py:367), granger_causality (var/diagnostics.py:34) and var.irf.irf (var/irf.py:7). Drop news_irf, or use it only as a cross-check.

10. Library gaps. File: news_maxshare zero-impact option and docstring, proxy_svar point-only path, an invertibility helper, and a population VAR(p) helper.

11. Scope. Keep the external-instrument part to one section comparing SVAR-IV, LP-IV and internal-instrument IRFs against the truth, so the notebook stays medium-sized.

vets.oracle_check:
The closed form holds: det = beta^4(1+w+w^2+w^3), w=z/beta, and max|eig| = 1/beta exactly (verified).

The R^2 'simulation truth' is not an oracle and one quoted number is wrong. The 0.947 at beta=0.99 is a 40-lag truncation artifact: a 40-lag projection on 20k periods gives 0.9488, 120 lags 0.9666, 300 lags 0.9691. The Riccati value is 0.96956 (converged: T=400 vs 3000 agree to 1e-5). The 0.671 at beta=0.9 matches Kalman 0.6724.

Stronger exact oracles, all verified here:
- R^2 of n on p alone = beta^(2(k-1)) = beta^6: Kalman matches to 1e-11 at beta = 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99 (a Blaschke factor).
- R^2 of n on da alone = 0.
- The population VAR(inf) Cholesky-2nd response of da at h=4 = sqrt(R^2). Yule-Walker VAR(200) gives 0.820 (sqrt 0.6724) and 0.984 (sqrt 0.9696).

VAR(4) is badly truncated even in population: da(h=4) = 0.385 at beta=0.9 and 0.436 at beta=0.99. The MC (T=200, p=4) therefore mostly measures truncation bias. It gets 0.377 and 0.446, inverting the intended 'higher beta, better recovery' message.

The Stock-Watson test in the merge note points the wrong way. SW 2018 (NBER w24216, fetched this session, Sec. 4 remark) say existing tests check 'the implication of invertibility that Zt does not Granger-cause Yt'. Sec. 5 Table 2 uses 'four lags of Z in each of the VAR equation'. Simulated: z->p is rejected in 20/20 draws and p->z in 0/20. So 'Granger causality of z by lagged y' has no power.

vets.oracle_check: The closed form is real and independent of puremacro, and I verified it. The observables are da_t = s_t + n_{t-4} and p_t = b^4 n_t + b^3 n_{t-1} + b^2 n_{t-2} + b n_{t-3}. The determinant is b^4(1+w)(1+w^2) with w = z/b, so all three roots have |z| = b < 1. From build(), L = diag(1, b^4). max|eig(G - N L^-1 F)| came out as 1.1111111111 at b=0.9 and 1.0101010101 at b=0.99 (|diff| = 0.0e0), with all three nonzero eigenvalues equal to 1/b. I read the condition itself in this session in Fernandez-Villaverde et al., NBER TWP t0308, sec. II: "D is invertible and the eigenvalues of (A - BD^-1 C) are strictly less than one in modulus". Its Example 1 is a permanent-income model. There is a second exact oracle the proposal misses: R^2(n | past p only) = b^6, i.e. 0.5314 and 0.9415, which the Kalman filter reproduces. The stated R^2 figures need care. The steady-state Kalman filter with sigma_s = sigma_n = 1 gives R^2(n | da, p) = 0.6724 at b=0.9 and 0.9696 at b=0.99. It is reproducible with puremacro kalman_filter, reading P_filt[-1] under a stationary or diffuse P0. The proposal's 0.947 at b=0.99 is off, probably because 40 lags truncate a near-unit MA root, and it never states sigma_s. One pitfall to flag in the lab: a P0 that treats the lagged n's as known returns R^2 = 1. No published table is claimed, and none is needed. The external-instrument claims are supported. I read in this session (NBER w24216, remark 4) that Stock-Watson's invertibility test is that "Z_t does not Granger-cause Y_t", so the proposal has the direction reversed. Their main test compares LP-IV with SVAR-IV (Hausman-type).

All six listed symbols exist and return correct results, and I ran all three examples' run_* functions this session. fevd is at puremacro/var/irf.py:22 and historical_decomp at :111. ideas.title: Aguiar-Gopinath (2007) for Mexico: data-moment card, then the trend-shock SOE with SGU closures
ideas.question: Does a trend-shock SOE model estimated on bundled Mexican data reproduce the paper's Mexico estimates and moments?
ideas.description: This is PLAN's replication with a course anchor and a data audit. The bundled Mexican quarterly accounts start in 1993Q1 (component file, not seasonally adjusted) or 1994Q1 (apertura, adjusted), so the paper's sample cannot be matched without INEGI historical series. Use the x11-adjusted components from the T02_B exercise for investment and net exports, and SGU (2003) closures from lesson 10b.
ideas.oracle_detail: The paper's Mexico estimates and moment tables, read from the paper in the implementing session (none are quoted here). The debt-closure eigenvalue check from lesson 10b is a second oracle.
ideas.data_detail: The bundle covers only 1993/1994 onward; the pre-1993 Mexican quarterly accounts would come from INEGI (fetch_inegi_panel, network).
ideas.library_gaps: No SOE, trend-shock or GMM/SMM estimation wrapper for this model in the library.
ideas.plan_overlap: Same as PLAN.md:102.

All three listed symbols exist and work. klein_solve is at puremacro/dsge/klein.py:285; its default div=1+1e-8 admits a unit root. x11_arima is at puremacro/sa/x11.py:309 (period=4, returns .sa). hp_filter is at puremacro/cycles.py:451 (returns a CycleResult) and puremacro/data.py:66 (returns a tuple). Toy smoke calls passed (scratch wf/ag07-feas/smoke.py). The proposal omits the piece that matters most: Model.theoretical_moments(hp_filter=1600) (puremacro/dsge/build.py:674, which calls spectral_moments at puremacro/dsge/_moments.py:94). It accepts a unit-root state when the HP filter is on, so HP moments of I(1) log levels come out analytically.

I wrote the JPE-version Aguiar-Gopinath model (Cobb-Douglas, SGU debt-elastic premium, with lgam = lgam(-1) + g - mug to carry log levels) as a roughly 20-line .mod and loaded it with load_mod. It solved with eu=(1,1), and the top |eig| values were 1.0 (trend) and 0.983 (debt). At the paper's Table 4 col 1 Mexico estimates (sigma_g=2.81, sigma_z=0.48) it gives:
- sigma(y)=2.399 (paper Table 5, spec 1: 2.40)
- sigma(c)/sigma(y)=1.265 (1.26)
- sigma(I)/sigma(y)=2.59 (2.60)
- sigma(NX)/sigma(y)=0.707 (0.71)
- rho(y)=0.78 (0.78)
- rho(y,NX)=-0.661 (-0.66)
- rho(y,c)=0.945 (0.94)
- rho(y,I)=0.924 (0.92)

Solving for the two shock sizes that exactly match sigma(y)=2.40 and sigma(c)/sigma(y)=1.26 gives sigma_g=2.798 and sigma_z=0.496 (paper: 2.81 and 0.48). A 20,000-period simulation followed by HP filtering agrees (2.36 / 1.26). One moment evaluation takes 0.014 s, so GMM is cheap. The one assumption: I set mug=log(1.0066); I did not read the value the paper uses for specs 1-3.

Two library quirks need workarounds:
- theoretical_moments' default fevd_horizons includes None, which raises ValueError on a unit-root model. Passing fevd_horizons=(1,) avoids it.
- Unfiltered moments (sigma(dy), rho(dy), E(dy)) are refused whenever G has a unit root, even for stationary growth variables (build.py, the else branch after line 757). They need a stationary companion model or a Lyapunov solve on the growth block.

Estimation: estimate_method_of_moments (puremacro/vfi/estimate.py:36) only returns a Nelder-Mead point estimate. There is no two-step optimal weighting, no Newey-West S matrix, no standard errors, no delta method and no J-test. newey_west_se (puremacro/inference/hac.py:10) works only for regressions.

ideas.title: Rebuild 14: score BP/RR/MR tax multipliers against the published tables, with honest proxy-SVAR bands (wild vs moving-block, weak-IV robust)
ideas.question: Do the three identification strategies reproduce their authors' headline multipliers on this data, rather than a 'ballpark'?

Keep the existing ReplicationCase regression.romer_romer_tax_multiplier_ols (target -3.0) in sync.

1. Replace the oracle. Score against MR 2014's common-dataset results:
   - BP (2.08): 0.48 / 1.35 after 2 years.

vets.capabilities_check:
The listed symbols exist. proxy_svar is at puremacro/var/identify/proxy.py:74; its impact is _proxy_impact_factory at proxy.py:23, and the wild bootstrap re-signs the proxy with the same Rademacher weight. olea_pflueger_f is at inference/weak_iv.py:272, cholesky_svar at var/identify/cholesky.py:181 and lp_hac at lp/jorda.py:18. Notebook 14 does not use cholesky_svar or lp_hac. It uses la_lp (lp/la_lp.py:99), and the real pieces for this proposal are la_lp_iv (la_lp.py:303), wild_bootstrap_var (inference/wild_bootstrap.py:77), moving_block_bootstrap (inference/moving_block.py:125, whose pass_index lets the proxy be resampled jointly with the residuals), anderson_rubin_test and msw_bands (weak_iv.py:350 and :418).

Smoke runs, all under 30 s, all in scratch wf/rev-tax14:
- On Mertens-Ravn's own JME 2014 replication data, a VAR(4) with constant, linear and quadratic trends and a 1975Q2 dummy reproduces the paper exactly. BP (theta=2.08): impact 0.48, peak 1.35 at h=7. Romer specification with 12 lags: impact 0.78, peak 2.96 at h=10. Proxy (puremacro's impact formula): impact 1.99, peak 3.19 at h=4. MR's theta decomposition gives thetaY = 3.133.
- The Olea-Pflueger effective F on MR's own data is 1.76, so the first stage is weak there too. la_lp_iv(anderson_rubin=True) returns unbounded or all-real AR sets at every h from 0 to 8 (MOP F about 2.3).
- A 150-replication Monte Carlo with a sparse (12% nonzero) proxy gives 90% bands at h=0 that cover 23-27% of the time with the wild bootstrap and 89-93% with an uncentered joint moving-block bootstrap. Jentsch-Lunsford's mechanism is that the Rademacher weights leave u_t*m_t unchanged in every draw.

Gaps:
1. No VAR routine takes deterministic terms (trends, dummies): not estimate_var (var/estimate.py:8), _ols_var (inference/bootstrap.py:11), wild_bootstrap_var, proxy_svar or moving_block_bootstrap (intercept only). Without them the proxy on MR's data gives 1.76 impact and a 3.81 peak at h=10 (constant only), or 2.42 impact (series detrended beforehand), instead of the published 2.00/3.19.
2. The proxy_svar bands are for a one-standard-deviation shock. Unit-normalised multiplier bands need a custom impact_fn; the w= hook makes that possible.
3. msw_bands is a single-equation Anderson-Rubin grid inversion, not Montiel Olea-Stock-Watson's delta-method set for SVAR-IV.
4. The moving-block bootstrap lacks Jentsch-Lunsford centering and a block-length rule.

ideas.title: From the Lucas tree to the equity premium: exact Mehra-Prescott and Burnside prices, perturbation accuracy, and Jermann (1998) habits with adjustment costs
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); follows 68, which names Epstein-Zin asset pricing as 'the natural next application'
ideas.question: How large an equity premium and how low a risk-free rate can a consumption-based model deliver, and how accurate are perturbation prices?
ideas.description: Price a Lucas (1978) tree three ways: (i) the Mehra-Prescott (1985) two-state Markov chain, whose price-dividend ratios and returns solve an exact linear system; (ii) Burnside's (1998) Gaussian AR(1) dividend-growth model, which has an exact series solution; (iii) load_mod at orders 1-3, repeating the Collard-Juillard (2001) accuracy exercise. Then cover the equity premium and risk-free-rate puzzles, a Hansen-Jagannathan bound from market data, Epstein-Zin prices (Tallarini 2000), where order 3 matters, and the Lucas (1987) welfare cost of business cycles.
ideas.paper: Lucas (1978); Mehra and Prescott (1985); Burnside (1998) JEDC; Collard and Juillard (2001) JEDC; Tallarini (2000) JME; LS4 'Asset pricing theory/empirics'; QuantEcon 'Asset Pricing: Finite State Models'
ideas.oracle_detail: Scratch probe (burnside_test.py; theta=-1.5, rho=-0.14, xbar=0.018, sigma=0.035, beta=0.95, an arbitrary calibration). The Burnside series v(xbar)=12.45783 matched an independent Gauss-Hermite grid fixed point to 1e-8 relative. The load_mod steady state plus 0.5*ghs2 gave relative errors of -1.44% at order 1 and -1.9e-4 at orders 2 and 3. The Mehra-Prescott finite-state solution is exact. Published MP (1985) and Collard-Juillard (2001) tables must be fetched and read before any number is cited. Dynare 8 is a second route.
ideas.data_detail: Model part is synthetic. The HJ bound needs market excess returns and the risk-free rate: Ken French F-F research factors (public), Shiller's long-run data, or FRED.
ideas.library_gaps: The Ken French fetcher downloads only the 30 industry portfolios (puremacro/fetch/kenfrench_industry.py:16), not Mkt-RF/RF. There are no asset-pricing helpers (returns and P/D from a solved model). Epstein-Zin in perturbation needs the value recursion written by hand in the .mod.
ideas.plan_overlap: PLAN's 'Order 3 you can trust ... then Tallarini (2000) or Basu-Bundick (2017)': notebook 68 shipped without Tallarini. Course 22_riesgo_orden3_es.py §5 covers Barro-Rietz and Andreasen, but from a frozen CSV (riesgo_desastres_momentos.csv) computed outside puremacro.

vets.required_changes: 1) Trim the scope to MP exact, Burnside exact vs load_mod orders 1-3, the admissible (rf, premium) region with the Weil risk-free-rate puzzle, and an HJ bound from the MP Table 1 moments. Drop Tallarini/EZ (the merge note already assigns it to repl-struct-16) and either drop Jermann or make it a second notebook. Keep Lucas-1987 as a short closed-form box at most. 2) Relabel the CJ exercise. load_mod reproduces only CJ's O1 column. Cite the CEPREMAP WP 9922 table as read, and flag or exclude the theta=-5, theta=0 and rho=0 rows that do not match. Present Dynare sigma-perturbation as a third method distinct from CJ's O2/O4 and DO2/DO4. Optionally implement CJ's stochastic perturbation in about 30 NumPy lines to reproduce the O2/O4 columns, and use the CJ benchmark calibration (0.0179, -0.139, 0.0348, -1.5, 0.95) rather than the rounded one. 3) For MP, state that the published 0.35% maximum depends on the beta bound: the exact supremum is 0.373% as beta->1, 0.36% at beta<=0.999, and 0.25% at beta<=0.99. Pass states=['x'] for the rho=0 case. 5) Correct the capability paths: decision_rules and stochastic_steady_state are in puremacro/dsge/pruning.py:320/730 (order 2) and :1643/1930 (order 3), and stochastic_steady_state is an ergodic mean. 6) If Jermann is kept, write it natively in standard timing with the adjustment-cost parameters computed in Python. Do not claim that order 3 changes the mean premium. Obtain the JME 1998 table through institutional access before citing any number, and state that the paper uses log-linear-lognormal pricing. 7) If modern returns are wanted, freeze an annual F-F Mkt-RF/RF CSV with provenance, or add a factors fetcher. vets.capabilities_check: load_mod exists at puremacro/dsge/dynare.py:2134 and solves the Burnside tree at orders 1, 2 and 3 in about 0.01 s. I reran the survey probe (scratch wf/lucas-tree-review/burnside_test.py). The series gives v(xbar)=12.457828, the quadrature fixed point gives 12.457828, and the relative errors are -1.44% at order 1 and -1.95e-4 at orders 2 and 3, so the survey's numbers reproduce. The other listed symbols are at the wrong path. decision_rules is at puremacro/dsge/pruning.py:320 (order 2) and :1643 (order 3). stochastic_steady_state is at pruning.py:730 and :1930. The DR containers are in puremacro/dsge/_results.py. stochastic_steady_state returns the pruned ergodic-mean deviation, not a risky steady state. The load_mod docstring (dynare.py:2166) still says order {1,2}, but order 3 works. With rho=0, load_mod raises ModelError('no predetermined state variables'), so the call needs states=['x']. EpsteinZinProblem (puremacro/vfi/epstein_zin.py:37) is a grid VFI for savings problems, not an asset pricer. It rejects psi==1 (lines 55-58), which is Tallarini's unit-EIS case. I did find a working route for an Epstein-Zin endowment economy: written as a .mod file, it solves in load_mod at orders 1-3 (probe_ez.py). So the klein_solve blocker cited in the merge note does not apply to the endowment version. There are no asset-pricing helpers in the library (no hits for price_dividend or hansen_jagannathan). The MP linear system, the HJ bound and the Lucas-1987 cost are 10-20 lines of NumPy each. The Jermann .mod is Pfeifer's GPL-3 file and load_mod cannot read it as shipped: (1) `lambda` as a variable name gives a SyntaxError in steady_state_model; (2) parameters assigned inside steady_state_model are unsupported ('no parameter named b'); (3) predetermined_variables is used as the complete state list with no Dynare timing shift (dynare.py:1792-1794, :2241). I confirmed (3) on a 3-variable RBC: 'predetermined_variables k' plus z(-1) raises BlanchardKahnError, while standard timing solves. After I rewrote Jermann in standard timing with the parameters computed in Python, it solves at orders 1-3 in 0.3-0.4 s. At order 2 the ergodic mean is rp_ann=6.32%, rf_ann=0.65% and rk_ann=6.97%. Order 3 gives identical means (the third-order terms have zero mean with symmetric shocks). A 50k-period pruned simulation runs in 6 s.
vets.oracle_check: Burnside: the closed form is exact. I checked the series independently with a Gauss-Hermite grid fixed point (agree to 1e-8), and the formula also appears in the CJ working paper, p.5. Mehra-Prescott: the two-state linear system is exact. I read MP (1985) from Mehra's site in this session: mu=0.018, delta=0.036, phi=0.43 (p.154); Table 1 gives consumption growth 1.83/3.57, riskless return 0.80/5.67, premium 6.18/16.67 and S&P 6.98/16.54 (mean/sd, %); p.156 states that 'the largest premium obtainable with the model is 0.35 percent'. My exact solve with alpha<=10 and rf in [0,4%] gives a supremum of 0.373% as beta->1 (alpha about 2.48, rf 3.99%), 0.36% with beta<=0.999, 0.31% with beta<=0.995 and 0.25% with beta<=0.99. So the 0.35% headline depends on the beta bound and is not reproduced to the digit. Collard-Juillard: I read the CEPREMAP WP co9922 (1999). The JEDC 2001 version is paywalled and was not read. Their benchmark is xbar=0.0179, rho=-0.139, sigma=0.0348, theta=-1.5, beta=0.95. load_mod order 1 matches Table 1's O1 column: benchmark 1.43/1.46 vs 1.43/1.46, theta=-10 23.52/24.47 vs 23.53/24.47, and beta=0.5, beta=0.99, theta=0.5, sigma=0.1, rho=0.5 within about 0.1 pp. Three cases do not match: theta=-5 (9.23 vs 8.57), theta=0 (0.00 vs 0.50) and rho=0 (1.85 vs 1.57). The CJ O2/O4 columns do not correspond to anything in puremacro. They come from CJ's own 'stochastic perturbation', a polynomial in x with all sigma-moments in every coefficient; their DO2/DO4 are certainty-equivalent. puremacro/Dynare sigma-perturbation is a third method: benchmark O2 0.02/0.05 vs CJ 0.00/0.00, and theta=-10 4.64/7.61 vs CJ O2 0.49/1.11 and DO2 23.14/23.16. puremacro has no order 4. Jermann (1998, JME) is paywalled and I could not read it. The paper uses log-linear-lognormal pricing, not perturbation, so there is no closed form and no published target I could verify. Dynare 8 remains a code-parity route only.
vets.data_check: The model parts are synthetic and need no data. The HJ bound can use the MP (1985) Table 1 moments read in this session: premium 6.18 mean and 16.67 sd give a Sharpe ratio of about 0.37. That needs no redistribution and is consistent with the MP calibration. The Ken French F-F_Research_Data_Factors_CSV.zip downloads from Python (13 kB; monthly and annual Mkt-RF and RF from 1926/1927). The server sends no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, so it cannot be fetched live under Pyodide and would have to be frozen with provenance, as notebook 18 does. Its cache also writes into data/raw. RF is nominal. For real rates, the bundled CPIAUCSL.csv covers post-1947 only. Using the MP Table 1 moments avoids that.

(b) The Burnside closed form v(x) = sum_i beta^i exp(a_i + b_i(x - xbar)) is real. I read it in Collard-Juillard CEPREMAP WP 9922 (fetched, p.4, eq. 8). ideas.title: Why are some countries rich? Development accounting, Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) distortions and Hsieh-Klenow (2009) misallocation
ideas.question: How much aggregate TFP is lost when idiosyncratic taxes and subsidies distort establishments, and can Hsieh-Klenow's TFPR dispersion recover it?
ideas.description: RR's model is effectively static (permanent productivity and distortions, exogenous exit) with free entry and conditional entry. The notebook replicates Tables 1-9 and then treats the model's simulated establishments as data for HK's accounting. Under joint lognormality, HK's TFP gap has a closed form in var(log TFPR), which checks the accounting against the model's truth. This teaches the misallocation literature without confidential microdata.
ideas.paper: Restuccia and Rogerson (2008, RED 11); Hsieh and Klenow (2009, QJE)
ideas.oracle_detail: RR Tables 1-9 and Figure 1. Kirkby's RestucciaRogerson2008.pdf says they 'essentially replicate perfectly' (0% median) and documents a bug in RR's own RR_model_RED.m, where the loop variable i overwrites the interest rate. HK's lognormal TFP-gain formula serves as a closed form on simulated firms.
ideas.data_detail: RR's calibration (US establishment size distribution) is in the paper. HK's plant-level data (Indian ASI, Chinese census, US Census) are confidential or need registration, so the HK part uses model-generated firms.
ideas.library_gaps: There is no RR solver. firm_dynamics provides free-entry pricing but not (s, tau) types, conditional entry or the capital market. A small numpy module is needed, or the notebook writes it inline.
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

ideas.title: Rebuild 32: DICE-2016R with equations that match the code, a real optimum or labelled grid search, and the GHKT (2014) closed-form carbon tax
ideas.question: What is the optimal carbon tax, and how close is DICE's numerically optimised path to GHKT's closed form, in which the tax is proportional to GDP?
ideas.description: The 09-20 review flagged notebook 32 for presenting a prescribed-tax, fixed-saving simulator as a welfare optimiser, with equations inconsistent with the code. Plan: (1) GHKT closed form, a tax/GDP ratio from damage elasticity, discount factor and carbon-depreciation weights, checked against a numerical GHKT solve. (2) A DICE optimum over (mu_t, s_t) by SLSQP, compared with Nordhaus's published SCC and optimal-path table. (3) The prescribed-tax simulator as a policy evaluator, labelled honestly. VERIFIED: dice.py is simulation-only ('Nothing is optimised', dice.py:6). Its initial state is a documented hybrid: _L0 = 7.79 billion, the 2020 population (dice.py:76), against pop0 = 7403 million in DICE-2016R-091916ap.gms (read from the GAMS documentation in this session).

Section 5.1 reports $56.9/tC at rho = 1.5% and $496/tC at rho = 0.1%, per ton of carbon and at 70 trillion $/yr of output. Reproducing these:
- The formula with beta = 0.985^10 gives 56.5. With beta = 1.015^-10 it gives 57.2.
- rho = 0.1% gives 495.6.
- Low and high damages give 25.2 and 485.9, against the published 25.3 and 489.
The closed form is therefore a valid oracle, provided the tC/tCO2 units, the annual-vs-decade output basis and the beta convention are all stated. Comparing DICE with GHKT is not an oracle, only a comparison. The prototype gives DICE optimal SCC/Ygross of 0.293, 0.296 and 0.307 ($/tCO2 per $T) for 2020, 2030 and 2050, so the ratio is nearly constant, as GHKT predicts.

- Section 4.2: gamma_bar=2.379e-5 (gammaL=1.060e-5, gammaH=2.046e-4, p=0.068).

ideas.question: How do announcement timing, capital adjustment costs and truncation horizon shape the transition and welfare after a permanent tariff, and when is a transition trustworthy?

ideas.title: Instrument strength versus validity: Wald, AR and tF coverage under weak and invalid instruments (rebuild 28), with the LP-IV residual fix and a Banxico application
ideas.question: Does a large first-stage F establish identification, and which intervals keep their coverage when instruments are weak or invalid?
ideas.description: Status: not implemented. Notebook 28 plants one weak and one strong instrument in a single sample and has no coverage Monte Carlo. DGP A (static, iid): z~N(0,1); (u,v) normal with correlation 0.8; x=pi*z+v; y=beta*x+gamma*z+u; beta=1; T=200. Grid: pi in {0.05,0.15,0.3,0.5} crossed with gamma in {0,0.05,0.1}. A further arm builds the 'instrument' from the regressor: z_tilde=x+0.3*eta. DGP B (dynamic): notebook 28's MA(11) response DGP (28_weak_iv_anderson_rubin.py:70-97), with instrument relevance pi and an exclusion leak gamma. Estimators: OLS; 2SLS with HC0 errors (inline numpy); anderson_rubin_test at the true beta (coverage is 1 minus the rejection rate); msw_bands on a grid (set length and unbounded share); olea_pflueger_f compared with stock_yogo_cv(1,10) and lp_iv's mop_cv_10; lp_iv(anderson_rubin=True) at h=0..12 on DGP B. Monte Carlo: R=1000 per static cell, about 0.2 ms per replication natively, so under 5 s for the whole grid; dynamic arm R=100 x 3 designs at about 77 ms per lp_iv call natively (about 25 s). Prototype (R=500, T=200): median effective F was 0.6, 4.5 and 50.0 for pi=0.05, 0.15 and 0.5. With gamma=0, AR 90% coverage was 0.904 in every strength cell and Wald coverage 0.84-0.90. With gamma=0.1, AR coverage fell to 0.564 and Wald to 0.36-0.64, whatever the F. The derived instrument had median F=2882 and coverage 0.000 for both. Figure: 2x2 panel with coverage heat maps (Wald, AR) over pi x gamma annotated with median F_eff, plus a scatter of F_eff against |2SLS-beta| coloured by gamma that shows the derived-instrument cloud. Exercise: pick pi and gamma (marked # <-). Assert that AR coverage is within 3 MC s.e. of 0.90 when gamma=0. Prompts: why can AR detect invalidity only through w=y-beta0*x, and why is its coverage under gamma!=0 independent of pi?
ideas.paper: Anderson and Rubin (1949); Staiger and Stock (1997); Stock and Yogo (2005); Montiel Olea and Pflueger (2013); Andrews, Stock and Sun (2019) survey
ideas.oracle_detail: beta is planted. Under iid normal homoskedastic errors with fixed instruments, the AR F-test (anderson_rubin_test uses the homoskedastic F, inference/weak_iv.py:350-410) has exact finite-sample size alpha, so AR coverage must be 1-alpha up to MC error sqrt(p(1-p)/R). The prototype reproduced 0.904 at R=500. The rest is simulation truth.
ideas.data_detail: Fully simulated with fixed seeds; no files.
ideas.library_gaps: (1) There is no public static 2SLS/IV estimator. Only lp_iv, dml_iv and lewbel_iv exist; tsls_hac is private (puremacro/inference/_ols_helpers.py:52), so the lab writes 5 lines of numpy. (2) anderson_rubin_test is the homoskedastic F. That is correct for DGP A, but notebook 28 prose (lines 21, 189) calls the HAC AR set 'exact', and this lab should replace that claim.
ideas.plan_overlap: Answers 09-20 REVIEW brainstorm item 3 and review finding 5 (28's exactness prose). Complements 50 (whose manufactured instrument was replaced) and supports PLAN.md's rebuild of 35 around Ramey-Zubairy 2018 (examples/ramey_zubairy_2018_multipliers.py). Option: rebuild 28 around this lab instead of adding 69.

ideas.title: Seasonal adjustment without the binary: native X-11 against Census X-13
ideas.anchor_notebook: new 69 (validation-style); links from curso T01_B/T01_C, which use only deseasonalize_x13 and mention x11 in exercise prose
ideas.question: Can the pure-Python X-11/ARIMA engine that runs under Pyodide reproduce the Census X-13ARIMA-SEATS seasonal factors, and where and why does it diverge?
ideas.description: Load the nine frozen X-13 outputs, run x11_arima on each input, and plot the gaps against the documented tolerances. Separate the interior from the series ends, where the binary uses asymmetric filters and the native engine uses backcasts. Check that henderson_weights sums to one and reproduces cubics (closed form); x11_arima(13) is [-0.01935, -0.02786, 0, 0.06549, 0.14736, 0.21434, 0.24006, ...]. Compare STL (deseasonalize_stl) with X-11 on the same series, and use residual_seasonality_F as the diagnostic on both. Finish with a Mexican NSA series (INEGI/ENOE, as in curso T01_C) where no binary exists in the browser. Exercise: toggle mode='add'/'mult' and measure the change in the seasonal factors.
ideas.paper: Census X-13ARIMA-SEATS v1.1.57 as reference software; Henderson (1916) trend filter
ideas.oracle_detail: The oracle is the frozen output of the Census X-13ARIMA-SEATS binary (v1.1.57, spec 'log|none + airline + no outlier + maxlead/maxback 60 + x11 msr') in tests/fixtures/sa_goldens/meta.json and tests/fixtures/sa_goldens_lb. It covers nine series: six LAUS counties, NSA INDPRO and two quarterly series. The measured tolerances are in docs/VALIDATION.md:76-103: interior medians 0.08-0.83%, maxima under 0.7% on smooth macro series, and seasonal-filter choice matching on every monthly series. The Henderson closed-form properties add a second check.
ideas.data_detail: The goldens and their inputs sit in tests/fixtures/sa_goldens and sa_goldens_lb (NSA INDPRO plus LAUS county CSVs), not in package data. They must be copied into package data, the same SW07-fixture issue noted in PLAN.md:177. The Mexican NSA series is fetchable through puremacro.fetch.realtime.inegi, or can be frozen.
ideas.library_gaps: The goldens are not shipped with the wheel, so an installed copy or Pyodide cannot load them. The native engine has no outlier or regression effects: the pinned spec has none. End-of-series filters differ from the binary's by design. x11_arima took about 1.5 s per 180-month series locally, which is fine.
ideas.plan_overlap: None in PLAN.md or REVIEW.md. The notebook complements curso T01_B (deseasonalize_x13, residual_seasonality_F, x13_available) and the T01_C exercise text that names puremacro.sa.x11.

ideas.title: How does a US shock reach Mexico? A Global VAR on the Mohaddes-Raissi database
ideas.anchor_notebook: new; pairs with 58/59 (Latin America real time)
ideas.question: Through which trade-weighted foreign variables do US output and interest-rate shocks propagate to Mexico and other emerging economies, and does weak exogeneity of the foreign block hold?
ideas.description: Build star_variables from the trade weights, fit gvar (country VARX* models), inspect stability (eigenvalues, max_eigenvalue) and the weak_exogeneity tests. Solve the global system (solve_gvar). Report generalized IRFs to a US GDP and a US short-rate shock (GVARResult.girf), GFEVD shares (GVARResult.gfevd), persistence profiles (.pp) and a conditional forecast (.forecast). Show the Mexico responses beside Brazil and Canada. The exercise swaps trade weights for financial weights.
ideas.paper: Pesaran, Schuermann & Weiner (2004); Dees, di Mauro, Pesaran & Smith (2007); Mohaddes & Raissi GVAR database
ideas.oracle_detail: The link identity G x_t = a0 + a1 t + sum H_l x_{t-l} + ... + eps_t holds exactly at every date (gvar docstring var/gvar.py:3058). GFEVD row sums, the persistence profile equals 1 on impact, and a single-country GVAR reduces to estimate_var; these are pinned in validation/cases_var.py (_gvar_link_identity_ref, _gvar_solo_girf_ref, _gvar_solo_gfevd_ref). An independent-software route, not yet verified, would freeze outputs of the Smith-Galesi GVAR Toolbox (MATLAB) on the same data.
ideas.data_detail: The GVAR quarterly database 1979Q2-2023Q3 (33 countries: real GDP, inflation, short and long rates, exchange rate, equity, oil) is public on Mendeley Data (kfp5fhgkvf), with earlier vintages in the Cambridge repository. Availability was confirmed in this session by web search; the licence is not yet checked. It includes trade-weight matrices. Freeze a country subset for Pyodide.
ideas.library_gaps: No loader exists for the GVAR database. No plotting preset shows a country's response to a foreign shock across countries. Runtime and memory for 33 countries x 6 variables under Pyodide are unmeasured.
ideas.plan_overlap: None. gvar has zero call sites in notebooks and in examples despite about 3,100 lines of code.

vets.capabilities_check: Every listed symbol exists at the stated line in puremacro/var/gvar.py: gvar :3058, solve_gvar :549, star_variables :1131, WeakExogeneityResult :1438, GVARResult.gfevd :1985, .pp :2023, .girf :2088, .forecast :2404. GVARResult (from :1852) also carries stable, max_eigenvalue, eigenvalues and weak_exogeneity. I ran the whole pipeline on the real Mohaddes-Raissi 2023 vintage in scratch (wf/gvar-rev/fit_gvar.py). Setup: 26 units, p=2, q=1, US star=(y,Dp,ep), poil held only by the US, allow_missing_variables=True. Result: k=134, T_eff=176. Timings: fit 0.16 s, girf 0.01 s, gfevd(20) 0.08 s, forecast instant, 50-draw bootstrap 1.24 s, so Pyodide runtime and memory are not a concern. Weak-exogeneity table: 153 tests, 6 reject_nominal. Mexico's F p-values run 0.42-0.78. max_eig is 1.013 (stable=False, warned). Equilibrated cond(G) is 107. Calling solve_gvar on res.link_matrices plus [I,-Lambda0] / [Phi_l, Lambda_l] rebuilt from CountryVARX reproduces res.G and res.F exactly (max diff 0.0), so the 'solve the global system' cell works. Caveats: (1) gvar already calls solve_gvar internally, so the separate call is only a demonstration. (2) .forecast (gvar.py:2404-2486) returns a deterministic point path that can be conditioned only on exog_future. It cannot condition on an endogenous US path, so the proposed 'conditional forecast' does not exist as described. (3) The plotting gap is overstated. GVARGIRFResult.plot(by_variable=True) (gvar.py:1755) already draws one line per country for each variable, but it has no country filter, so it would draw 26 lines.
vets.oracle_check: The internal cases exist as cited, in puremacro/validation/cases_var.py: _gvar_link_identity/_ref :377/:393, _gvar_solo_girf_ref :430, _gvar_solo_gfevd_ref :451, the pp(0)=1 and GFEVD row-sum cases :399/:413, registered from :460. They run only on a seeded 2-country toy DGP, not on this data. The weak-exogeneity size Monte Carlo is pinned at tests/test_var/test_gvar.py:746. I found a much stronger external oracle in this session. The database ships its own star series (ys, Dps, eqs, rs, lrs, and eps for the US) in 'Country Data (1979Q2-2023Q3).xls'. The database PDF, read here, says they are built from 2014-2016 average trade weights (its eq. 3). star_variables reproduces them to at most 4.4e-15 for mex, bra, can, usa and china. The inputs were weights from flows.xls averaged over 2014-16 with the 8 euro members aggregated, and puremacro's renormalisation over countries that carry each variable (wf/gvar-rev/star_oracle.py, extra.py). That check is independent of puremacro. The proposed GVAR Toolbox route should be dropped. The Toolbox estimates VECX* models with cointegration and restricted trends, and puremacro fits unrestricted levels VARX* with no cointegration (gvar.py:84-97, docs/gvar.md §8), so their GIRFs are not comparable. The Read Me also says Toolbox 2.0 needs patches for MATLAB 2021 and later. No published GIRF figure can serve as a target either: the literature uses VECX* and a different vintage.

ideas.title: Regional spillovers across US states: spatial econometrics on Munnell's public-capital panel
ideas.question: Does public capital raise output in neighbouring states, and how much do the weights, the model (SAR/SEM/SDM/SLX) and the standard errors change the answer?
ideas.description: Build contiguity, kNN and distance weights for the 48 contiguous states from the bundled load_us_state_centroids (lat/lon and a 'neighbors' column). Run Moran's I and Geary's C on state output growth, then the Anselin LM battery (lm_spatial_tests) on the pooled OLS residuals to choose between SAR and SEM. Fit sar, sem, sdm and slx cross-sections and the spatial_panel SAR/SDM/SEM with individual and two-way effects, with LeSage-Pace direct, indirect and total effects. Compare Conley SEs (conley_se) with clustered SEs. Run spatial_lp of state employment on a state shock and its spatial lag. Add a spatial_did demonstration with exposure_rings on bundled county centroids, where naive DiD is contaminated by spillovers (simulation truth). Probe this session: spatial_panel(model='sar', effects='individual') on Produc gives rho=0.274688719, and spreg.Panel_FE_Lag gives 0.274688713, with betas identical to 6 decimals (lpcap -0.04658, lpc 0.18743, lemp 0.62509, unemp -0.00448).
ideas.oracle_detail: PySAL spreg 1.9.0 and esda 2.10.0 (installed locally) as frozen goldens, following validation/goldens/spatial.json. Verified agreement to about 1e-8 for the SAR fixed-effects panel. Simulation truth for spatial_lp and spatial_did.
ideas.data_detail: Rdatasets plm/Produc.csv (Munnell 1990, 48 states x 1970-1986, 64 KB; fetched OK; 'TENNESSE' must be mapped). Geography is bundled: puremacro/datasets/data/us_state_centroids.csv (with neighbors) and us_county_centroids.csv. State employment and unemployment for spatial_lp come from FRED/BLS through build_subnational_panel.
ideas.library_gaps: None blocking. spatial_panel needs unit_col/time_col for long frames. The 'neighbors' column must be filtered to the sample states.
ideas.plan_overlap: None. Notebook 55 covers quantitative spatial GE (AllenArkolakisModel, CaliendoParroModel), not spatial econometrics. Apart from those two models, the whole puremacro.spatial package has 0 notebook and 0 example call sites.

ideas.title: Build the capital stock and the Solow residual yourself: OECD quarterly accounts against Fernald's TFP
ideas.question: How far can a perpetual-inventory capital stock and a Solow residual built from public quarterly national accounts go toward a published TFP series, and which assumptions (initial stock, depreciation conversion, aggregation, labour share) matter?
ideas.description: Fetch qna_panel(assets=True, real=True, labor=True) for the US and a few OECD countries. Build per-asset stocks with qna_capital: geometric against linear quarterly depreciation, Harberger K0 and its k0_sensitivity, Torngvist services against a summed stock, and invariance to rebasing. Compute qna_tfp with a Gollin-adjusted labour share (gollin_adjusted_ls). Compare US TFP growth with Fernald's quarterly TFP (fetch.fernald). Extend to the long annual G9 panel (build_g9_long_panel, splice_audit, load_klems_country) and to the capital-skill and cross-nest elasticities (fit_korv_country, fit_cross_nest_pooled, sato_wald_test). Probe this session: qna_panel(['USA'], assets=True, real=True, labor=True) returns 126 quarters, and qna_tfp runs, returning tfp, labor and labor_share.
ideas.oracle_detail: Fernald's utilization-unadjusted quarterly TFP (FRBSF xlsx cached at data/raw/www.frbsf.org/wp-content_uploads_quarterly_tfp.xlsx): growth correlation and the dating of the productivity slowdown. It is approximate by construction (business sector, BLS capital). Internal checks: Torngvist invariance to rebasing (capital.py docstring reports 2.6e-15) and the closed-form steady-state bias of linear depreciation (+5.3% equipment, +8.5% IPP, same docstring).
ideas.data_detail: OECD QNA via puremacro.fetch.qna_panel, cached under data/raw/sdmx.oecd.org (423 cached responses). Fernald xlsx is cached. EU-KLEMS and PWT through the klems and long_panel loaders.
ideas.library_gaps: None blocking for the QNA part. KORV and cross-nest need the EU-KLEMS downloads, and build_g9_long_panel writes a CSV by default (write_csv=True). Pass False in a notebook.
ideas.plan_overlap: Not in PLAN.md. Course 10_b1 uses Fernald TFP, course 21 fits KORV (fit_korv_pooled, fit_sigma_su_pooled), and curso T01_B uses load_klems_panel and gollin_adjusted_ls once each. qna_capital and qna_tfp have 0 call sites.
