ideas.title: Life-cycle SMM with a known truth: recovering beta and risk aversion from age-wealth profiles
ideas.question: Can simulated method of moments recover a life-cycle model's discount factor and risk aversion from mean wealth by age, and do its confidence intervals cover the truth?
ideas.description: Solve a finite-horizon income-risk model with survival (FiniteHorizonProblem), build cohort distributions and age profiles, and simulate a data panel at known parameters. Estimate with estimate_method_of_moments and compute efficient-GMM or sandwich SEs from numerics.numerical_gradient on a smoothed moment map. Repeat over about 100 seeds for coverage, and show the beta-sigma identification ridge. Include the check that the panel histogram matches the cohort distribution, and compare Farmer-Toda with Tauchen income chains.
ideas.paper: Gourinchas and Parker (2002) as the later published target
ideas.oracle_detail: The true (beta, sigma) generate the data; the check is Monte Carlo coverage of nominal 95% intervals. Internal checks: empirical_distribution of a large simulated panel converges to life_cycle_distribution, and without income risk the Euler equation (consumption growth (beta*s_j*R)^(1/sigma)) holds up to grid error. Smoke test here: a 400x5x40 life-cycle solve plus distribution took 0.2 s, so hundreds of solves are affordable.
ideas.data_detail: A simulated panel. SCF or PSID age-wealth moments can follow later (PLAN's published-moment version).
ideas.library_gaps: estimate_method_of_moments returns no Jacobian, weighting-matrix update or standard errors (EstimationResult has only theta, objective, moments, success, n_evals). Discrete-grid policies make the moments step functions (its own docstring says so), so gradients need lottery or EGM smoothing, or finite-difference steps larger than the grid spacing. FiniteHorizonProblem has no numba backend and its 'options' field is unused. simulate_panel starts every agent at one asset index.
ideas.plan_overlap: PLAN's bigger bet 'life-cycle method of moments' (published moments, high cost). This version adds a cheap simulation-truth first stage and a coverage study, and uses the finite_horizon and simulate modules that PLAN did not survey.

vets.required_changes:
1. Replace simulate_panel with an age-indexed panel simulator (notebook-local, or a new simulate_life_cycle_panel in puremacro/vfi/simulate.py). Keep empirical_distribution for the per-age histogram check.
2. Estimate on a smooth moment map. Write a notebook-local finite-horizon EGM with survival and age-varying income (about 25 lines), push the distribution with lottery_push (distribution.py:36), and simulate the data by lottery draws so the truth is exact for the estimator. Keep FiniteHorizonProblem VFI as a cross-method check (profiles agree within about 1-2%) and show its step-function moments and step-dependent SEs as a warning panel.
3. Hand-code the GMM sandwich and efficient-GMM covariance with a central-difference Jacobian using parameter-scaled steps. Do not use sandwich_vcov, and do not use scalar numerical_gradient except per moment.
4. Relabel the method as minimum-distance/GMM with simulated data, or simulate model moments with common random numbers and apply the (1+1/tau) SE factor.
5. Replace the per-age Euler oracle. Report the mean error, or its convergence in n_a, for VFI without income risk, and headline the VFI-vs-EGM and panel-vs-distribution checks.
6. Calibrate so the moment ages have positive wealth (ages 9 and older, or a flatter income profile) and a_max does not bind (about 80 with a quadratic grid).
7. Budget and assertions: 100 seeds take about 90 s on desktop. Use 50-100 seeds, allow for Pyodide slowdown, and assert coverage within a Monte Carlo band (for example above 0.8), not near 0.95. Measured coverage is 0.89/0.90. Report the undercovering efficient-GMM SEs honestly and add an identity-W comparison.
8. Frame Tauchen vs Farmer-Toda as a misspecification exercise: data from a fine chain, estimation with a coarse chain, bias shown in units of SE.
9. Drop "extends 53" (IFT-on-collocation does not transfer). Anchor to 03 and cross-link 28 and 10 for coverage.
vets.capabilities_check:
All 11 symbols exist at the stated paths: FiniteHorizonProblem finite_horizon.py:47, life_cycle_distribution :174, cross_section :200, age_profile :214, simulate_panel simulate.py:22, empirical_distribution simulate.py:64, estimate_method_of_moments estimate.py:36, farmer_toda discretize.py:104, numerical_gradient numerics.py:27, sandwich_vcov numerics.py:66, stationary_age_weights olg.py:22. Three of them cannot do what the proposal needs.
(1) simulate_panel takes only a time-invariant 2-D policy: `n_a, n_z = pol.shape` at simulate.py:34. Passing the life-cycle policy_aprime (J,n_a,n_z) fails with "ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)" (verified). It also starts every agent at one asset index and has no age dimension, so it cannot simulate the data panel.
(2) sandwich_vcov is a quasi-MLE sandwich over per-observation negative log-likelihoods (numerics.py:66-109). It is not the GMM sandwich (G'WG)^-1 G'WSWG (G'WG)^-1 / N.
(3) numerical_gradient returns the gradient of a scalar function with one step h for every parameter. A 7x2 moment Jacobian therefore needs a loop over moments, and beta and sigma need different step sizes.
Smoke tests with scratch smoke1-5.py, n_a=300 or 400, 5 Farmer-Toda states, J=40, survival:
- One VFI solve plus distribution takes 0.21 s.
- The moment map is a step function. A beta change of 5e-5 moves age-10 mean wealth by 3%.
- The VFI finite-difference Jacobian depends on the step. It is garbage at h<=1e-4, and se(sigma) is 0.177 at h=1e-3 but 0.028 at h=5e-3.
- One Nelder-Mead estimate takes 21 s and 92 evaluations, so 100 seeds would take about 35 min.
The smoothed fix works:
- A notebook-local finite-horizon EGM (about 25 lines) with lottery_push (distribution.py:36) runs in 6 ms per solve.
- Its Jacobian is identical for h from 1e-6 to 1e-3.
- Its profile matches VFI within about 1% ([0.136 0.955 2.911 5.282 6.611 5.507 1.243] vs [0.137 0.943 2.921 5.294 6.602 5.483 1.241]).
The library has no finite-horizon EGM. solve_egm (egm.py:27) is infinite-horizon only, and DCEGMProblem (dcegm.py:678) has income that does not vary with age.
vets.oracle_check:
The simulation-truth coverage oracle works, but only with the smooth EGM plus lottery moment map. I simulated a lottery-draw panel, 100 seeds with N=2000, 7 mean-wealth moments at ages 9,14,...,39 and efficient W. Results:
- Coverage of nominal 95% intervals is 0.89 for beta and 0.90 for sigma. The Monte Carlo SE is about 2.2 points, so the intervals undercover modestly.
- Mean estimates are 0.9499 and 1.986 (truth 0.95 and 2.0).
- The standard deviation of the estimates is 0.0057 and 0.221, against mean SEs of 0.0049 and 0.189.
- The correlation between the beta and sigma estimates is -0.989 and cond(G) is about 2000, so the ridge is real.
- Runtime is 88 s on desktop.
This teaches something real: efficient-GMM SEs understate the spread along the ridge. The coverage experiment itself is sound.
Internal checks:
- The empirical_distribution-vs-cohort check passes. The total-variation distance between a 200k-agent panel and the distribution is 0.003-0.009, and the mean-wealth gap is under 0.2%.
- The Euler check as proposed fails per age. Discrete VFI with no income risk has a maximum consumption-growth error of 0.027 at n_a=400 (0.009 at n_a=1500), while theoretical growth is only 1.002-1.008. It holds only on average or as n_a grows.
- EGM satisfies the Euler equation by construction, so it is not an independent check there.
- A comparison of the VFI and EGM profiles is a better cross-method oracle.
- The data must be simulated from the same approximation the estimator uses (lottery draws), or grid error biases the coverage result.
vets.data_check:
The data are purely synthetic: a simulated panel from known parameters. Nothing needs to be fetched and there are no licensing issues. It runs offline and under Pyodide with numpy and scipy only.
Calibration pitfalls I found:
- With a hump income profile kappa=exp(0.1j-0.0025j^2) and beta=0.95, nobody saves at ages 0-7. The age-4 moment is identically zero, which makes S singular. Use moment ages of 9 or older, or flatten the profile.
- a_max=40 binds (the top grid point is occupied). a_max=80 with a quadratic grid occupies up to about 54.
The Gourinchas-Parker (2002) published target needs PSID/CEX-based moments that are not bundled; that is correctly deferred. No published numbers were used or needed in this review.
vets.novelty_check:
No existing notebook runs a structural (VFI or life-cycle) estimation coverage study. Coverage appears in 06, 07, 10, 11, 17 and 28, all reduced-form. Notebook 53 does GMM with IFT gradients on continuous collocation. That machinery does not apply to discrete-grid FiniteHorizonProblem, so "extends 53" is a stretch; the real anchor is 03, which only calls life_cycle_profile.
tests/test_vfi/test_vfi_estimate.py:53 recovers beta from noiseless mean assets with a 5e-3 tolerance, which is a grid-step caveat. This proposal fills PLAN.md:120 (life-cycle method of moments) as a cheap first stage and the uncertainty/coverage lab from the 09-20 REVIEW.md:138. It is not a duplicate.

vets.oracle_check:
The simulation truth is obtainable: the author sets the truth. Because the same model code generates the data, it tests the estimator and the inference, not the solver. I measured everything below in scratch runs under .../scratchpad/wf/lcsmm-review/probe1-7.py.

Coverage study (J=40, Tauchen-5 chain, beta=0.96, gamma=2, six age-bin mean-wealth moments, N=2000, efficient W=Omega^-1, smooth EGM moments):
- 100 seeds ran in 65 s native.
- Wald coverage for beta and gamma was 0.87/0.88 on one set of seeds and 0.93/0.91 on another. The Monte Carlo SE is about ±2.2 percentage points, so the tables must report it.
- A Stock-Wright/Hansen S-statistic at the truth covered 0.95.
- At N=20000 (60 seeds), Wald coverage was 0.97.
- A diagonal-W sandwich covered only 0.80-0.88, even at N=20000. The likely causes are Nelder-Mead on the ridge or finite-difference noise.
- The ridge is real: corr(beta_hat, gamma_hat) = -0.994 and the columns of G are about 30:1 proportional in every bin. Adding log-consumption moments cuts the SEs by 35% but leaves corr at -0.997.

Internal checks with some independence:
- VFI on a 400-point curved grid and EGM on 200 points with lottery moments agree within 0.014 (0.4%).
- Means from a panel of 200,000 agents differ from the lottery moments by at most 0.005, about 10% of an N=2000 SE.

The proposed Euler check is weak as stated. With VFI on 2000 points, the error in consumption growth is median 0.0044 and max 0.013, while net growth is only about 0.01. Use the closed-form deterministic consumption path in levels instead (flat income, no risk, unconstrained start). For EGM the Euler check is tautological.

Published anchor: the econometricsociety.org abstract, fetched this session, says Gourinchas-Parker (2002) matches age profiles of consumption, not wealth. The IDEAS/RePEc abstract of Cagetti (2003, JBES 21(3):339-353), also fetched this session, says it matches simulated median wealth profiles to PSID and SCF data to estimate time preference and risk aversion. Cagetti is the right later target for wealth moments. I read no table values.
vets.data_check: The data are synthetic, as proposed, and the notebook must say so at the top. Two design points. First, ages 0-9 hold about zero wealth because the borrowing constraint binds, which makes Omega singular; bin ages from 10 upward (six 5-year bins worked). Second, simulate continuous-asset agents from the EGM policy, not agents on grid nodes. A later empirical version needs SCF or PSID median-wealth profiles, as Cagetti used; none are bundled.
vets.novelty_check:
Not a duplicate. Notebook 53 (notebooks/53_exact_analytic_ift_gradients.py:88 onward) recovers beta and sigma by GMM on a deterministic continuous model. Its objective at the truth is about 1e-12, and it has no sampling noise, SEs or coverage. Notebook 03 and the course copy T06_B only solve the life-cycle model and do no estimation. Notebook 10 and the review's uncertainty lab do coverage for DiD, not for structural SMM.

No notebook, course file, example, replication or validation case calls estimate_method_of_moments, FiniteHorizonProblem or simulate_panel on a life-cycle model; grep found them only in tests, puremacro/vfi and notebook 03's wrapper. PLAN.md:120 lists "life-cycle method of moments" as a bigger bet with published moments. This proposal is its cheap first stage and complements it.

ideas.title: MCMC diagnostics you can check against closed forms
ideas.anchor_notebook: new short lab; prerequisite for PLAN's 'Three samplers, one posterior'; links 42 and 47
ideas.question: Do puremacro's convergence diagnostics and standard-error helpers report what they claim on problems whose answers are known?
ideas.description: Pass AR(1) chains with known integrated autocorrelation time to effective_sample_size and geweke_z. Run random_walk_metropolis on a conjugate normal linear-regression posterior and compare posterior moments, trace_summary and gelman_rubin with the closed form. Compare mle_fit Hessian and sandwich SEs under correct specification and under heteroskedastic misspecification, with Monte Carlo coverage. Check fan-chart coverage from simulate_var_paths and fan_chart_quantiles on a known VAR.
ideas.oracle_detail: Checks: ESS = n(1-rho)/(1+rho) for an AR(1) chain; Geweke z ~ N(0,1) under stationarity (5% two-sided rejection); conjugate posterior moments; sandwich = inverse information under correct specification. Run here: ESS was 9,909 against a closed form of 10,526 (rho 0.9, n 200,000). geweke_z rejection at |z|>1.96 over 400 stationary AR(1) chains of 5,000 draws was 2.8% at rho 0, 5.5% at 0.5, 29.7% at 0.9 and 57.8% at 0.97.
ideas.data_detail: Simulated chains and regressions only; runs offline in seconds.
ideas.library_gaps: geweke_z is miscalibrated for persistent chains. _spectral_density_zero (mcmc.py:17-34) uses a Bartlett bandwidth of int(4(n/100)^0.2) lags per segment (about 5 lags for a 500-draw first segment), far below the autocorrelation time of typical RWMH chains, so it flags stationary chains as not converged (30% at rho 0.9). Fix it (batch means, an n^(1/3) Newey-West bandwidth or an AR spectral estimate) before any notebook relies on it. random_walk_metropolis, trace_summary, sandwich_vcov and numerical_gradient have no notebook call sites.
ideas.plan_overlap: PLAN's 'Three samplers, one posterior' tests DSGE samplers against the Herbst-Schorfheide book. This lab is different: closed-form oracles on the generic mcmc, numerics and posterior modules, and it exposes a bug that notebook would inherit. It also fits the 09-20 'uncertainty lab'.

vets.required_changes: 1. Before the notebook, a library PR: reimplement geweke_z's segment variance as an AR(p)-by-AIC spectral density at zero, matching coda's spectrum0.ar. Do not use batch means or a bandwidth tweak (still 12-32% false alarms at rho 0.9-0.97). Add a calibration regression test in tests/test_mcmc_coverage.py: 400 AR(1) chains, rho 0.9, n 5000, rejection ≤ ~9%. Recheck estimate_dsge_bayesian geweke_z_max and tests/test_dynare_bayesian.py:138. Keep the old Bartlett estimator inline in the notebook as the 'before' curve. 2. Correct the effective_sample_size docstring, or implement the monotone step. 3. Add a split option to gelman_rubin (default split=True, or at least available) and have notebook 42 use it. 4. Report ESS as a distribution over replications, not one draw. Add the MCSE check (MCMC mean - closed mean)/(post sd/sqrt(ESS)) ~ N(0,1) so that ESS is also validated on genuine RWMH output. 5. Replace the 'sandwich = inverse information' oracle with the exact identities se_classical = sqrt(diag(s2_MLE (X'X)^-1)) and se_sandwich = HC0, plus the coverage table (74.6% vs 95.0% under heteroskedasticity). 6. For gelman_rubin, use the AR(1) oracle sqrt(1+(tau-1)/n) and a drifting-chain split-vs-non-split demo. 7. Restrict the fan-chart check to the true-parameter (degenerate posterior) case against closed-form Gaussian quantiles, or drop it. Do not present frequentist coverage of an estimated-posterior fan chart as a closed-form oracle. 8. Link to notebooks 42 and 47 and to PLAN's 'Three samplers'. Cite Geweke (1992) and coda's geweke.diag.
vets.capabilities_check: All 11 symbols exist where the proposal says and fit the lab. I smoke-ran each one: every experiment took under 10 s, about 25 s in total, using numpy/scipy only, so it is Pyodide-safe. Symbols: geweke_z mcmc.py:37, gelman_rubin :58, autocorrelations :78, effective_sample_size :94, trace_summary :118, random_walk_metropolis :159, numerical_hessian numerics.py:41, sandwich_vcov :66, mle_fit :112, simulate_var_paths posterior.py:14, fan_chart_quantiles :60. Results. (1) effective_sample_size is calibrated. Mean ESS over replications divided by the closed form n(1-rho)/(1+rho) was 0.98-1.03 for rho 0-0.97 and n 5k and 200k. At rho 0.9, n 200k it was 10,309 (sd 368, 10 chains) against 10,526; the proposal's 9,909 is a single draw. (2) random_walk_metropolis on a conjugate known-sigma regression (4x20k draws, accept 0.24) matched the closed-form posterior means and sds to 3 decimals, with R_hat 1.000. The MCSE z-scores were +1.05, -1.43 and -1.69. (3) mle_fit on the Gaussian regression QMLE matched the closed forms to 5 digits: se_classical = sqrt(diag(s2_MLE (X'X)^-1)) and se_sandwich = HC0. Slope 95% coverage (T 200, 500 reps): 93.6% classical and 92.2% sandwich when correctly specified; 74.6% and 95.0% under sd=exp(0.8x) heteroskedasticity. (4) simulate_var_paths plus fan_chart_quantiles, given the true VAR(1) parameters, matched the closed-form Gaussian quantiles. The maximum error was 0.095 sd at D=4k and 0.023 sd at D=40k, which is Monte Carlo noise. 80% band coverage over 300 reps was 77-82% across horizons. (5) The geweke_z bug is confirmed; details are under gaps.
vets.oracle_check: The oracles are independent and obtainable, with three corrections. (a) The ESS and AR(1) Geweke oracles are exact closed forms. Geweke should also be checked against its reference implementation. The coda source I fetched this session (github.com/cran/coda R/geweke.R) uses frac1=0.1, frac2=0.5 and spectrum0.ar(y)$spec for each segment, an AR spectral estimate rather than a Bartlett kernel. (b) 'Sandwich = inverse information under correct specification' holds only asymptotically: in one correctly specified sample the slope SE was 0.0684 classical against 0.0636 sandwich. Use the exact finite-sample identity instead: in Gaussian linear-regression QMLE the beta block equals HC0 (the Hessian is block-diagonal at the MLE). (c) gelman_rubin has no closed form on the conjugate posterior. A usable oracle for stationary AR(1) chains is E[R_hat] ≈ sqrt(1+(tau-1)/n), which checked out at 1.0166 vs 1.0178 (rho 0.9, n 500) and 1.071 vs 1.063 (rho 0.97). (d) Frequentist coverage of a fan chart built from estimated posterior draws is not a closed-form oracle. Only the degenerate true-parameter case, or prior-drawn truths (SBC-style), gives one. No published table values are needed.
vets.data_check: Data are fully synthetic (simulated AR(1) chains, a regression and a VAR), so there are no licensing or network needs. It runs offline in seconds; my full battery took about 25 s.
vets.novelty_check: The material is novel as a calibration lab. Nothing in notebooks 00-68, the course or curso checks diagnostics against known answers. Existing uses: notebook 42 (lines 83, 173-174) computes non-split gelman_rubin and ESS on 2x100 SW07 draws; curso T02_E_bayesian_dsge_local.ipynb cell 11 uses ESS to compare RWMH with NUTS; notebook 47 uses the fan-chart functions. Two example scripts, puremacro/examples/mcmc_diagnostics.py and mle_sandwich_demo.py, are usage demos without oracles or coverage. tests/test_mcmc_coverage.py:57-106 tests geweke_z only on iid chains, which is why the bug went unnoticed. The validation gallery checks HC0 only through conley_cov (cases_spatial.py:519), not mle_fit. PLAN's 'Three samplers, one posterior' uses the Herbst-Schorfheide book as its oracle, so there is no duplication. This lab is a prerequisite for it and fits the 09-20 'uncertainty lab'. The fan-chart section overlaps notebook 47 most and is the weakest part.

ideas.title: Model doctor: diagnosing a DSGE that will not solve
ideas.anchor_notebook: fold into PLAN's 'DSGE from a Python function', or a new lab after 41
ideas.question: When a DSGE steady state or solution fails, can the library say which equations are to blame?
ideas.description: Plant defects in small models written with dsge.build and steady: a duplicated and a missing equation (Dulmage-Mendelsohn blocks), a unit root, a bad guess repaired by homotopy, a Taylor coefficient below one (indeterminacy) and an explosive rule (no stable solution). For each, show what steady, check, model_diagnostics, klein_solve (BlanchardKahnError) and gensys report. Compare Klein and gensys on the healthy model.
ideas.oracle_detail: Every planted defect has a known answer. The over- and under-determined equation and variable sets are known by construction. RBC steady-state capital (alpha/(1/beta-1+delta))^(1/(1-alpha)) is matched to machine precision by steady (checked here: 37.98925). The Taylor-principle determinacy boundary of the three-equation NK model is transcribed from Bullard and Mitra (2002). Klein and gensys decision rules must agree to rounding.
ideas.data_detail: Hand-written toy models only.
ideas.library_gaps: When the equation-variable matching is incomplete, steady() (steady.py:545-552) tries hybr before the Dulmage-Mendelsohn diagnosis. If hybr finds any root, it returns converged=True with only info['fallback_from_block']=True. The singular system {x-a, 2(x-a), y*z-2} came back as (1, 2, 1), 'converged', and StructuralSingularityError was never raised. The fallback needs at least a warning or an opt-out. Neither dsge.build with a callable nor steady has a notebook call site.
ideas.plan_overlap: PLAN's workflow notebook 'DSGE from a Python function' (build, steady, diagnostics, Klein vs gensys). This adds the planted-defect oracle, the structural-singularity diagnostics and the silent-fallback finding, and can be merged into it.

vets.required_changes:
1. Merge into PLAN's 'DSGE from a Python function' (PLAN.md:105) rather than creating a separate lab.
2. Drop the Taylor-principle indeterminacy cell and the Bullard-Mitra frontier, already covered in curso T02_C cells 4-5 and 14-15, course 10c:529-583 and examples/dsge_nk_sketchpad.py:137. Point to them in one line. For no stable solution, use rho_r=1.05 (closed-form root 1.05) or a lagged-data rule (phi_pi 20 gives (1,1), 40 gives (0,0) with phi_x=0), with the boundary taken from the analytic characteristic polynomial or a fetched paper.
3. Redesign the DM defect:
   - Show StructuralSingularityError with an inconsistent over-determination, e.g. Euler replaced by a-1.02, which names over {a_target,tfp}/{a} and under {resource,prod}/{k,c,y}.
   - Show the consistent duplicate separately as the failure case: steady returns a wrong k, and build then raises an unnamed SingularPencilError.
4. Small library fixes first, with tests, so the notebook does not bake a bug into its asserts:
   - a. At steady.py:545-552, emit a warning, or raise unless allow_fallback=True.
   - b. Add equation_names= to build, forward it through _solve_steady_state, and keep steady's info on LinearModel (build.py:2329-2345).
   - c. After convergence in _solve_block_system, run a rank check on the Jacobian at the solution and flag a non-isolated root.
   - d. In model_diagnostics, downgrade the static-rank and 'empty equation' findings when a unit root or dynamic incidence explains them (diagnostics.py:438-449, 559-570).
   - e. Give the lab a route to model_diagnostics on singular pencils, e.g. build(strict=False) returning a flagged model, or a diagnostics entry point that takes (f, ss).
   - f. Optional: fix the missing-root selection at diagnostics.py:141-143.
5. Remove find_steady_state from the capability list, or present it as a documented limitation (perfect_foresight.py:409).
6. Homotopy cell: use a curated path (alpha 0.6->0.36 from k=5000, or A 1->50 as in test_steady.py:294) and explain that it is parameter continuation from a fixed guess.
7. Present check() loadings as co-movement, not blame. The oracle is the eigenvalue modulus. State that model_diagnostics passes indeterminate and explosive models, and that check and model_diagnostics answer different questions.
8. Klein vs gensys:
   - Ship the explicit 6-variable gensys mapping, imported from puremacro.dsge.gensys.
   - Align the rn timing: build shifts rn by one period relative to gensys.
   - Add the undetermined-coefficients closed form as an oracle independent of the shared _qz code.
9. Bilingual twin and catalog entries as usual.
vets.capabilities_check:
All 12 symbols exist at the cited lines. I smoke-ran them in wf/modeldoc-rev/smoke1-3.py; the three scripts take about 10 s in total. Most fit the lab, but find_steady_state does not, and some behaviour contradicts the lab's premise.
(1) Healthy RBC through build(guess=...): k_ss=37.989253538152624 against a closed form of ...255 (difference 3.7e-13). check() reports BK satisfied and model_diagnostics passes.
(2) A consistent duplicated equation never reaches StructuralSingularityError:
- Euler replaced by a copy of the TFP equation: steady returns k=16.23 through the hybr fallback (steady.py:545-552), flagged only in info.
- Euler replaced by 2*resource: the matching is complete, so the block path itself returns k=12.29 with converged=True and no flag. _solve_coupled_block (steady.py:482-513) and the final check (626-651) test only the residual, never rank or uniqueness.
- In both cases build then raises SingularPencilError from klein.py:368 without naming which equations are dependent.
- Only an inconsistent over-determination, such as Euler replaced by a-1.02, triggers the DM report: over={a_target,tfp}/{a}, under={resource,prod}/{k,c,y}. tests/test_dsge/test_steady.py:216-291 also uses only inconsistent cases.
(3) build discards equation names and the info dict (build.py:2329-2345, `ss, _ = steady(...)`), so the DM message says eq_1..eq_4 and fallback_from_block is invisible through build.
(4) model_diagnostics cannot run on singular-pencil models, because build raises before any LinearModel exists (strict=False does not help). Its pencil and collinear-equation branches (diagnostics.py:463-475, 586-604) are unreachable for the very models this lab targets.
(5) On a legitimate random walk (NK with rho_r=1), model_diagnostics returns passed=False with two false errors: 'Static Jacobian rank-deficient' and 'Redundant/empty equations: eq_1 involve zero variables' (diagnostics.py:438-449, 559-570). check() reports that model as determinate with one unit root.
(6) check() is suggestive about blame, not a reliable diagnosis:
- phi_pi=0.9 names the missing root 0.9616 (pi, i, x).
- rho_r=1.05 finds the excess root |lambda|=1.0500 but ranks i=1.0 above rn=0.29.
- phi_pi=-0.5 or -3 selects the exogenous 0.9 root and blames rn, because the heuristic at diagnostics.py:141-143 takes the largest stable root.
- check never names equations at all.
(7) model_diagnostics reports passed=True with no findings on the indeterminate and explosive models; it carries no BK status.
(8) find_steady_state (perfect_foresight.py:409-480) does not fit build-style callables: it raises AttributeError ('ndarray' has no attribute 'c'). It ignores solve_algo, and with a bad guess it returns the guess with NaN residuals instead of raising.
(9) Homotopy works only with a curated start. Guess k=5000 fails directly, and the beta or delta paths fail at s=0; alpha 0.6->0.36 recovers k=37.98925 in 4 steps. steady.py:764-769 is a parameter continuation from a fixed guess.
(10) gensys is not exported from puremacro.dsge (__init__.py mentions it only in the docstring), and no helper maps a LinearModel to gensys form. I wrote a 6-variable mapping (rn,x,pi,i,Ex,Epi): Klein F and L match gensys Impact to 2.0e-15 and 6.7e-16, and gensys returns eu (1,0) at phi_pi=0.9 and (0,0) at rho=1.05.
(11) The explosive-rule defect needs a lagged-data rule. The contemporaneous rule at phi_pi=-10..1.5 is never (0,0). A lagged rule with phi_x=0 gives eu (1,1) at phi_pi=20 and (0,0) at phi_pi=40.
vets.oracle_check:
Obtainable but partly overstated:
(a) The RBC closed-form K is independent and matches to 3.7e-13 absolute, 1e-14 relative.
(b) The 'known by construction' equation and variable sets hold only for inconsistent over-determination. For a consistent duplicate the correct answer is a rank deficiency that the library never names; that is a finding, not a pass.
(c) The Taylor-principle boundary kappa(phi_pi-1)+(1-beta)phi_y>0 is already stated and checked in curso/notebooks/T02_C_new_keynesian_local.ipynb (cells 4-5 and 14-15), which I read in this session. I did not fetch Bullard-Mitra. A lagged-rule upper boundary must be read from the paper or derived from the analytic characteristic polynomial (np.roots), not typed from memory.
(d) Klein and gensys agree (2e-15), but both call the same _qz.ordqz_sorted and _check_regular, so a common-mode QZ error would go unseen. Add the undetermined-coefficients closed form of the NK response to rn as the independent oracle.
(e) Eigenvalue oracles are closed-form: the excess root equals rho_r (check prints 1.0500), and the indeterminate root is a root of the NK quadratic. Eigenvector loadings have no 'blame' oracle and must not be scored as one.
(f) Homotopy: use the closed-form k from tests/test_dsge/test_steady.py:294-348 (A 1->50) or the alpha path.
vets.data_check: Synthetic hand-written models only, so there are no data or licensing issues. Everything runs in seconds and needs only numpy and scipy (Pyodide-safe).
vets.novelty_check:
Partial duplication.
- The Taylor-principle, indeterminacy and BK-flag material is already covered by curso T02_C (a phi_pi sweep plus a 2-D determinacy region against the analytic frontier), notebooks/course/10c_rigideces_nominales_es.py:529-583 (which separates indeterminacy from non-existence), puremacro/examples/dsge_nk_sketchpad.py:137-145 (BlanchardKahnError at phi_pi=0.9), and notebooks 46 and 47 in prose.
- check, resid and model_diagnostics on healthy models appear in curso T02_B and T02_C.
- New material: build with a callable plus steady, the DM/Hopcroft-Karp/Tarjan block report, homotopy, the silent-fallback findings, and gensys with a Klein-vs-gensys comparison. PLAN.md:54 lists these under 'No notebook'.
- It is essentially PLAN's 'DSGE from a Python function' (PLAN.md:105-107) plus planted defects, so merge rather than create a new lab.
- Notebook 64 is about trade/CGE continuation and does not overlap.

ideas.title: Hamilton (1989) recession dating on US GNP: MS-AR done right
ideas.anchor_notebook: notebooks/16_regime_girf.py (mentions ms_var_fit only in prose at :365 and :389)
ideas.question: Does ms_var_fit recover Hamilton's expansion and recession regimes and transition probabilities on his own GNP sample?
ideas.description: Promote puremacro/examples/ms_var_business_cycle.py (synthetic, 98% classification) to Hamilton's data, 1951Q2-1984Q4. Add: a math cell for the Hamilton filter, the Kim smoother and EM; smoothed recession probabilities against NBER dates (the data file carries a recession flag); a comparison of the MSM(2)-AR(4) and MSIH specifications; an exercise on EM starting values and local optima.
ideas.paper: Hamilton (1989) Econometrica 57(2)
ideas.oracle_detail: statsmodels 0.15 MarkovAutoregression(order=4, switching_ar=False) on stata-press rgnp.dta reproduces the statsmodels documentation table read this session: p00 0.7547, p10 0.0959, constants -0.3588 and 1.1635, sigma2 0.5914, AR terms 0.0135, -0.0575, -0.2470, -0.2129 (llf -181.263 in the session run). Like-for-like with puremacro's MSIH class: statsmodels MarkovRegression (switching constant and variance, 4 AR lags as exog) gives llf -179.328. puremacro ms_var_fit(K=2, p=4) converges after 373 EM iterations to llf -180.553 with mu 0.97/0.40 and Sigma 0.42/1.21, which is a volatility split rather than recession dating. Hamilton (1989) itself is a second oracle (not read this session).
ideas.data_detail: https://www.stata-press.com/data/r14/rgnp.dta (returns 403 without a User-Agent header; 135 growth observations after dropping the leading NaN; includes a recession flag). Freeze it as CSV.
ideas.library_gaps: ms_var_fit is a shared-A MSIH model only (puremacro/var/regime/ms_var.py:1-12), yet its docstring says it 'reproduces the Hamilton (1989) recession dating result'. It has no MSM (switching mean with lagged regimes) specification, no constant-variance option, no multiple EM starts and no standard errors. In the session run EM stopped at a local optimum below statsmodels' MSIH llf.
ideas.plan_overlap: Not in PLAN.md.

vets.required_changes: 1. Fix ms_var_fit before the notebook. Update (mu_k, A) jointly by regime-weighted GLS with Sigma_k^{-1} weights (scalar case shown in scratch run2.py em_correct; vec-GLS for n>1). Add a test that the log-likelihood never decreases across EM iterations. Correct the docstring at ms_var.py:12-14. Re-run the example, notebook 16 and the girf and ms_var tests. 2. Add real multi-start (random P/mu starts, n_starts), a variance floor that flags degenerate spikes, and a warning or larger default when converged=False. 3. Add MSM-AR(p), Hamilton's model, for example ms_ar_fit(y, K=2, p=4) or a switching='mean' option. Use the 2^(p+1)-state expansion reusing _hamilton_filter and _kim_smoother, with scipy BFGS MLE and numerical-Hessian standard errors (about 100 lines). Do not ship an MSIH-only 'Hamilton replication'. 4. Make the primary oracle Hamilton's own Markov1.zip EXAMPLE1.OUT: parameters, standard errors, loglik -60.882447 without the constant (-181.2634 with it) and smoothed probabilities. Freeze it as a validation golden in puremacro/validation. Keep statsmodels 0.15 as a frozen secondary check only. For the MSIH comparison, align the initial-state convention (ergodic vs free pi0) and report the multiple optima and the unbounded spike. 5. Data: freeze Hamilton's GNP82.DAT as a CSV with a loader. Take the recession flag from a fetched NBER chronology or FRED USRECQ with its convention stated, not from the Stata flag. 6. Reframe the exercise as 'wrong M-step vs local optimum vs unbounded likelihood', with the smoothed-probability plot against NBER quarters.
vets.capabilities_check: ms_var_fit is at puremacro/var/regime/ms_var.py:118. It runs on univariate (T,1) input with K=2, p=4, but it fits MSIH only (a shared A with switching mu and Sigma). It has no switching-mean MSM model, no constant-variance option and no standard errors. The proposal understates a worse defect: the EM M-step is wrong. At ms_var.py:194-201 the shared A is updated by unweighted OLS of Y - smoothed@mu, and that step ignores the regime-specific Sigma_k. When the variances switch, this is not the conditional maximiser, so the algorithm is not a valid (G)EM. On Hamilton's data I ran verbose, n_iter=400: the log-likelihood fell on 72 of the steps. The default n_iter=100 stops unconverged at -180.4825, which is higher than the final value, -180.553 after 373 iterations. The endpoint is therefore not a local optimum. A corrected M-step (joint GLS for mu_k and A with weights w_tk/s2_k), started from ms_var_fit's own converged point, climbs in 136 iterations to ll -179.1567 with mu -0.061/1.208, s2 1.044/0.544 and P diagonal 0.788/0.904: a recession/expansion split. The seed does nothing. Seeds 0-5 all gave the same result, because the start is a deterministic quantile clustering plus 0.05 jitter (:155-166). NBER agreement (smoothed prob >0.5) is 61% for ms_var_fit and 92% for the corrected EM. The docstring claim at :12-14 is false. On the positive side, the private _hamilton_filter (:79) and _kim_smoother (:99) work for any number of states. With a 32x32 expanded transition matrix and scipy BFGS, a scratch MSM-AR(4) of about 60 lines reproduces Hamilton exactly in 1.9 s using numpy and scipy only (scratch run3_msm.py).

**Bug, not a local optimum.** The proposal reads the llf gap as a local optimum. It is an M-step bug. At ms_var.py:195-198 the AR matrix A is updated by unweighted OLS on Y minus (smoothed probs @ mu). The exact step would weight each observation by xi_tk/Sigma_k. On rgnp with K=2, p=4, the fit ends after 459 iterations at llf -180.5532 (tol 1e-10). At that point the likelihood gradient with respect to the AR coefficients is [-4.44, -6.55, -3.31, -3.76], while the gradients for mu and Sigma are 0. So the point is not stationary.

An exact ECM step (weighted GLS for mu and A together) converges to the same answer from three different starts: puremacro's own fixed point, a puremacro-style quantile start and a start split by the recession flag. That answer is:
- llf -179.1567 with the initial regime probabilities estimated freely (pi0 = smoothed[0])
- expansion mean 1.208, other regime -0.061
- variances 0.544 and 1.044
- P00 0.904, P11 0.788
- AR terms 0.122, 0.021, -0.135, -0.139

This matches the statsmodels MSIH optimum, llf -179.3276. statsmodels starts the filter from the ergodic probabilities, which explains the small llf difference.

ideas.question: How should an unknown initial level enter the likelihood, and does puremacro's exact-diffuse MLE match a reference implementation?
ideas.description: Promote exact_diffuse_kalman and mle_sandwich_demo using the Nile flow series. Show: finite, approximate and exact diffuse initialisation; MLE of the two variances via mle_fit with sandwich SEs; smoothed level and auxiliary residuals; the log-likelihood constant convention. The exercise adds a break dummy.

ideas.oracle_detail: Verified this session. statsmodels UnobservedComponents('llevel') with initialize_diffuse() gives MLE sigma2_eps 15098.5, sigma2_eta 1469.2 and llf -632.546. puremacro kalman_smoother(diffuse_states=[0]) plus Nelder-Mead gives the same 15098.5 and 1469.2 with loglik -633.465. The 0.919 gap equals 0.5*log(2*pi), the constant term for the diffuse observation (a convention to document). Approximate-diffuse init gives -640.99 at the same parameters. All three symbols exist and I ran them on the Nile data (whole run under 1 s). StateSpaceModel is at puremacro/state_space.py:41. kalman_filter/kalman_smoother take diffuse_states (state_space.py:227,397). The exact-diffuse update is at :113-170. mle_fit and sandwich_vcov are at numerics.py:112 and :66. Results:

ideas.title: Growth-at-Risk (Adrian, Boyarchenko and Giannone 2019) on real NFCI data, then Mexico
ideas.anchor_notebook: notebooks/09_growth_at_risk.py (simulated FCI and GDP); notebooks/49; curso T03_C_growth_at_risk
ideas.question: Do financial conditions move the lower quantiles of US four-quarter-ahead growth but not the upper ones, and does the same hold in Mexico?
ideas.description: Quarterly averages of weekly NFCI and annualised GDP growth, 1973Q1-2015Q4, with quantile regressions of h = 1 and h = 4 growth on NFCI and current growth. Fit the skewed-t, compute entropy measures, and run out-of-sample densities from 1993Q1. Mexico: GDP growth against BIS credit-to-GDP gap and policy-rate spreads (fetch_bis_macroprudential, used in no notebook).
ideas.paper: Adrian, Boyarchenko & Giannone (2019 AER) 'Vulnerable Growth'
ideas.oracle_detail: statsmodels QuantReg in the work environment gives exact qar coefficients. ABG publish figures only (quantile-slope and skewed-t plots, SR 794 checked this session: no coefficient table), so the targets are to transcribe from ABG (2019) figures; ABG's MATLAB replication package can be frozen as a second oracle.
ideas.data_detail: puremacro/datasets/data/NFCI.csv and GDPC1.csv (Chicago Fed via FRED; BEA public domain). Mexico: BIS stats API (reachable this session; BIS terms to check) and bundled OECD QNA Mexico.
ideas.library_gaps: None blocking. Check that fit_skewt_to_quantiles matches ABG's quantile-matching objective.
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

vets.required_changes:
1. Build ABG's regressions explicitly. Set y_{t+h} = (400/h)·(log GDP_{t+h} - log GDP_t), or ABG's formula once confirmed. Regress on [1, NFCI_t, g_t] over 1973Q1-2015Q4, using puremacro.regress.quantile.quantreg or _qreg. Do not use qar(horizons=(1,4)). Optionally add target='average' to qar and fix notebook 49's h=4 call.
2. Upgrade puremacro/gar/skewt.py: vectorized CDF/ppf, nu >= 1 (or ABG's integer grid), least_squares with multi-start, and a stored match residual. Test it against an independent quad-based quantile oracle. Assert on the residual, not on exact pass-through, because current-vintage 2008Q4 quantiles are outside the skew-t family's reach (best SSR 0.42).
3. Add relative_entropy(f_cond, g_uncond, side) following ABG eq. 5-6, with the unconditional density from a constant-only QR plus skew-t, and add longrise. Rename or re-document SkewTFit.downside_entropy as Shannon entropy, and correct notebook 09's claim about it.
4. For OOS, use forecast.density.pit plus log scores and a GDP-only benchmark. Label the KS/Berkowitz bands as substitutes for Rossi-Sekhposyan, or implement RS critical values from the paper, not from memory.
5. Oracle: present statsmodels agreement as a solver check only. Use qualitative ABG targets, cited to SR794 figure numbers: lower-quantile NFCI slopes strongly negative, upper ones near zero or positive, OOS close to in-sample. Ask the user to download openICPSR E113169V1 (login needed) and freeze ABG's data vintage and MATLAB outputs, run on local R2026a, as the quantitative oracle.
6. Keep runtime to minutes. Use the faster fitter or cache the fits. The Spanish twin doubles the runtime.
7. Drop Mexico from this rebuild, or make it a follow-up that first fixes fetch_bis_macroprudential (URL key Q.{cc}.P.A., CG_DTYPE A/B/C), freezes the BIS Mexico credit gap with attribution, and uses the tracked curso Mexico GDP (1993Q1-). It must frame the credit gap as a slow vulnerability measure, not a financial-conditions index, and it must say that about 130 quarters, dominated by 1995 and 2009, give a weak 5% quantile.
8. Open the notebook with what is new relative to course/23, curso T03_C and notebook 49, and cross-link them.
vets.capabilities_check:
All four symbols exist at the cited lines: qar at puremacro/gar/qar.py:28, fit_skewt_to_quantiles at puremacro/gar/skewt.py:259, lp_quantile at puremacro/lp/quantile.py:49 and fetch_bis_macroprudential at puremacro/fetch/financial.py:525. Smoke runs (scratch wf/gar-abg-review/smoke1-6.py) found five problems.
(1) qar cannot produce ABG's h=4 target. SR794 p.7 defines y_{t+h} as the annualized average growth between t and t+h, but qar regresses single-quarter growth at t+h (qar.py:111, y_h = y[max_lag + h:]). On bundled data, qar(h=4) reproduced the single-quarter-at-t+4 regression exactly (tau=.95 NFCI slope +0.757 in both), while the ABG average target gives +1.227. qar also drops the first usable row, because it starts at t=p. Workaround: build the design by hand and fit it with the public puremacro.regress.quantile.quantreg (regress/quantile.py:691), which matched the LP to 3 d.p., or with lp.quantile._qreg. Alternatively, add a target='average' option to qar.
(2) fit_skewt_to_quantiles has the right objective but the wrong parameter space and optimizer. SR794 eq. 4 matches the 5/25/75/95 quantiles with nu in Z+. The library clamps nu to at least 2.5 (skewt.py:83, :302) and runs Nelder-Mead with maxiter=200 (:263, :319). success=False at all three ABG Figure-7 dates. At 2008Q4 its quantile-match SSR is 1.54; an independent fitter over integer nu (tan-grid CDF plus least_squares) reaches 0.42 at nu=2, a value the library cannot use. Exact fit is not attainable on current-vintage quantiles either, so 'passes through all four quantiles' cannot be asserted.
(3) The fitter is slow: 3.1 s per fit, because the CDF is a Python loop of 600-point trapz calls inside brentq. The full ABG program needs about 344 in-sample fits plus about 360 OOS fits (two models), roughly 37 min in CPython per language edition, and longer in Pyodide.
(4) SkewTFit.downside_entropy (skewt.py:237) computes the Shannon entropy of the fitted density's lower half, not ABG's relative entropy. ABG eq. 5-6 is the KL-type divergence of the unconditional density g, taken from the constant-only QR plus skew-t, relative to the conditional f, below and above the conditional median. At 2008Q4 the library value is 1.46; my ABG L^D is 1.02 and L^U is -0.13. There is no upside entropy, no longrise, and no test of either. expected_shortfall matches ABG's SF definition.
(5) OOS tools: forecast/density.py:23 pit, the KS test and berkowitz_test exist, and the log score is trivial to compute. Rossi-Sekhposyan PIT bands are absent.
Mexico: fetch_bis_macroprudential returns an empty frame. Run with an in-memory fetch (no repo writes), its _BIS_CREDIT_GAP_URL (financial.py:195, key Q.ALL.ALL.ALL) returns HTTP 404. The live CSV column is CG_DTYPE with codes A/B/C, but the code looks for CG_DATA_TYPE/DATA_TYPE and maps GAP/RAT/TRD (financial.py:596, :611-617). The key Q.MX.P.A.C works (1990Q4-2026Q1). The function has no policy-rate spreads; those need fetch_policy_rates (:395) or compute_sovereign_spreads (:851).
vets.oracle_check:
statsmodels QuantReg is a solver check, not a replication oracle. statsmodels 0.15 in the work env matched puremacro's LP _qreg on 15 regressions (targets y1, y4-average and single-quarter t+4, each at 5 taus, n=172) with max coefficient difference 9.4e-5. The ABG targets are figure-level only. I read NY Fed SR794 (Sep 2016, rev. Nov 2017) this session: 14 figures, no tables. It confirms the specifics: NFCI is the quarterly average of weekly values under the FRED week-attribution rule (fn 4), the regressors are current GDP growth plus NFCI, the skew-t is Azzalini-Capitanio, and the OOS exercise is an expanding window from 1973Q1-1992Q4 with first forecasts for 1993Q1 and 1993Q4, run to 2015Q4, evaluated with predictive scores and PITs with Rossi-Sekhposyan (2017) bands. The Figure 4 bands come from a VAR(4) bootstrap with 1000 draws.
Replication package: the AEA article page lists doi 10.3886/E113169V1. The openICPSR page loads (licenseId 16), but the file list and downloads require a login, so I could not verify its contents or data vintage. It needs the user to download it manually. MATLAB R2026a is available locally to run it.
Qualitative target: the asymmetry reproduces on current-vintage data (my estimates, 1973Q1-2015Q4). h=1 NFCI slopes at tau .05/.25/.50/.75/.95 are -2.42/-1.68/-0.78/-0.76/-0.03. h=4 average-target slopes are -2.21/-1.23/-0.67/-0.27/+1.23.
vets.data_check:
US data is sufficient but a revised vintage.
- puremacro/datasets/data/NFCI.csv is weekly, dated on Fridays, 1971-01-08 to 2026-07-17 (ABG's vintage started in 1973). Dating by the Friday reproduces ABG's FRED week-to-quarter rule.
- GDPC1.csv runs 1947Q1-2026Q1. 1973Q1-2015Q4 gives 172 rows with no NaNs.
- The NFCI vintage differs from ABG's (revised index), so only qualitative comparison is possible unless the openICPSR data are frozen. The exact ABG growth formula (log vs compound annualization) is unverified; the package code would settle it.
- I did not verify Chicago Fed reuse terms this session.
Mexico:
- 'Bundled OECD QNA Mexico' is wrong for the repo cache: data/raw/sdmx.oecd.org is gitignored (.gitignore:44). A tracked copy does exist at curso/notebooks/data_curso/oecd_qna_mex_componentes_VQ.csv (B1GQ_S1 volume, 1993Q1-2026Q1, 133 quarters).
- No BIS data is cached or tracked. The BIS Mexico credit gap (Q.MX.P.A.C) is reachable from Python, 1990Q4-2026Q1, but would need a frozen CSV.
- BIS terms page (read this session): limited extracts, non-commercial use, BIS cited as source. The separate 'About BIS statistics' terms were not read.
- Showcase notebooks run offline, so every series must be frozen.
vets.novelty_check:
Real-NFCI growth-at-risk is not new in the repo.
- notebooks/course/23_growth_at_risk_es.py already runs qar on real NFCI plus A191RL1Q225SBEA (1971Q1-2019Q4, p=4, h=1), skew-t fits at 2005Q2 vs 2008Q4, the GaR fan, lp_quantile and ALFRED real-time vintages. It is Spanish only.
- curso/notebooks/T03_C_growth_at_risk.ipynb section 4 is 'Empirical Growth-at-Risk with Real US Macroeconomic and Financial Data' (GDPC1 plus NFCI qar); section 5 is historical stress.
- notebooks/49 uses real nfci through load_macro_monthly with qar at h=4. That is the wrong target: a single quarter, as noted above.
- notebooks/09 and puremacro/examples/vulnerable_growth.py are simulated only. The replication and validation galleries have no ABG case.
- PLAN.md and REVIEW.md do not overlap.
Genuinely new: ABG's exact specification (h=4 average target, [1, NFCI, g] regressors, 4-quantile skew-t each quarter), time series of conditional quantiles and densities (Figs 5-8), relative entropy and longrise (Fig 9), recursive OOS with a GDP-only benchmark, predictive scores and PIT (Figs 10-11), and any Mexico GaR. BIS credit-gap data appears in no notebook.

ideas.title: How rare are uncertainty shocks? Bloom (2009) and JLN (2015) with bundled indices, extended to Mexico
ideas.question: How many uncertainty episodes does each proxy flag, and do Bloom-style VAR responses of IP survive swapping the stock-volatility indicator for macro uncertainty, EPU or GPR, in the US and in Mexico?
ideas.description: (1) Rebuild Bloom's volatility-shock indicator (volatility > 1.65 s.d. above its HP trend) and audit puremacro's hard-coded event list. (2) Count JLN months above 1.65 s.d. (session check on the bundled jln_macro_usa.csv, 2026 vintage: 54 of 618 months for 1960:07-2011:12). (3) Run Bloom's 8-variable monthly VAR on FRED data. (4) Mexico: EPU Mexico and GPRC_MEX shocks to Mexican IP (oecd_mei_mex_log_ip) and the BIS policy rate, as LP and Cholesky VAR.
ideas.paper: Bloom (2009 Econometrica); Jurado, Ludvigson & Ng (2015 AER); Baker, Bloom & Davis (2016 QJE); Caldara & Iacoviello (2022 AER)
ideas.oracle_detail: Read this session in JLN NBER WP 19456, PDF p.6: over 1960:07-2011:12, macro uncertainty exceeds or comes close to exceeding 1.65 s.d. in only 49 of 618 months, in three episodes (1973-74, 1981-82, 2007-09); half-life 53 months against 4 for stock volatility; Bloom's 17 dates are listed in his Table A.1. Bloom's IRF (Figure) and Table A.1 dates: to transcribe from Bloom (2009). Second oracle: Bloom's Econometrica replication files (numbers only).
ideas.data_detail: puremacro/replication/data/speccurve17_panel.csv (epu, wui, jln, vix, ip, emp, ffr) and curso jln_macro_usa.csv, epu_mex_mensual.csv (to 2023-02), oecd_mei_mex_log_ip.csv. The cached data/raw/www.policyuncertainty.com/media_All_Country_Data.xlsx has Mexico, Chile and Brazil EPU to 2026-07. data/raw/www.matteoiacoviello.com/gpr_files_data_gpr_export.xls has GPRC_MEX/BRA/CHL/COL/ARG (columns checked this session). EPU and GPR: cite and follow the site terms. Pre-1986 S&P volatility for Bloom's indicator needs Shiller's data; VXO/VIX are subject to Cboe terms.
ideas.library_gaps: puremacro/instruments/literature/bloom_2009.py docstring says '17 dates from Table A.1 plus October 2008', but BLOOM_2009_EVENTS has 17 entries including 2008-10-01; verify against Table A.1. examples/bloom2009.py:41 and examples/caldara_iacoviello.py:23 need data/processed/panel_Q.parquet, which is absent, so tests/test_replication_bloom2009.py and the Caldara-Iacoviello smoke test skip, and the bloom test carries an xfail.
ideas.plan_overlap: Overlaps the 09-20 'uncertainty/coverage lab' and existing notebook 17; keep it as the replication-card version.

vets.required_changes:
1. Replace "8-variable VAR on FRED data" with Bloom's own VARDATA.csv from the Econometrica supplement (VAR.zip), bundled as puremacro/replication/data/bloom2009_vardata.csv with provenance and a terms check. Assert parity with irf.dta "kitchen" oirfcvolatblclipm, max|diff| < 1e-3 over h=0..36 (the session got 2.0e-5; trough -0.976 at h=4). Optionally add the do-file's robustness rows as further oracles (fkitchen, okitchen, vkitchen, hfkitchen, ldkitchen).

2. Fix BLOOM_2009_EVENTS: change 2008-10-01 to 2008-03-01, citing vardata_2008.do. Correct the docstring, the loader span (1962-07 to 2008-06), the _catalog.py description and test_bloom_2009.py. Consider exporting the first-month and oil/war/terror lists.

3. Step (1): run the mechanical rule on Bloom's VOLATBL and report the result as-is: 21 runs, 16 of 17 recovered, OPEC II at z=1.63. Present this as "the 17 dates are curated".

4. JLN: cite NBER WP 19456 by page and footnote (49/618 "exceeds or comes close", 3 episodes, half-life 53 vs 4, fn 18's 5 HP episodes). Assert only 3 episodes and a half-life near 53. Show 54 against 49, and the altered fn-18 episodes, as vintage drift.

5. Do not redo T01_C §3 (the VIX rule for 1990-2026, the LP on the indicator, the VIX/JLN/EPU innovation LPs); link to it. The proxy swap should happen inside Bloom's VAR on his sample, with JLN h1 in place of the indicator.

6. Mexico: bundle a CSV with EPU_MEX to 2026-07 and GPRC_MEX. Use IR3TIB01MXM156N, since no BIS Mexico rate is bundled. End the sample at 2019-12 or handle 2020 explicitly. Label the section exploratory, with no oracle. Pass controls to lp_hac lagged, because it enters them contemporaneously.

7. Drop identify_maxshare from the capabilities list.

8. Optionally retarget tests/test_replication_bloom2009.py to the bundled CSV so it stops skipping.
vets.capabilities_check:
All four symbols exist with the stated signatures: cholesky_svar at puremacro/var/identify/cholesky.py:181 (residual bootstrap; n_boot=0 gives the point estimate only), lp_hac at puremacro/lp/jorda.py:18, identify_maxshare at puremacro/var/identify/maxshare.py:272, and hp_filter at puremacro/cycles.py:451 (the lamb argument accepts 129600).

I smoke-ran Bloom's baseline "kitchen" VAR on Bloom's own Econometrica replication data. The recipe was: HP-filter every variable with lambda 129,600, then drop months without VOLATBL (552 months, 1962:07-2008:06). The variable order is [clstock, clean, cffr, clwage, clcpi, choursm, clempm, clipm], with 12 lags. I took the IP response to a unit shock in the indicator, in %. It matches Bloom's Stata irf.dta (oirfcvolatblclipm) to a maximum absolute difference of 2.0e-5 over h=0..36. The trough is -0.976 at h=4, and Bloom's own +/-1 s.e. at h=4 is [-1.374, -0.577]. A 300-draw bootstrap takes 2.3 s.

The Mexico part also runs, over 1997-2019 in a Cholesky VAR [log EPU_MEX, log IP, 3-month interbank rate] with p=6. The IP trough is -0.58 at h=15 (90% band -0.79 to -0.19). The same VAR with GPRC_MEX gives a trough of -0.12 with a band of [-0.42, +0.26].

identify_maxshare is not used by any step of the plan. The notebook needs no new estimator.
vets.oracle_check:
The oracle is obtainable, and stronger than proposed.

(1) Bloom's Econometrica supplement is downloadable with Python from econometricsociety.org: ".../impact-uncertainty-shocks/supp/6248_data and programs_0.zip". Inside it, VAR.zip holds VARDATA.csv, vardata_2008.do and irf.dta, and irf.dta contains his IRF numbers for 11 specifications. This is an exact numeric oracle, and puremacro matches it to 2e-5. Transcribing numbers from the figure is not needed.

(2) The 17 event dates come from Bloom's do-file (vardata_2008.do, "Maximum month timing"). The 17th date is 2008-03; the first-month timing list gives 2007-08 instead. I also read the 2007 NBER WP w13385: its Table A.1 has only 16 events and its sample is 1963:07-2005:07, so the WP should not be cited for the dates. I did not read the published Table A.1 itself.

(3) The JLN claims check out against NBER WP 19456 (Sept 2013), as read this session:
- Intro: "exceeds (or come close to exceeding) 1.65 standard deviations from its mean a total of only 49 (out of 618) months", in three episodes. The half-life is 53 months, against 4 for VXO.
- Footnote 18 adds a second checkable number. Under Bloom's HP criterion, U(1) has 5 episodes: 1973:09-1974:11, 1980:02-1982:02, 1990:01, 2001:10 and 2008:07.

The bundled 2026 vintage does not reproduce these numbers exactly:
- 54 months strictly above 1.65 sd (57 above 1.5 sd).
- The same 3 episodes.
- AR(1) half-life 53.1, which matches.
- The HP criterion gives 5 runs, but different ones: no 1990:01, 1980-82 splits into two, and 2001-09/10 appears.

So the JLN comparison has to be framed as vintage drift, not parity. I did not read the AER 2015 published text, and the original 2015 vintage was not obtained.
vets.data_check:
Bundled and tracked:
- curso/notebooks/data_curso/jln_macro_usa.csv (1960:07-2025:12, h1/h3/h12).
- epu_mex_mensual.csv, which ends 2023-02.

Novelty is partial. curso/notebooks/T01_C_high_frequency.ipynb §3 (cells 18-27) already covers:

ideas.title: Ins and outs of unemployment: Shimer (2012) for the US and a 4-state formal/informal version for Mexico
ideas.question: How much of unemployment variation comes from job finding rather than separations, and how does informality change the answer in Mexico?
ideas.description: US: Shimer's job-finding and separation rates from UNEMPLOY, UEMPLT5 and CLF16OV with time-aggregation correction, the steady-state decomposition and beta-shares, checked against CPS gross flows. Mexico: monthly F/I/U/N matrices recovered from the ENOE 3-month transitions (principal-log method), steady-state shares and a variance decomposition across formal, informal and unemployment margins.

vets.oracle_check:
The US oracle is obtainable and strong, but it is not the one the proposal names. Everything below was read this session from fetched sources.
(a) Shimer's posted data (sites.google.com/site/robertshimer/research/flows, downloaded via Google Drive): quarterly job-finding probability F and exit probability X, 1948Q1-2007Q1. The page describes them as 'quarterly averages of monthly transition probabilities, corrected for time-aggregation'. Terms of use require the statement 'This data was constructed by Robert Shimer. For additional details, please see Shimer (2012).'
  - 1948-1993, our series from bundled FRED data: corr 1.000, max |dF| 0.002, max |dX| 0.0003.
  - 1994-2007: corr F 0.95. Mean F is 0.415 vs posted 0.438 with the constant 1.1 (footnote 38 of the Shimer RED 2012 author PDF says multiplying by 1.1 after 1994 'delivers very similar results'). A factor of 1.158 = 43.2/37.3 (short-term shares in the incoming rotation groups vs the full sample, RED p.28-29) matches the mean exactly (0.437).
  - Decomposing the posted series gives 0.76/0.24 against NBER WP 13421 Table 1 column 1 (0.76/0.25, 1948-2007).
(b) RED 2012 author version (Feb 17 2012, from Shimer's Drive), Table 1 on PDF p.34: 1948-2010 0.77/0.24; 1967-2010 0.83/0.17; 1976-2010 0.85/0.15; 1987-2010 0.90/0.10; men 25-54 0.69/0.32. Method: regress HP(1e5) quarterly averages of xbar/(xbar+f_t) on the actual u_{t+1}/l_{t+1}, not on u*. Ours with factor 1.1: 0.83/0.22, 0.88/0.18, 0.91/0.15, 0.98/0.09 (filtering the full sample once). That is about 0.06-0.08 high after 2007, so it needs a stated tolerance.
(c) RED Table 2 column 2 (1987-2010, p.35): EU 0.17, EI -0.05, UE 0.51, UI 0.16, IE 0.09, IU 0.13. BLS flows 1990-2010 with logm time aggregation give 0.15, -0.03, 0.49, 0.14, 0.07, 0.10. Every hazard is within 0.03, which makes this the right participation-margin oracle.
(d) Elsby-Hobijn-Şahin, FRBSF WP 2013-05, Table 3 (samples end Feb 2012): unadjusted flows from 1978 give U-E 57.4, U-N 35.5, E-N 0.8. The abstract says 'around one-third'. Their flows start in 1967 or 1978 (Shimer microdata and Ritter), and they use a dynamic non-steady-state decomposition with margin-error correction. Bundled BLS flows start in 1990 and neither of those methods is in the library, so EHS can only be a qualitative oracle. I did not check the published JME numbers.
(e) Bosch-Maloney (2010) was not fetched. Their ENEU 1987-2004 urban sample has no overlap with ENOE 2005-2024 (loaders not ported, labor_flows_enoe.py:44-49), so it cannot be a numeric oracle. The Mexico part has no independent published target.

vets.capabilities_check:
panel_lp_dk (puremacro/lp/panel_dk.py:19, engine _panel_helpers.py:207-276) exists and works. In a smoke test on a 17x40 synthetic panel its betas matched linearmodels 7.0 PanelOLS(entity+time FE, cov_type='kernel') to 4 decimals. Its DK SEs came out about 4-5% smaller than linearmodels', which is consistent with linearmodels' FE degrees-of-freedom correction. It runs in about 0.03 s.

panel_lp_iv (puremacro/lp/panel_iv.py:14) is NOT a valid 2SLS:
- Its first stage (lines 45-50) regresses x on z plus contemporaneous controls only.
- It sets x_hat = pi_z*z (line 54), then runs panel_lp on x_hat with lags of x_hat and y (line 55). The first stage therefore omits exogenous controls that the second stage includes.
- Its SE is the cluster SE from x_hat residuals, not residuals built from actual x, and there is no DK option.
- first_stage_f (line 58) is a single cluster-based number for all horizons.

Two tests show the effect:
- Synthetic DGP: beta is off by 1-4% and the SE is understated by 28-38% against linearmodels IV2SLS with dummy FE (h=1: 0.085 vs 0.117).
- Real annual GLP-style panel (DGLP Table A1 plus OECD EO GDPV and NLGXQ, 1978-2009): panel_lp_iv gives -1.07 at h=1 and -1.38 at h=5. A consistent 2SLS with lags of x and y gives -0.74 and -0.95. With the very same second-stage controls it gives -0.90 and -1.14. The reported F is 16.5, against a partial F of 71-91.

Existing tests only check that the F column is present and >5 (tests/test_lp/test_panel_parity.py:101-121) and row-order invariance (tests/test_dgp_adversarial.py:92). Single-country lp_iv (iv.py:367) is sound but not panel.

The descriptive part reproduces GLP's qualitative point on real data:
- OLS on dCAPB: +0.23 at h=0 (expansionary).
- Narrative consolidation with DK SEs: -0.20 at h=0, -0.54 at h=1, -0.73 at h=5 (90% band -1.40 to -0.07).
- Split: tax-based -1.06 vs spending-based -0.22 at h=1.
These are smoke numbers, not citable.

vets.capabilities_check: Smoke-ran all four on RR 1969-1996 shocks summed to quarters plus current FRED GDPC1, GDPDEF and FEDFUNDS. Core LPs take 0.14 s. (1) lp_state_dep (puremacro/lp/state_dep.py:107) exists and is exported. Its logistic F=1/(1+exp(-gamma(s-c)/sd)) with c on the raw scale (state_dep.py:47-95) is exactly TT's transition, so theta=3 and c = 20th percentile of z are expressible. But it interacts only the shock: F*x and (1-F)*x at state_dep.py:218-222, with unregimed controls, no F level term and no trend. Passing a trend through controls= fails with LinAlgError "X'X is singular (rank 6 of 7)", because the contemporaneous value and lags of the trend are collinear. TT eq. (1) needs a linear trend plus a regime-specific intercept and controls. This matters: with shock-only interaction and no trend, the recession GDP response is positive (+0.075 cumulative at h=12). The full TT spec, hand-rolled with inference._ols_helpers.ols_hac, gives -0.010. TT Section IV.B itself reports the no-trend recession IRF as uniformly positive. (2) lp_smooth_transition_irf (state_dep.py:253) is unfit and should not be used. It imports statsmodels at :321, which breaks the Pyodide contract. It regresses the level y_{t+h} (:330), standardizes the state on each horizon's own sample (:349), uses a different HAC bandwidth (:368), and is not exported from puremacro.lp. (3) lp_asymmetric (puremacro/lp/asymmetric.py:25) matches TT's max/min split, but has no trend and no FFR-impact scaling. (4) lp_hac (jorda.py:18) works. There are two unlisted pieces. lp_state_dep_iv (state_dep.py:395) can do TT's per-regime scaling to 1 pp FFR, but the recession first-stage F is only 0.3-1.3 (weak). puremacro.inference.moving_block_bootstrap can stand in for TT's block bootstrap. There is no time-series Driscoll-Kraay estimator across horizons (DK exists only in the panel code: regress/lp.py, lp/panel_dk.py). RR eq. (2) is a monthly ADL with 11 dummies, 24 lags of dy and 36 lags of S, and no helper exists for it. I hand-rolled it in about 20 lines of numpy.

The coefficients match Table 1 (p.1063) to 3 decimals: constant 0.171 (0.141), initial rate -0.021 (0.012), dY0 innovation 0.152 (0.030), unemployment -0.048 (0.021), R2 0.28, N=263. Eq. (2) on the appendix's LNIPNSA reproduces Table 3 (p.1070), e.g. S1 0.0038 (0.0018), S10 -0.0047 (0.0018), dy12 0.287 (0.060), N=324, R2 0.86. It also reproduces the text (p.1069): -4.3% flat over months 22-27 (mine -4.23/-4.31/-4.34) and -1.7% at month 48 (mine -1.69). TT side: I read the published version (LSE eprint 69214). Its numbers are cumulative GDP responses at h=12. Table 1 baseline (nonlinear shocks, 1969-2002): expansion -0.0751, recession -0.0240. Table 4 (linearly identified shocks): expansion -0.0939, recession -0.0257. Table 2 (sign): positive -0.0754, negative -0.0269. My approximation (full spec, RR to 1996, today's vintage) gives expansion -0.125 vs recession -0.010, and positive -0.099 vs negative +0.077. The ordering matches, the levels do not. So TT can only be a qualitative, ordering-based oracle: TT's shocks come from a state-dependent RR regression extended to 2002 (eq. 3, p.51) on a ~2014 Philadelphia Fed vintage. The proposed second oracle is misdescribed. TT's openICPSR package (doi 10.3886/E114109V1) is MATLAB, not Stata (runme_aejm_final.m, generate_shocks.m, data.xlsx, NeweyWestDK.m). Downloading it requires an ICPSR login, so the build cannot use it; at most it is a one-off manual cross-check in local MATLAB.
