ideas.title: Peso-dollar and US yields: GARCH and DCC on real data (Engle 2002)
ideas.question: How does the correlation between the peso and US yields or equities move in stress episodes (1994-95, 2008, 2016, 2020)?
ideas.description: Fit daily GARCH(1,1) and DCC(1,1) on MXN/USD returns, 10-year Treasury changes and a US equity factor. Compare with the arch package fits and report persistence, half-lives and the correlation path.
ideas.paper: Engle (2002 JBES) 'Dynamic Conditional Correlation'
ideas.oracle_detail: The arch package (already the golden source in puremacro/validation/goldens/garch.json) gives GARCH parameters and conditional variances. For DCC, R rmgarch dccfit output as numbers only. Engle (2002) empirical tables: to transcribe (only as a qualitative anchor; the data differ).
ideas.data_detail: FRED DEXMXUS (Board H.10, public domain) and DGS10; equities via the Ken French factors (fetch/kenfrench_industry.py; free with citation). Avoid Yahoo and S&P redistribution.
ideas.library_gaps: dcc_fit supports only a zero mean; there are no Student-t innovations.
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

vets.required_changes:
1. Fix the library-gaps text. dcc_fit supports mean="constant" (dcc.py:60, 114). Real gaps: no Student-t, no standard errors, no public GJR (a private one exists at lp/_garch_utils.py:48), and mean is demeaned with the sample mean rather than estimated jointly.
2. Oracle for DCC: replace R rmgarch, which is not installed. Use the MFE Toolbox dcc.m (bashtage/mfe-toolbox) in the local MATLAB R2026a and freeze its numbers. Add the Engle (2002) Appendix-1 RATE-DJ anchor (alpha 0.037372, beta 0.950269 from dccfinal.pdf): -ΔDGS30 against the CRSP market, 1990-03 to 2000-03, reproduces a=0.041, b=0.947, positive ρ around 0.35, negative in summer 1998 and near zero in Q1 2000. Label it a proxy replication because the DJIA is not freely available.
3. Oracle for GARCH: compare with arch mean='Zero' on the demeaned series, not "Constant". Compare parameters on the full sample and σ paths after the 200-observation burn used in cases_garch.py:29. State that σ²₀ differs (sample variance vs arch backcast).
4. Sample: estimate from 1996 onward. Handle 1994-95 (band regime, then 13-20% daily devaluation moves) either by filtering it with the post-1996 parameters or by making it an explicit structural-break lesson (full-sample MXN persistence 0.918 vs 0.985). Do not treat it as one more stress episode inside the fit.
5. Timing: say that DEXMXUS is the noon New York rate and the other series are end of day, which attenuates daily correlations (daily -0.30 vs weekly -0.42 for MXN with the market; lag-1 correlation -0.17). Add a weekly Wednesday-to-Wednesday DCC as a robustness check.
6. Data: freeze DEXMXUS, DGS10 and DGS30 slices, plus Ken French daily Mkt-RF+RF with attribution, as CSVs with FUENTES entries. Write a daily-factor loader, because kenfrench_industry.py is monthly industry data. Define bond return as minus the yield change.
7. Fit DCC once per specification; do not refit per episode. Report episode means of R_t from the single fit. The notebook must ship as an EN/ES pair.
vets.capabilities_check:
Both symbols exist and ran on the real data. garch11_fit is at puremacro/garch/fit.py:46 and dcc_fit at puremacro/garch/dcc.py:60 (exported in puremacro/garch/__init__.py).

Smoke run (scratch .../wf/garch-dcc-mxn-rev/smoke.py and smoke2.py): daily 100·Δlog DEXMXUS, 100·ΔDGS10 (bp) and Ken French Mkt-RF+RF, aligned on common days, 1993-11-09 to 2026-08-31, T=8176.
- GARCH fits take 0.02-0.03 s each and all converge.
- The 3-variable DCC takes 9.1 s at T=7646. The 2-variable DCC takes 8.2 s. The cost is the Python loops at dcc.py:32 and dcc.py:48, so Pyodide will be several times slower.
- A Nelder-Mead polish from the L-BFGS-B point left (a,b)=(0.021056, 0.973432) unchanged, so dcc.py:129 reaches the optimum.
- Results from 1996 on: MXN persistence 0.985 (half-life 45 days), 10-year yield 0.994 (113 days), market 0.980 (34 days). DCC a+b=0.9945.
- Mean correlations by episode, MXN with 10y / MXN with market: GFC 2008-09 to 2009-03 -0.27 / -0.30; taper 2013 +0.07 / -0.36; Nov-Dec 2016 +0.24 / -0.21; COVID Mar-Apr 2020 -0.38 / -0.50; calm 2017 +0.07 / -0.13. The sign flip between flight-to-quality episodes and US-rate or election shocks is a real teaching result.
- Half-life is not a library field, but log(0.5)/log(α+β) is one line.
vets.oracle_check:
GARCH: the arch oracle (8.0.0 in the work env) works, but only when the specification matches. garch11_fit(mean="constant") subtracts the sample mean (fit.py:112), while arch "Constant" estimates mu jointly by maximum likelihood. On the same data that gives visibly different fits: from 1995-03, MXN log-likelihood -7140.13 (puremacro) vs -7085.38 (arch) and persistence 0.9845 vs 0.9825. With arch mean='Zero' on the demeaned series the two agree: MXN α 0.13120 vs 0.13123 and β 0.85349 vs 0.85348; 10y α 0.03947 vs 0.03934; log-likelihood gaps 0.02-0.6. The remaining gap is the starting variance (sample variance vs arch's backcast), as documented at puremacro/validation/cases_garch.py:24-29.

DCC: the proposed R rmgarch oracle cannot be obtained here, because Rscript and R are not installed and there is no Python DCC package (arch has none). A feasible independent oracle is Kevin Sheppard's MFE Toolbox multivariate/dcc.m, which I confirmed exists at github bashtage/mfe-toolbox through the GitHub API, run in the local MATLAB_R2026a.app and frozen to numbers.

Engle 2002 is better than a qualitative anchor. Its Appendix 1 (read this session from pages.stern.nyu.edu/~rengle/dccfinal.pdf using pypdf) reports for stocks-bonds ("RATE DJ", ten years of daily data ending March 2000, bond return = minus the change in the 30-year yield) a mean-reverting DCC with alphaDCC=0.037372 and betaDCC=0.950269. The paper's text says these correlations run around 0.4, turn highly negative in summer 1998 and are about zero at the end of the sample. dcc_fit on -ΔDGS30 against the CRSP market (Ken French), 1990-03-23 to 2000-03-22 (T=2501), gives a=0.0408 and b=0.9465: mean ρ 0.35, Jul-Oct 1998 -0.26 (minimum -0.50 on 1998-09-14), Q1 2000 +0.04. The series are proxies (CRSP value-weighted rather than the DJIA, FRED constant-maturity rather than the benchmark bond), so this is a partial replication. It also removes the proposal's stated risk of having no published target.
vets.data_check:
DEXMXUS (daily from 1993-11-08, noon buying rates in New York) and DGS10 are both licensed "public domain: citation requested"; I confirmed this on the FRED series pages fetched this session. Both download without a key from fredgraph.csv (158 KB and 269 KB).

The Ken French daily factors file (F-F_Research_Data_Factors_daily_CSV.zip, 178 KB, built from the 202608 CRSP database) ends with "Copyright 2026 Eugene F. Fama and Kenneth R. French". Bundling it is possible only with attribution under the repo's data-rights policy (curso/notebooks/data_curso/FUENTES.md:12,196). There is precedent: Cboe's VIXCLS is already bundled.

The fetcher the proposal cites is wrong. puremacro/fetch/kenfrench_industry.py downloads monthly 30-industry portfolios, not daily factors, so a small daily-factor loader or frozen CSV is needed. Notebooks that must run under Pyodide read frozen CSVs (puremacro/datasets/data, notebooks/course/data), so the sliced series have to be frozen and registered. Nothing in the repo uses DEXMXUS, DGS10 or DGS30 yet.

Three data problems the proposal missed:
1. The peso traded in a band until December 1994. The largest daily moves are 19-20% (1994-12-22, 1994-12-27) and 18% (1995-03-10). A full-sample GARCH gives MXN persistence 0.918 (half-life 8 days) against 0.985 from 1996, so 1994-95 cannot sit inside a single-regime fit.
2. Timing does not line up: FX is fixed at noon in New York, while the yield and equity data are end of day. dMXN_t correlates -0.304 with same-day market returns but -0.169 with the previous day's, and the weekly (Wednesday) correlation is -0.42 against -0.30 daily. Daily DCC therefore attenuates the peso-equity correlation.
3. DGS10 changes are in yield units. Engle defines bond return as minus the yield change, so the sign convention has to be fixed.
vets.novelty_check:
Novel, with partial overlap.
- notebooks/08_garch_volatility.py and the example puremacro/examples/dcc_volatility.py use simulated data only.
- notebooks/27_garch_midas_macro_risk.py is simulated GARCH-MIDAS.
- notebooks/course/03_riesgo_incertidumbre_es.py:243-253 fits GARCH to quarterly GDP innovations.
- curso/notebooks/T03_B_garch_volatility.ipynb already fits real daily VIX with arch GARCH and GJR, including stress-regime subsamples (cells 24 and 29: 2008 GFC, COVID). So "GARCH on real data across stress episodes" is partly covered.
- No notebook, course file, example, replication or validation case fits DCC on real data or uses DEXMXUS or DGS10.
- PLAN.md has no overlap; its only Mexico item is Aguiar-Gopinath 2007, which is unrelated.
- The Engle (2002) stocks-bonds anchor is not replicated anywhere.

ideas.title: A Taylor rule for Banxico, benchmarked on Clarida-Galí-Gertler (2000)
ideas.anchor_notebook: curso T01_C_high_frequency (Mexican LP-IV with the Banxico announcement direction, cells 35-37); notebooks/66_optimal_policy_cgg1999_replication.py (model side)
ideas.question: Did Banxico's reaction to expected inflation exceed one after inflation targeting (2001 onward), as CGG found for the post-Volcker Fed?
ideas.description: Forward-looking GMM Taylor rules with smoothing: US pre- and post-1979 samples for the published anchor, then Mexico 2001-2019 with the BIS policy rate, CPI inflation and an IP gap. Report Hansen J and weak-IV diagnostics.
ideas.paper: Clarida, Galí & Gertler (2000 QJE) 'Monetary Policy Rules and Macroeconomic Stability'
ideas.oracle_detail: CGG (2000) Table II coefficients (beta, gamma, rho) for the pre- and post-Volcker samples: to transcribe. For Mexico there is no verified published target, so the oracle is internal plus statsmodels/linearmodels IV2SLS on the same data as independent software.
ideas.data_detail: The BIS WS_CBPOL M.MX CSV returned 200 this session with no token ('From 21 Jan 2008 onwards: Central Bank target...'); Banxico SIE needs a token. Bundled curso CPALTT01MXM659N (12-month inflation to 2024-07), oecd_mei_mex_log_ip.csv, IR3TIB01MXM156N. US: FRED FEDFUNDS, GDPDEF, GDPPOT.
ideas.library_gaps: No public single-equation linear GMM/2SLS estimator: tsls_hac in puremacro/inference/_ols_helpers.py:52 is private, and lp_iv at h=0 is a workaround. fetch_policy_rates appears in no notebook.
ideas.plan_overlap: Complements PLAN notebook 66 (the CGG 1999 model); not listed.

vets.required_changes:
1. Add a public puremacro.inference linear_gmm (or iv_gmm). Scope: k endogenous regressors, included exogenous variables, two-step and iterated weighting, Bartlett HAC with explicit L, J with its df, and a delta-method helper for nonlinear functions of the coefficients. Test it against linearmodels IVGMM with the kernel and centring aligned. Do not use lp_iv.
2. Fix fetch_policy_rates:
- Query _BIS_CBPOL_SINGLE_URL per country; M.MX works.
- Warn or raise instead of silently falling back to discontinued INTDSR series.
- Bundle snapshot CSVs so the notebook never calls fetch: US quarterly 1958-1997 (FEDFUNDS first month, GDPDEF, GDPC1, GDPPOT, M2SL, GS10, TB3MS, PPIACO) and BIS M.MX. Record the BIS break note from COMPILATION.
3. Weak-IV diagnostics:
- Fix kleibergen_paap_f for k>=2 (the real KP rank statistic via SVD) or document it as a test of Pi=0.
- Report Cragg-Donald and Sanderson-Windmeijer F per endogenous regressor.
- Do not quote Stock-Yogo critical values that are not tabulated.
4. US anchor:
- Cite QJE Table II and Table III from the CREI PDF, not the NBER WP 6442 Table 1.
- Pin one spec: two-step, L=0 (MA(0) for k=q=1 per footnote 13), CBO gap, four lags, M2 included, and state the M2 ambiguity.
- Assert a qualitative band: pre beta<1, post beta>1, each within 2 published SE.
- Disclose the substitutions: PPIACO for CRB, GS10 for FYGL, current-vintage GDPPOT.
- Show the L and iterated-GMM sensitivity, and J p going to 1, as the many-moments lesson, with a two-lag instrument set as robustness.
5. Mexico:
- Split at 2008-01-21, bank funding rate vs target.
- Use 12-month CPI with k=4 and HAC L>=3, so HC0 hansen_j is not enough.
- Report a weak-IV-robust set for beta, and frame the answer as weak identification or a specification-sensitive one, not a yes/no on beta>1.
6. Ship it as a lab that replaces notebook 47's OLS rule or as a new notebook 69 plus its Spanish twin, and link T01_C and notebook 66.
vets.capabilities_check:
Only one of the four listed capabilities does its job for this spec, and one of them is broken. I read the source and ran two scratch scripts (fetch.py, cgg_gmm.py and mx_gmm.py in scratchpad/wf/taylor-cgg2000/, each under 5 s).
(1) lp_iv, puremacro/lp/iv.py:367, cannot estimate CGG. It takes one endogenous regressor (x: str), while CGG has two: pi_{t+1} and x_t. At h=0 its dependent variable is y_t - y_{t-1}, and it adds lags of x as included controls, but the inflation lags must be excluded instruments. Its HAC lag is h+1. So "lp_iv at h=0 as a workaround" is false.
(2) hansen_j, puremacro/inference/over_id.py:40, works with k>=2 but uses only the HC0 weight and returns only J, with no estimates or standard errors. HC0 is valid for k=q=1, where CGG footnote 13 says the error is MA(0). It is not valid for k=4 or for Mexico's 12-month inflation (MA(3)). Smoke run: J p = 0.131 pre-1979 and 0.383 post, against 0.133 and 0.346 from my hand-rolled GMM.
(3) olea_pflueger_f, weak_iv.py:272, handles one endogenous regressor only.
(4) kleibergen_paap_f, weak_iv.py:164: for k>=2 it computes a Wald test of Pi=0 divided by l*k (lines 259-266, described there as an "Approximation"), not the KP rank test. On the same US data it gave rk F 67-141 while cragg_donald_f (weak_iv.py:59) gave 4-10. It would report weak instruments as strong.
(5) stock_yogo_cv, over_id.py:158, tabulates only k=1, l=3..8. It has nothing for CGG's k=2, l=22.
(6) anderson_rubin_test, weak_iv.py:350, handles one endogenous regressor, is homoskedastic, and tests a reduced-form coefficient. It cannot test beta=b/(1-rho1-rho2) with the gap as a nuisance endogenous regressor.
(7) fetch_policy_rates, puremacro/fetch/financial.py:395, is broken for BIS. _BIS_CBPOL_URL (M.ALL, financial.py:193) returned HTTP 404 in this session. _BIS_CBPOL_SINGLE_URL (line 194) is defined but never used. MEX silently falls back to FRED INTDSRMXM193N, a discount rate covering 2008-01 to 2013-04 (64 obs), labelled policy_rate. It also needs requests, which Pyodide lacks, and caches into the repo's data/raw (fetch/_http.py:24).
A two-step HAC GMM written by hand in about 40 lines of numpy runs in under 1 s.
vets.oracle_check:
The published anchor can be obtained, but the match will be qualitative, not to the decimal.
Source: I read QJE 2000 Table II this session from Galí's CREI copy, https://crei.cat/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/cgg_qje2000.pdf (pypdf text, line 60).
- Pre-Volcker: pi* 4.24 (1.09), beta 0.83 (0.07), gamma 0.27 (0.08), rho 0.68 (0.05), J p 0.834.
- Volcker-Greenspan: pi* 3.58 (0.50), beta 2.15 (0.40), gamma 0.93 (0.42), rho 0.79 (0.04), J p 0.316.
- Table III, detrended-output rows: beta 0.75 (0.07) pre and 1.97 (0.32) post.
Paper's spec: k=q=1, rho over two rate lags, four instrument lags, CBO gap, GDP deflator, FYFF in the first month of each quarter. The text lists M2 among the instruments, but the Table II note omits it. The number of HAC lags is not stated.
Watch the version: NBER WP 6442 (fetched this session) has a different Table 1 (beta 0.80 and 1.80, quadratic-trend gap, one rate lag). The two versions must not be mixed.
Smoke replication on current-vintage FRED data, with PPIACO in place of the proprietary CRB PSCCOM and GS10 in place of FYGL (two-step, HC0 weight, CBO gap, with M2):
- Pre-1979: beta 0.842 (0.079), gamma 0.314, rho 0.760.
- Post-1979: beta 2.105 (0.298), gamma 1.036, rho 0.825.
- Beta and gamma land within one published SE; rho is 1-2 SE high.
The results are fragile. Iterated GMM with Newey-West L>=4 gives post-1979 beta 3.3-5.1 and a negative gamma, and J p goes to 0.99 at L=8 (25 moments, T=70-78).
The independent software oracle is linearmodels IVGMM, a dev dependency (pyproject.toml:87). With bandwidth 4 it gave 0.863/0.331/0.669 pre and 2.359/1.344/0.809 post. It should match exactly once the kernel conventions and centring are aligned, and it belongs in a test, not the notebook.
Mexico has no published target.

US: every series I fetched through fetch_fred with no key: FEDFUNDS, GDPDEF, GDPPOT, GDPC1, M2SL, GS10, TB3MS, PPIACO. All are public-domain sources (Fed, BEA, CBO, BLS). Nothing in notebooks 00-68, the course, curso, examples or PLAN.md estimates a forward-looking GMM Taylor rule (grep over the whole repo).

ideas.title: Credit booms and deep recessions: Jordà-Schularick-Taylor local projections
ideas.question: Are recessions preceded by excess credit growth deeper and longer across 18 advanced economies since 1870?
ideas.description: Identify business-cycle peaks, then run panel LPs of real GDP per capita paths conditioned on excess credit in the preceding expansion (normal against financial recessions), with Driscoll-Kraay SEs and a Latin American contrast using Cerra-Saxena-style crisis dates (Laeven-Valencia).
ideas.paper: Jordà, Schularick & Taylor (2013 IMF Econ Rev) 'When Credit Bites Back'; JST (2017 NBER Macro Annual)
ideas.oracle_detail: JST (2013) recession-path tables: to transcribe from the paper. Second oracle: JST's Stata code output (numbers only).
ideas.data_detail: https://www.macrohistory.net/app/download/9834512469/JSTdatasetR6.xlsx returned 200 this session (1.1 MB). The licence, read via macrohistory.net/database, is Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 with a required citation of JST (2017 NBER Macro Annual). Fetch at run time and do not bundle it into the MIT package; any derived fixture inherits ShareAlike. Laeven-Valencia crisis dates are IMF public data with no fetcher.
ideas.library_gaps: No JST or Laeven-Valencia fetchers; no Bry-Boschan peak dating (check regime_dates.py).
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

1. Correct the paper: JMCB 45(s2):3-28 (2013), NBER WP 17621; 14 countries, 1870-2008, 223 recessions. Set the question to "14 advanced economies 1870-2008", then add an "update to R6: 18 countries, 1870-2020" section.
2. Replace the capabilities:
   - Drop panel_lp_dk and lp_state_dep. Two-way demeaning absorbs the N/F intercepts, their left-hand side is y_{t+h}−y_{t−1}, and a single time series is the wrong design.
   - Use puremacro.regress.ols (regress/ols.py:1289) on a peak-event table: y = Δ_h log rgdpbarro×100, regressors [N, F] with no constant, cov_type nonrobust to match the paper, f_test("N = F").
   - Show cluster-by-country standard errors only as a robustness aside, noting there are only 14 clusters.
   - No Driscoll-Kraay.
3. Oracle and tolerances:
   - Hard-code Table 1 peaks and labels and Table 4 from the fetched NBER w17621 (Oct-2012 revision), after checking them against the JMCB print.
   - Assert |coef − published| ≤ 0.2, |SE − published| ≤ 0.1, and sample 224 vs 223.
   - Report the own-dating agreement with Table 1 (288/298).

ideas.title: The cost of business cycles: Lucas (1987) closed form, perfect insurance, and Imrohoroglu (1989) liquidity constraints
ideas.question: How large is the welfare cost of business cycles once agents cannot insure unemployment risk, and which published welfare numbers survive an exact check?
ideas.description: The notebook reproduces Imrohoroglu's Tables 1 and 2 and adds two closed forms. The first is Lucas's lognormal cost, 0.5*gamma*var(log c). The second is an exact cost for the perfect-insurance column, since consumption is then aggregate income on a two-state Markov chain. VERIFIED in scratch runs: VFIProblem on the storage economy (na=1501, 4 exogenous states) returns CE 0.102% (sigma=1.5) and 0.268% (sigma=6.2) with mean storage 2.346, identical to Kirkby's VFI Toolkit replication; each sigma takes about 25 s. At sigma=6.2 mean storage of 6.34 sits near the grid top a_max=8, so the grid must be widened. The exact perfect-insurance cost comes to 0.089% (sigma=1.5) and 0.298% (sigma=6.2). The paper has .080 and .300; Kirkby's replication has 0.051 and 0.065. The closed form sides with the paper, and it scales roughly linearly in sigma while Kirkby's column does not. The storage column confirms Kirkby, not the paper (.300 and 1.500). The notebook teaches consumption-equivalent welfare, why linear-quadratic welfare numbers fail (Kirkby's main finding), and how a closed form adjudicates between two oracles. A second part covers the intermediation economy, which borrows at rb=0.08 with a kinked return.
ideas.paper: Imrohoroglu (1989, JPE 97(6)); Lucas (1987, Models of Business Cycles; 2003 AER address)
ideas.oracle_detail: Three oracles. (1) Exact perfect-insurance CE from the 4x4 (s,z) chain and the no-cycle 2x2 chain, both read from Kirkby's Imrohoroglu1989.pdf (github.com/vfitoolkit/vfitoolkit-matlab-replication, GPL-3: freeze numbers only), plus Lucas's lognormal formula. (2) Published tables: the original Table 1 (.080/.300 perfect insurance; .300/1.500 storage) and Table 2 (intermediation: borrowed .480, stored .220, saved .700, income .940, consumption .935; storage .000/2.400/2.400/.940/.940), read in this session from the scanned images on pp. 2-3 of that PDF. Confirm against the JPE scan. (3) Independent software: Kirkby's replicated values (0.051, 0.102, 0.065, 0.268; Table 2: 0.614, -0.437, 0.177, 0.934, 0.934; storage 2.346, 0.940), which Ayse Imrohoroglu confirmed by an independent replication (Kirkby WP, footnote 5).
ideas.data_detail: No data. The calibration (beta .995, theta .25, sigma 1.5/6.2, rl 0, rb .08, the transition matrices) comes from the replication PDF. An optional Lucas section uses the variance of per-capita consumption from FRED (fetchable).
ideas.library_gaps: None blocking. Optional helpers: a consumption_equivalent() utility and a kinked-interest return function for the intermediation economy. The 1501-point grid runs in about 50 s total on numpy; the notebook could cache or use numba.
ideas.plan_overlap: None. PLAN's Bewley row (67, done) covers Huggett and Aiyagari only; no notebook or course file mentions Imrohoroglu or Lucas's cost of cycles.

Published tables: read in this session from the scanned images in Kirkby's Imrohoroglu1989.pdf (repo vfitoolkit-matlab-replication; p.2 image Im1, p.3 image Im2).

Three premises fail.
(1) Kirkby's "perfect insurance" column is not perfect insurance. His Imrohoroglu1989.m sets a_grid=0 for Environment C, which is hand-to-mouth autarky. The closed form E[u(e(s))] under the 4-state vs 2-state stationary laws gives exactly 0.0505/0.0648. That cost comes only from the unconditional unemployment gap (0.08031 vs 0.08004). The diagnosis is a wrong environment, not "does not scale".
(2) The "exact" perfect-insurance cost of 0.089/0.298 assumes aggregate unemployment depends on z alone. It does not: with a continuum of agents, u' = u*pi_uu(z,z') + (1-u)*pi_eu(z,z') depends on history (fixed points 0.040 and 0.123; 0.081 on impact). A 4M-period simulation gives 0.100/0.322. Removing the 0.02% mean-income gap gives 0.067/0.276 (z only) and 0.071/0.293 (with history). The Lucas lognormal formula gives 0.0671/0.2773. So the perfect-insurance oracle is a band of about 0.067-0.100 and 0.276-0.322, not a point. It rejects Kirkby's column, but it cannot confirm .080 to three digits.
(3) Kirkby's sigma=6.2 storage value of 0.268 is an artifact of truncating the grid at a_max=8: 8.9% of the business-cycle stationary mass sits in the top 5 grid points. On a_max=16 (na 1501 or 3001) and a_max=24, the cost converges to 0.151-0.152%. Neither Kirkby nor the paper (1.500) holds at sigma=6.2. The storage cost then falls below the perfect-insurance cost, which reverses the paper's headline. Per Kirkby's code comment, the paper's own grid was [0,8] with 301 points. The independent replication Kirkby's PDF cites (by Imrohoroglu and Aggarwal) matched his numbers, so it probably shares the same truncation.

ideas.title: The liquidity trap three ways: Eggertsson-Woodford closed form, Markov-switching solver, and OccBin
ideas.question: What happens in a New Keynesian economy when the natural rate falls below zero for a random duration, and why does the answer explode as expected duration rises?
ideas.description: In the two-state absorbing-Markov liquidity trap of the 3-equation NK model, x_L and pi_L have closed forms. VERIFIED: solve_ms_dsge with an absorbing transition and regime intercepts K reproduces x_L = sigma*r_L*(1-beta*mu)/((1-mu)(1-beta*mu)-sigma*mu*kappa) and pi_L = kappa*x_L/(1-beta*mu) to printed precision at mu/r_L = (0.8,-0.01), (0.85,-0.005), (0.7,-0.02). Sections: (1) closed form versus solve_ms_dsge at 25 random calibrations. (2) The existence boundary where the denominator vanishes (the deflationary black hole), plotted in (mu, kappa). (3) The government-spending multiplier at the ZLB in closed form versus the solver. (4) OccBin with a known spell of length 1/(1-mu) versus the Markov solution, showing that duration uncertainty amplifies the slump. The OccBin arm is optional. (5) Forward guidance: holding i=0 after exit.
ideas.paper: Eggertsson and Woodford (2003, BPEA); Eggertsson (2011, NBER Macro Annual); Christiano, Eichenbaum and Rebelo (2011, JPE); Woodford (2011, AEJ:Macro)

ideas.title: Hansen (1985) indivisible labor: Table 1 by perturbation, linear-quadratic, and global methods
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase or section 1 of PLAN's 'Business-cycle moments done right'
ideas.question: Why does indivisible labor with lotteries raise the volatility of hours and output by about 30%, and how much do Table 1's numbers depend on the solution method and the shock specification?
ideas.description: The divisible and indivisible models are written natively in logs, solved at order 1, and their HP(1600) theoretical moments compared with Hansen's Table 1. VERIFIED: theoretical HP s.d. (%) are y 1.38, c 0.43, i 4.32, k 0.38, h 0.71, y/h 0.70 for the divisible model and 1.80, 0.52, 5.76, 0.50, 1.37, 0.52 for the indivisible one. Hansen's values are 1.35, 0.42, 4.24, 0.36, 0.70, 0.68 and 1.76, 0.51, 5.71, 0.47, 1.35, 0.50, read from the transcription in Kirkby's Hansen1985.pdf. stoch_simul(periods=115, simul_replic=100, hp_filter=1600) runs in 0.6 s, which matches the paper's small-sample design. Findings to show: corr(k,y) comes out at 0.35 against the paper's 0.06, which Pfeifer's DSGE_mod notes as a likely typo; productivity is proportional to consumption in the indivisible model; and Hansen's shock is AR(1) in levels with lognormal innovations, which LQ and first order ignore but Kirkby's global solution does not. HP-filtered theoretical moments have no notebook call site today.
ideas.paper: Hansen (1985, JME 16(3)); Rogerson (1988)
ideas.oracle_detail: Hansen Table 1 as transcribed in Kirkby's Hansen1985.pdf (vfitoolkit-matlab-replication, GPL-3), read in this session; confirm against the JME scan. Kirkby's global-VFI replication values from the same PDF (divisible y 1.37, indivisible 1.80) serve as an independent method, and Kirkby's WP Table 2 reports a 2.9% median absolute difference. Pfeifer's Hansen_1985.mod (GPL-3) can run in Dynare 8 through MATLAB R2026a as a frozen third route.
ideas.data_detail: Model moments need no data. The US column (1955Q3-1984Q1) is in the paper; an optional refresh uses FRED GNP, consumption, investment and hours.
ideas.library_gaps: None for a native model. Pfeifer's Hansen_1985.mod does not load: the parameter 'lambda' collides with a Python keyword (eval at puremacro/dsge/dynare.py:1878), and B is assigned inside steady_state_model, which is unsupported. The existing test_hansen_1985_rbc_1st_and_2nd_order (tests/test_dynare_advanced.py:94) never checks Table 1. A global VFI with an hours choice at Kirkby's 101x501x31 grid makes a return tensor of about 786M entries, too large for numpy; use coarser grids or EGM.
ideas.plan_overlap: Partial. It shares machinery (HP theoretical moments, simul_replic) with PLAN's 'Business-cycle moments done right: BKK (1992) or King-Rebelo (1999)'; the two could be merged, with Hansen as the first model. course/07_competitivos_laboral_es covers the lottery theory only.

vets.oracle_check:
Hansen's Table 1 was read in this session (pypdf) from Kirkby's Hansen1985.pdf, page 3, 'Table 2: Original Table 1 from Hansen (1985)'. Source: raw.githubusercontent.com/vfitoolkit/vfitoolkit-matlab-replication/master/Hansen1985/Hansen1985.pdf. Divisible s.d.: 1.35, 0.42, 4.24, 0.36, 0.70, 0.68. Indivisible: 1.76, 0.51, 5.71, 0.47, 1.35, 0.50. corr(y,k) is 0.06 and 0.05. These match the proposal.
Footnote b says these are means over 100 simulations of 115 periods. The primary target is therefore the simul_replic output; the theoretical HP moments are the population reference.
Two of the proposal's findings are refuted.
(a) corr(k,y). Pfeifer's .mod header (fetched from DSGE_mod) calls it a likely typo. It is a timing convention. With beginning-of-period capital kb = k(-1), theoretical corr(y,kb) is 0.07 and the 100x115 simulations give 0.06-0.07, matching Hansen. The 0.35-0.36 comes from Dynare's end-of-period k.
(b) Kirkby's global method is not a clean independent oracle for the shock specification. On an identical 801x15 grid, the level-AR(1) lognormal and log-AR(1) normal specifications give the same moments: y 1.43/1.43, c 0.45/0.45, i 4.52/4.54, h 0.74/0.75. Coarse capital grids inflate c and i and lower corr(c,y): 0.67 at 201 points, 0.82 at 401, 0.87 at 801. Kirkby's deviations (c 0.49, corr 0.70) go in the same direction. His hours grid (101 points on [0,1], step 0.01, about 3.3% of h_ss ~0.30) is coarser than the hours s.d. it measures (0.7-1.4%).
Not verified this session: the JME scan (not fetched) and Kirkby's WP '2.9% median absolute difference'.

ideas.title: OccBin you can trust: Guerrieri-Iacoviello (2015) against Dynare 8's occbin
ideas.question: Does puremacro's piecewise-linear OccBin reproduce the published toolkit on its own examples, including regime durations and asymmetric responses?
ideas.description: The notebook replicates GI's Figure 3: an RBC with irreversible investment under positive and negative shocks of increasing size. It then runs the NK/ZLB example and compares regime sequences, paths and binding spells with Dynare 8's occbin. solve_occbin is used in 5 notebook sources (41, 46, 57 and Spanish twins) and curso T02_D, always on toy models and never checked against the original toolkit. Extensions: solve_multiconstraint_occbin on a two-constraint case, and the piecewise Kalman likelihood against Dynare's occbin filter.
ideas.paper: Guerrieri and Iacoviello (2015, JME 70)
ideas.oracle_detail: Dynare 8's occbin (the snapshot at /Applications/Dynare/8-2026-05-26-1803, examples/occbin/rbc_occbin.mod, run via MATLAB R2026a -batch; freeze paths as fixtures, and do not ship the GPL model files), plus GI's published Figure 3. Pfeifer/Mutschler's Guerrieri_Iacoviello_2015_rbc.mod and _nk.mod (GPL-3) record a typo in GI's Euler equation (11).
ideas.data_detail: Calibrated models only. Dynare paths are frozen as fixtures.
ideas.library_gaps: Pfeifer's GI mod fails at load with NameError on the steady_state() operator in the model block, which is unsupported; writing the model natively avoids this. Comparing shadow-rate paths may need an output option that exposes OccBin's guessed regime sequence per iteration.
ideas.plan_overlap: None in PLAN. The replication contract's Dynare-through-MATLAB route is reused.

vets.oracle_check:
The oracle can be obtained. I ran it: Dynare 8 snapshot plus MATLAB -batch with nograph. Both runs exited 0 and printed DONE_OK in about a minute. The outputs are in scratch dyn/ and dyn2/ (.mat files).
Mismatches in the proposal:
(a) examples/occbin/rbc_occbin.mod is not GI Fig. 3. It is a two-constraint IRR+INEG model with psi=5 adjustment costs and a 200-period surprise-shock sequence. It serves only the multi-constraint extension, and only once initial_state exists.
(b) GI Fig. 3 is two symmetric ±4% TFP shocks, not shocks of increasing size. I read this in this session from the JME PDF at https://www.matteoiacoviello.com/research_files/JME_2015.pdf. The figure plots the piecewise-linear solution against dynamic programming and first-order perturbation. No numbers are published, and the DP curves cannot be reproduced.
(c) Published numbers exist in Table 2 of the same PDF. Piecewise-linear row: log I mean -1.015, s.d. 5.3%, skewness 1.33; log C mean 0.152, s.d. 3.62%, skewness -0.23; correlation 0.80; binding frequency 38%. The simulation length is not stated. My scratch simulations with surprise shocks (table2_sim.py, table2_log.py) give log I mean -1.020 to -1.023, s.d. 5.0-5.45%, skewness 1.09-1.19, and binding frequency 36.5-37.2%. Log C skewness ranges from -0.10 to -0.37 across seeds. This is a loose band check only.
(d) Fig. 5 caption: a shock of 4 s.d. with sigma=0.005 (Table 3) should give 0.02, yet beta moves to 1.019 and 0.969. Under Dynare's level linearization those values imply an innovation of 0.025, and 0.994*1.025=1.01885 matches. Mutschler's GPL mod file makes the same point.
(e) The Eq. (11) typo is confirmed in the PDF text: the equation ends in -(1-delta)lambda_t.
(f) GI's own toolkit (occbin_20140630/model_irrcap/dynrbc.mod, downloaded to scratch) writes c, k and i in logs, with constraint i<log(PHII). Dynare 8 and Mutschler work in levels, with threshold (phi-1)*Iss=-0.025 against log(0.975)=-0.0253. The two specs therefore bind at different points, and the notebook must say which one each oracle uses.

All the named symbols exist. solve_occbin is at puremacro/dsge/occbin.py:1250, solve_multiconstraint_occbin at occbin.py:2202, build_dynare at puremacro/dsge/dynare.py:244, OccBinConstraint (with relax_variable, relax_threshold and relax_operator) at occbin.py:96, and piecewise_kalman_filter at occbin.py:2573.

I ran scratch probes with the conda work python; the scripts are in scratchpad/wf/occbin-gi-rev/.
(1) I wrote GI's one-constraint RBC (I >= phi*Iss, relax_variable Lambda<0) as native build_dynare callables and gave it a -4% TFP shock (eps = log 0.96). solve_occbin converges with a 14-period binding spell and log I stays at log(0.975) = -2.53%. It matches Dynare 8 occbin, run on my own .mod file, to at most 1.1e-15 in every variable over 60 periods.
(2) Dynare's two-constraint example (examples/occbin/rbc_occbin.mod: IRR plus INEG adjustment costs), run with single shocks of -4% and -0.01. solve_multiconstraint_occbin matches to at most 2.4e-15 with horizon>=200. (3) Dynare's own shocks(surprise) sequence over 200 periods: it matches to at most 1.2e-15 (regimes 2 and 3 are reproduced), but only after a 2-line scratch patch.

Without this, neither sequential surprise shocks nor stochastic simulations for moments (GI Tables 2 and 4) are possible.

The proposal's library_gaps text is partly wrong. The STEADY_STATE operator in the model block does parse (_parser.py:737). load_mod raises NameError('steady_state') only when the occbin_constraints block is present. With that block removed, the bind/relax tags are ignored, so the duplicate equations give "8 residual(s) for 7 variables" (ModelError). Writing the models natively is fine.

Published anchors, read from the GI FEDS 2014-47 working-paper PDF fetched from federalreserve.gov/pubs/feds/2014/201447/201447pap.pdf (not the JME 70 version, so figure and table numbers may differ in the journal):
- Figure 3 (p.34 caption): "RBC Model with Constraint on Investment: An Unexpected Decrease in Technology (left column) and an Unexpected Increase in Technology (right column)". The shocks are ±4% (A=0.96/1.04). The figure overlays piecewise, dynamic programming and first-order solutions. It is not "shocks of increasing size"; the shock-size sweep is Figure 1, a simple asset-pricing model, naive splice vs piecewise.

- Table 2, piecewise row: log I mean -1.015, sd 6.3%, skewness 1.33; log C mean 1.152, sd 4.7%, skewness -0.23; correlation 0.80; binds 41% of periods.

- Table 4, piecewise: ZLB frequency 4.2%.

- The p.23 sentence says a +4 s.d. shock "brings beta up to 1.019", but 0.994*exp(4*0.005) is about 1.014. Resolve the shock mapping against Dynare rather than the prose.

ideas.title: Ireland (2004) by maximum likelihood: technology shocks in the New Keynesian model
ideas.question: Do technology shocks matter in a NK model estimated by maximum likelihood on output, inflation and the interest rate, and how do the pre- and post-1980 samples differ?
ideas.description: The notebook estimates the 4-shock NK model by Kalman-filter ML on full, pre-1980 and post-1980 samples. It then reports variance decompositions and IRFs, and reproduces Ireland's point estimates and standard errors. The lesson on inference at bounds: several estimates lie at zero, so Ireland used one-sided derivatives. VERIFIED: Pfeifer's Ireland_2004.mod loads in puremacro as a LinearModel. This would be the catalog's first maximum-likelihood DSGE replication.
ideas.paper: Ireland (2004, REStat 86(4))
ideas.oracle_detail: Ireland's Table 1 estimates and SEs (paper to be fetched), plus Pfeifer's Ireland_2004.mod ML replication. Its header records that Ireland demeans each subsample's observables and imposes [0,1] bounds by transformation. Run it through Dynare 8 + MATLAB and freeze.
ideas.data_detail: Pfeifer's repo ships gpr.dat and data_full/pre/post_1980.m (listing verified); Ireland's website hosts the originals. A FRED rebuild is possible, but vintages differ.
ideas.library_gaps: Dynare-style ML is not implemented: build.py:958 raises when estimated_params has no prior shape. A flat-prior workaround through estimate_dsge exists; the proper fix is an ML front end with bounded optimisation and Hessian or OPG SEs, including one-sided derivatives at bounds.
ideas.plan_overlap: None (PLAN's DSGE estimation items are all Bayesian: SW07 and Herbst-Schorfheide).

vets.required_changes:
1. Add a public ML front end rather than relying on the flat-prior hack. Suggested shape: LinearModel.estimate_ml(data, varobs, prefilter=True, start='calibration'|dict, transform='bounded' (logit/log), method='csminwel', n_starts=k, se='hessian'|'opg'|'sandwich', rel_step=1e-3, one_sided_at_bounds=True). It should return estimates, loglik, SEs, at-bound flags and all local optima found. At minimum, expose a public log_likelihood(params, data).
2. Fix estimated_params_init(use_calibration) so it seeds init from the calibration (_estimated_params.py:453).
3. Use the paper as the oracle, not a Dynare freeze.
   - Point estimates: 4 decimals against Tables 1 and 3.
   - FEVD: within 0.2 pp of Table 2 at finite horizons, noting the infinity-row truncation.
   - IRFs: the p.929 impact numbers (scale unit IRFs by the shock SD).
   - SEs: assert only Table 1, within about 5%.
   - Present Table 3 subsample SEs as the fragility-at-bounds lesson (indefinite Hessian, step sensitivity, SEs meaningless when the gradient at the bound is nonzero), not as a reproduction target.
4. Bound omega to [0,1].
5. Main estimation: transformed space, started from the published values, like Pfeifer's use_calibration. Add a small frozen multi-start panel that shows the local optima (log-lik gaps of 2.5 to 13.4) so the notebook is not circular.
6. Write the model block inline from Ireland's eqs (15)-(17) and (20)-(24), crediting Pfeifer's findings. Do not copy the GPL .mod.
7. Bundle gpr.dat (220x3) with provenance: Ireland's data via Pfeifer's repo, the sha256, and a note that Ireland's progs page is dead. Demean each sample separately.
8. Keep the build runtime bounded: one or two optimiser runs per sample at about 3-40 s each; cache the multi-start results.

ideas.title: Firing costs in general equilibrium: Hopenhayn-Rogerson (1993)
ideas.question: How much do firing taxes of 0.1 and 0.2 of a year's wage reduce employment, productivity and welfare once entry, exit and labor supply adjust?
ideas.description: This extends notebook 04 (Hopenhayn 1992) with lagged employment as a state, a firing tax on reductions, exit that pays the tax on all workers, free entry and a Hansen-Rogerson household. The targets are Tables 2-5: benchmark statistics, the effect of tau on prices, output, employment and utility-adjusted consumption, inaction bands (n_l, n_u), and MPL deviations. The teaching point, from Kirkby: HR's coarse employment grid (201 to 250 log-spaced points) acted like an extra fixed adjustment cost, so a grid-refinement section explains the 13.1% median gap.
ideas.paper: Hopenhayn and Rogerson (1993, JPE 101(5))
ideas.oracle_detail: HR Tables 2-5 as images on pp. 4-7 of Kirkby's HopenhaynRogerson1993.pdf (fetched in this session; the images were not transcribed). Kirkby's replicated values are in text there, for example Table 3 at tau=0.1: price 1.021, consumption 98.2, employment 98.8. Kirkby's WP Table 2 gives a median absolute difference of 13.1%. Parameter a=0.078 and the entrant distribution come from Floden's notes, as the PDF documents.
ideas.data_detail: Calibrated. The parameters are in the replication PDF, and HR's Table 1 data are not needed.
ideas.library_gaps: firm_dynamics.py handles only a productivity state with no endogenous firm state. A two-state (n,z) problem with exit (V=0), free entry and a non-mass-conserving distribution with entrants is missing. It can be built on VFIProblem with an absorbing exit node, but a first-class solver (hopenhayn_rogerson or a generic entry_exit option) is cleaner.
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

ideas.title: Gains from trade: the ACR formula and the Costinot-Rodríguez-Clare multi-sector ladder
ideas.question: How large are the gains from trade, and how much do multiple sectors and input-output linkages raise them relative to the one-sector ACR formula?
ideas.description: VERIFIED: CaliendoParroModel with J=1, no IO and balanced trade satisfies the ACR identity W_hat = pi_nn_hat^(-1/theta) to a relative error of 2.3e-16 across 6 random iceberg shocks in a 5-country economy. The notebook then climbs CRC's ladder (one sector, multiple sectors, multiple sectors with IO) on real input-output data. It compares autarky gains with CRC's Table 4.1 and shows the sectoral ACR generalisation holding inside the CP solver. EK (2002) enters as the Ricardian microfoundation of theta.
ideas.paper: Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodríguez-Clare (2012, AER); Costinot and Rodríguez-Clare (2014, Handbook of IE vol. 4); Eaton and Kortum (2002)
ideas.oracle_detail: The ACR identity and its multi-sector and IO generalisations are exact within the model, and one was verified in this session. The published target is CRC (2014) Table 4.1 (NBER w18896 is free; not read in this session). The EK paper is free at Cowles (p1866); EK's 1990 bilateral data were not found in this session.
ideas.data_detail: WIOD 2013 release (the 2008 table) or OECD ICIO must be fetched and reduced to a fixture. The bundled icio_77c_11s.npz must NOT be used: it is corrupted-derived, with world VA about 8,800 times too large (memory note).
ideas.library_gaps: No autarky counterfactual helper (a d_hat going to infinity limit, or the closed form directly). A loader from WIOD or ICIO to CP inputs with consistent balanced-trade adjustment (a Dekle-Eaton-Kortum purge of deficits) is also missing.
ideas.plan_overlap: Partial. PLAN's 'Three trade models, one tariff' studies a tariff under four demand systems, not gains from trade or ACR. 'Is this IO table safe' is complementary and provides the data hygiene.

ideas.title: Caliendo-Parro (2015) NAFTA against the paper
ideas.question: Does the package's CP solver reproduce the published welfare, trade and real-wage effects of NAFTA's tariff cuts on Mexico, Canada and the US?
ideas.description: The module is named after the paper, but notebook 55 runs it on a 3-country, 2-sector toy calibration. This notebook would load CP's 1993 data (about 31 countries plus RoW and 40 sectors, sector thetas and tariffs), apply NAFTA's tariff changes, and compare welfare and its terms-of-trade and volume-of-trade decomposition with the paper's tables.
ideas.paper: Caliendo and Parro (2015, REStud 82(1))
ideas.oracle_detail: CP's welfare-effect tables (to be fetched). The authors' replication package is presumed public, but its availability was NOT confirmed in this session (a web search found nothing), so check the ReStud supplement or the authors' pages first.
ideas.data_detail: CP's 1993 input-output, trade, tariff and theta data. Source and licence are unverified.
ideas.library_gaps: A welfare-decomposition method (CP eq. 25-style ToT/VoT split) is probably missing; check CaliendoParroResult. A data loader for CP's format is also needed.
ideas.plan_overlap: None (PLAN's trade items use the newer condensed and MRIO engines).

vets.required_changes:
1. Build a new standalone notebook (e.g. 69_caliendo_parro_nafta plus the _es twin) and link it from 55. Do not replace 55's toy CP cell: 55 also hosts Allen-Arkolakis, and the toy cell runs in seconds.
2. Vectorise CaliendoParroModel._solve_expenditures and _solve_baseline_expenditures with einsum. Make the solver converge on CP data at the default settings, using a better damping or Newton-type update, or a documented tol and max_iter. Add a regression test on the CP baseline.
3. Add a loader, e.g. puremacro.trade.load_caliendo_parro_1993(). It should fetch Data_and_Codes_CP.zip through fetch._http.cached_get with a SHA-256 pin and read initial_condition_1993_noS.mat and tariffs2005.txt. Do not bundle the data unless the licence is cleared; document the sources and terms.
4. Run NAFTA through solve_counterfactual(tariffs_new=tau_1993 with the 2005 rates on the six CAN/MEX/USA pairs), not simulate_tariff_shock. Pass explicit ISO country codes and never rely on the alias map.
5. Implement CP eq. (16) exactly as Welfarelineal.m does, with the bilateral split from welfare_stats.m, as a library function or notebook helper. Do not use TradePolicySimulator's decomposition; fix or relabel it separately.
6. Oracles: Table 2 (all four columns), Table 3 and Table 5, asserted at the table's rounding. Table 4 is optional. Next to them, report the module's exact welfare_pct (MEX about 0.01%) and explain that Table 2's Total is a first-order approximation driven by lost tariff revenue. A short, precomputed path-integration demo is optional.
7. Keep to one or two counterfactuals so the notebook's runtime stays manageable, especially under Pyodide.
vets.capabilities_check:
Both symbols exist. CaliendoParroModel (puremacro/trade/caliendo_parro.py:189) loads the authors' zero-surplus 1993 baseline without changes: N=31, J=40, nontradables=20..39. It reproduces CP's X0 to within 9e-8 relative, with a baseline labour-market residual of 7e-8. The loader is in scratch at wf/cp15-nafta-review/cpload.py.

simulate_tariff_shock (:801) is the wrong entry point. It sets one uniform rate for one pair across all sectors, but NAFTA needs the sector-level 2005 tariffs on six CAN/MEX/USA pairs. Use solve_counterfactual(tariffs_new=...) (:569).

Run on CP's data, the module's output matches the paper:
- Real wages MEX/CAN/USA +1.715/+0.323/+0.112%, against Table 2's 1.72/0.32/0.11.
- Table 5 import growth matches to 2 decimals: 116.60, 118.31, 58.57, 9.49, 109.54, 6.57.
- A scratch port of CP's Welfarelineal.m, applied to the module's equilibrium, gives Total/ToT/VoT = MEX 1.312/-0.412/1.724, CAN -0.064/-0.108/0.044, USA 0.085/0.044/0.041. Table 2 has 1.31/-0.41/1.72, -0.06/-0.11/0.04, 0.08/0.04/0.04.

Problems:
(1) The module's own welfare_pct (exact I-hat/P-hat, :758) is MEX 0.007%, CAN -0.110%, USA 0.074%, far from Table 2's Mexico 1.31%. Integrating eq. (16) along an 8-step tariff path gives 0.097/-0.107/0.073, converging to the exact values. So CP's 'Total' is a one-step linearisation at 1993 tariff weights; Mexico loses tariff revenue worth 2.04% to 0.37% of income. The module is internally right, but welfare_pct is not the published number.
(2) Speed. The unvectorised _solve_expenditures loop (:477-522, innermost loop at :507) takes 0.62 s per iteration. The NAFTA run took 1049.6 s and stopped at max_iter=1500 with converged=False (residual 1.26e-8 against tol 1e-8, :730). A scratch einsum patch cut this to 0.056 s per iteration and 85 s in total, with identical results.
(3) The result object does not store c_hat, which the decomposition needs.
(4) The alias map in _resolve_country_index (:538-542) hard-codes USA=0, CHN=1, ROW/DEU=2. In CP's country order, 'US' silently resolves to ARG.
(5) TradePolicySimulator._compute_welfare_decomposition (puremacro/models/trade_policy.py:423-455) is labelled the 'CP exact decomposition' but is an ACR-style domestic-share formula plus a residual, not CP eq. (16). The notebook must not use it.

- Table 3, p.21: bilateral NAFTA vs RoW split.
- Table 4, p.23: sectoral shares.
- Table 5, p.24: import growth.
- Table 1, p.18: theta_j. The 99% column matches T.txt (petroleum 64.85).

The paper's p.21 text says welfare comes from eq. (16) and real wages from eq. (15). The package's results_counterfactualsCP.m and welfare_stats.m give the exact formula behind each table, so matching can be to the table's rounding. Caveat: 'Total' welfare is the linearised eq. (16), not an exact welfare change. Real wages and trade growth can be compared directly with module outputs.

ideas.title: Credit crunch and deleveraging: Guerrieri-Lorenzoni (2017) transition
ideas.question: How does a tightening of the household borrowing limit depress the interest rate and output along the transition, and when does the zero lower bound bind?
ideas.description: This is a Huggett economy with endogenous labor, a 12-state income process plus unemployment, and a government bond. The borrowing limit falls permanently, and transition_path solves the interest-rate path. The paper has only figures. Following Kirkby, a section shows that changing the Tauchen hyperparameter can make the ZLB bind for decades, a discretisation lesson that continues notebook 67.
ideas.paper: Guerrieri and Lorenzoni (2017, QJE)
ideas.oracle_detail: GL figures (approximate targets) and Kirkby's GuerrieriLorenzoni2017 replication (GPL-3; freeze numbers). GL's own MATLAB code is reported to be public, but this was not verified in this session.
ideas.data_detail: Calibrated from the paper.
ideas.library_gaps: transition_path supports price-only paths with a constant P_z, which is enough. Endogenous labor in the return function is standard. The ZLB variant needs an NK wage or price block (not in vfi).
ideas.plan_overlap: Partial. PLAN lists MNS forward guidance and Krusell-Smith, both heterogeneous-agent dynamics but different experiments.

vets.required_changes:
1. Engine: use a numpy EGM backward step with endogenous labour (n = max(0, 1 - fac·c^(gam/eta)), constrained segment as in GL) and lottery_push forward, either in the notebook (about 60-100 lines) or as a small library helper. Examples: a continuous-policy mode or backward_step hook for transition_path that returns extra policies (c, n) per period, or an egm_labor_transition. Do not headline transition_path; its discrete VFI takes about 49 s per iteration. If kept at all, use it only as a coarse, small-T cross-check.
2. Oracle: switch to GL's author outputs (trans.mat, trans_fix.mat, steady.mat from the Lorenzoni zip). Assert the flexible path within 0.05 pp annual at all 100 quarters, trough about -2.07% at q4, 5 negative quarters, and 7 quarters at the ZLB in the fixed-wage case. Freeze those numbers in the notebook with the URL; do not ship the .mat files.
3. Calibration: use the par.mat values and the paper's 6-quarter phi path and T = 100. Explain Kirkby's point that Table 1 reports B and phi relative to annual GDP.
4. ZLB: implement it as GL's labour-wedge path (r_t, omega_t) with r_t floored at 0 and goods-market clearing. Drop the phrase "needs NK block".
5. Timing: pair r_t with bonds chosen at t. GL's own pairing leaves r_1 fixed at the initial guess, and in my port it diverged from a flat guess.
6. Rewrite or drop the "Tauchen makes the ZLB bind for decades" section. If kept, state Kirkby's actual finding: with a wider grid (q = 3) the crunch has little effect. Recalibrate beta, psi and nu for each grid so the initial rate is 2.5%, or compare GL's grid against a variance-matched Rouwenhorst chain. Cross-reference notebook 67 instead of repeating its lesson. If a persistent-ZLB lesson is wanted, use GL's median-wealth alternative calibration and say that it needs a permanent wedge.
7. Make it a new showcase notebook (69) with an _es twin, not an addition to 02. Keep each transition to about 1 minute with a warm start or a Broyden update.
vets.capabilities_check:
All three listed symbols exist, but transition_path is the wrong engine for this model. transition_path (puremacro/vfi/transition.py:40) is a discrete-grid VFI solver. It rebuilds the return tensor for every period in every iteration (lines 63-68) and keeps only the a' index, `flat % n_a` (line 71), so the labour policy is lost and output has to be recomputed by the user. P_z is fixed for the whole path (line 53), which is fine here. A time-varying borrowing limit through build_problem params works. A two-column (r_t, omega_t) price path is accepted: I smoke-tested it with shape (5,2).

Smoke test with GL's own code calibration (par.mat), a 200-point grid and labour solved inside return_fn:
- VFIProblem (problem.py:213) with stationary_equilibrium (equilibrium.py:35) gives initial r = 2.713% and terminal r = 1.551% (annual). GL's values are 2.500% and 1.500%. Each steady state took about 40 s.
- transition_path with T=100 took 49 s per iteration. The return-tensor build alone is 0.47 s per period. GL's update scheme needs hundreds of iterations, so a run takes hours. That is not viable for a notebook or for Pyodide.

What does work: a numpy port of GL's EGM step with endogenous labour, using puremacro's lottery_push (distribution.py:36) for the distribution. One backward-forward pass takes 0.10 s. From a flat initial guess, with r_t paired to bonds chosen at t, 400 iterations (39 s) came within 0.027 pp (annual) of GL's own interest-rate path at every quarter, including r_1 (-0.969 vs -0.961).

Existing library pieces cannot do this directly. solve_egm (egm.py:27) has no labour choice and no time-varying limit. solve_continuous_transition is hardwired to Aiyagari with a >= 0 and a Cobb-Douglas firm. tauchen (discretize.py:19) exposes the width m.
vets.oracle_check:
The claim that the paper offers only figures understates what is available. GL's own MATLAB replication zip is public. Link found on Lorenzoni's page: https://sites.northwestern.edu/guidolor/files/2017/03/replication-codes-for-Credit-Crises-2017-1f7cb32.zip. It ships solved numeric outputs, all read in this session:
- trans.mat: the 100-quarter flexible-price r_t path. Annualised: -0.961% in q1, trough -2.070% in q4, negative for 5 quarters, ending at 1.500%.
- trans_fix.mat: the fixed-wage path, with r_t = 0 for 7 quarters, plus the omega_t wedge path.
- steady.mat: r1 = 0.00625 (quarterly), r2 = 0.0037510, Y1 = 0.41738, Y2 = 0.41667, D1 = 0.30051, D2 = 0.13356, MPC1 = 0.02277.

In my numpy port both author paths clear the markets: flexible-price bond RMS 5.19e-6; fixed-wage bond 1.04e-5 and goods 5.7e-6. Output on impact from the port is -1.11% (flexible) and -1.74% (fixed wage). The paper's Figure 3 output axis runs from -1.2 to 0 (from the Nov 2016 working paper PDF on the same site).

Caveat: GL's compute_transition.m pairs r_t with bonds held entering t, so BM(1) is identically 0 and r_1 is never updated. With that pairing my port diverged from a flat guess. Pair r_t with bonds chosen at t.

Kirkby's GPL-3 replication (vfitoolkit-matlab-replication/GuerrieriLorenzoni2017) has figures only and no frozen numbers. It is useful for parameter notes, not as the oracle.
vets.data_check:
The model is calibrated and synthetic; no fetch is needed. Use the parameters from GL's code (par.mat), not the paper's Table 1: bet = 0.97744, gam = 4, eta = 1.5, pssi = 15.88188, nu = 0.16695, B = 2.67123, phi1 = 1.60054, phi2 = 0.8767. The borrowing limit falls linearly over 6 quarters, T = 100, and the grid is b = -2 + 52(i/200)^2. Kirkby's GuerrieriLorenzoni2017.m explains that Table 1 reports B and phi divided by annual GDP.

Income grid: GL's 12 equally spaced log points (up to ±1.06032) plus unemployment, with job-finding 0.882 and separation 0.0573. puremacro's tauchen(12, 0.967, sqrt(0.017), m=2.1) comes close but not exactly: top point 1.0747 vs 1.0603, variance 0.254 vs 0.268, largest transition-probability gap 0.033. Either hard-code GL's 12x12 matrix with a citation or recalibrate beta.

Licensing: the GL zip has only a readme and no licence. Freeze a few numbers with a citation; do not vendor the .mat or .m files. Kirkby's code is GPL-3: cite it, do not copy it.

Runtime: pure numpy/scipy, about 40 s per transition in CPython and slower in Pyodide. A warm start or a Broyden update would cut this.
vets.novelty_check:
There is no Guerrieri-Lorenzoni or credit-crunch content anywhere in the repo; the only grep hits are Guerrieri-Iacoviello OccBin. PLAN.md and REVIEW.md do not list it. It differs from the pending MNS forward-guidance and Krusell-Smith items, and from notebook 52, which is Aiyagari TFP shocks with a >= 0, and notebook 02, which is a discrete-grid Aiyagari MIT shock.

The proposed Tauchen section partly repeats notebook 67, which already varies the Tauchen width (notebooks/67_bewley_classics_replication.py:159). Anchoring in 02 would bloat that notebook, so this should be a new showcase, number 69.

vets.capabilities_check: The symbols exist, but the proposed engine is the wrong one. transition_path (puremacro/vfi/transition.py:40) runs discrete VFI only. Each period of each iteration rebuilds the full return tensor (:68) and takes a greedy Bellman step (:70). P_z is fixed along the path (:53), and the stored policy is only the a' index (:71). A GL-sized period step measured in this session took 0.46 s at 201 asset points and 2.36 s at 501. At T=100 that is roughly 4 minutes per fixed-point iteration. Grid bias is also large: at GL's own r1, discrete VFI gives bond demand 2.509 (201 points) and 2.632 (501 points) against B=2.671. The only notebook that uses it, notebooks/02_aggregate_shocks.py:200-201, works at n_a=100 with tol=2e-3 (quarterly), about 0.8 annual points. GL's result, a rate below zero for 5 quarters, needs roughly 0.01-point accuracy. No EGM transition fits either. solve_egm (puremacro/vfi/egm.py:27) takes exogenous income only. solve_continuous_transition (puremacro/vfi/continuous_transition.py:744) is Aiyagari-specific (shock_var z/r/beta) and has no borrowing-limit path, bond supply B or labor choice. Reusable pieces: young_lottery_weights and continuous_push_distribution (puremacro/vfi/continuous_distribution.py:84, :293), tauchen (puremacro/vfi/discretize.py:19), and the intratemporal-labor pattern in puremacro/vfi/aiyagari_endogenous.py:36. stationary_equilibrium (puremacro/vfi/equilibrium.py:36) is a scalar brentq over VFI and fine only for coarse checks. VFIProblem is at puremacro/vfi/problem.py:213. The EGM needed is small. With separable utility labor is closed form, n = max(0, 1 - (psi/theta)^(1/eta) c^(gamma/eta)). A numpy transliteration of GL's backward-EGM plus Young-forward pass (scratch gl_egm_check.py) runs in 0.08 s for T=100 on GL's 200-point grid, so a full solve of 100-400 iterations takes about 10-30 s and is Pyodide-safe. The proposal's gap statement is wrong: the ZLB variant needs no NK block (see oracle_check).
vets.oracle_check:
The oracle is much stronger than 'figures only'. The authors' own replication package is public and was downloaded in this session from sites.northwestern.edu/guidolor/files/2017/03/replication-codes-for-Credit-Crises-2017-1f7cb32.zip (MATLAB). Its contents:
- par.mat: calibration, including the 13x13 chain.
- grid.mat: 200 points on [-2, 50].
- steady.mat: Y1=0.41738, Y2=0.41667, r1=2.5% and r2=1.5004% annual, debt/GDP 0.18 and 0.08, plus policies and distributions.
- trans.mat: the flexible-price r_t over 100 quarters.
- trans_fix.mat: the ZLB r_t and the wedge omega_t.

The saved paths are equilibria. Re-run through the numpy EGM transliteration, the bond-market residual is at most 2.6e-5 (B=2.67) and the goods residual Y-C at most 3.8e-5. The re-run also matches the published text in the author-posted Nov-2016 final version (sites.northwestern.edu/guidolor/files/2017/03/Credit-Crises-November-2016-18p6etp.pdf):
- Flexible prices: r_t = -0.96, -0.97, -1.55, -2.07, -1.56, +0.02 (annual %), negative in quarters 1-5; the text says 'negative for the first 5 quarters'.
- Output impact -1.112%; the text says 'contracts by 1.1% on impact'.
- ZLB: r_t = 0 in quarters 1-7; the text says 'in period 7 ... still stuck at zero'.
- ZLB output impact -1.744%; the text says 'about 1.7%'.

The QJE typeset text was not compared. In that version the ZLB is modelled with fixed nominal wages and a labor wedge, (1-omega_t) theta U_c + U_n <= 0, with r_t>=0, omega_t>=0 and one of the two binding. That is a two-component price path (r_t, omega_t), not an NK block.

Calibration caveat: the paper's Table 1 (beta 0.9711 in the final version, 0.9713 in NBER WP 17583; psi 12.48; nu, B and phi in yearly-output units) does not match the code (beta 0.97744, eta 1.5, psi 15.88188, nu 0.16695, B 2.67123, phi 1.60054 to 0.8767, linear over 6 quarters). Use par.mat and document the gap.

Kirkby's replication (github vfitoolkit/VFItoolkit-matlab-replication/GuerrieriLorenzoni2017, doc and .m fetched) is secondary. It says 'everything replicates just fine' but gives no numbers, and its GPL-3 license was not verified. The replication zip's readme states no license, so freeze a small numeric fixture with a citation rather than vendoring the .mat files or code.
vets.data_check: Synthetic and calibrated, with no external data. All inputs come from the authors' par.mat and inc_process.mat (13 states: unemployment theta=0 plus 12 Tauchen states; transition probabilities 0.057 and 0.882). The paper's figures normalise yearly output to 1, while the code has quarterly Y1=0.417, so figure axes differ by about 4*Y1 (Kirkby notes the same). Report both units.
vets.novelty_check:
Novel. A grep for 'Lorenzoni' across all .py, .md, .ipynb and .json files in the repo returns no hits, and 'deleverag' matches nothing relevant. There is no borrowing-limit-shock transition in notebooks 00-68, notebooks/course, curso/notebooks (T00-T09), puremacro/examples or PLAN.md.

ideas.title: Recursive preferences at order 3: Tallarini (2000), Caldara et al. (2012), Basu-Bundick (2017)
ideas.question: Can Epstein-Zin models be solved at order 2 and 3 with the value function as a variable, and do quantities stay invariant to risk aversion while the market price of risk moves (Tallarini)?
ideas.description: VERIFIED BLOCKER. Pfeifer's Caldara_et_al_2012.mod, with 'lambda' renamed, fails klein_solve at order 1 with KleinResidualError: row-scaled residual 1.573e-03 at equation 8, 'numerical breakdown of the QZ decomposition'. It fails the same way with eta=0 (no stochastic volatility) and with gamma=2, so the EZ auxiliary-variable structure s = V(+1)^(1-gamma), not stochastic volatility, is implicated. Dynare solves this file. EpsteinZinProblem VFI rejects psi=1 (epstein_zin.py:55), which is Tallarini's unit EIS. Plan: first diagnose and fix (scaling or classification of V and s), then (a) Caldara's comparison of Euler errors and moments at orders 2 and 3 against VFI, and (b) Tallarini's invariance result and market price of risk. (c) BB's uncertainty-shock IRF at the ergodic mean is a stretch goal.
ideas.paper: Tallarini (2000, JME); Caldara, Fernández-Villaverde, Rubio-Ramírez and Yao (2012, RED); Basu and Bundick (2017, Econometrica)
ideas.oracle_detail: Pfeifer's Caldara_et_al_2012.mod replicates the paper at orders 2 and 3 and lists seven errors in the paper (for example, nu=0.36218 not the Table 1 value, and sigma_bar=log(0.007)). Basu_Bundick_2017.mod replicates BB's IRFs and notes that BB's 200-period burn-in is too short. Run both via Dynare 8 and freeze. Tallarini's published tables and the Caldara/BB figures must be fetched.
ideas.data_detail: Calibrated.
ideas.library_gaps: (1) KleinResidualError on an EZ RBC at order 1; root cause unknown. (2) EZ VFI without the psi=1 (log) aggregator. (3) Parser: 'lambda' keyword, parameters assigned in steady_state_model, and steady-state .m files (BB). (4) Stochastic-steady-state IRFs for pruned order 3, which Pfeifer notes Dynare also lacks.
ideas.plan_overlap: Partial. PLAN's pending 'Order 3 you can trust ... then Tallarini (2000) or Basu-Bundick (2017)'. Notebook 68 did the fixtures and closed forms but not this economics part.

vets.required_changes:
1. Replace the "VERIFIED BLOCKER" text with the correct diagnosis:
   - The benchmark (gamma=5) already solves at orders 1 to 3 and matches Dynare 8 to 1e-13.
   - The extreme calibration (gamma=40) fails only because s=V^(1-gamma)~2e6. Rescaling to s=(V(+1)/Vbar)^(1-gamma), as BB's V_normalization does, fixes it.
   - The gamma=2 and eta=0 evidence came from edits to the inactive macro branch.
   Teach the rescaling as a lesson rather than blocking on a Klein fix.

2. Load a stripped copy of Pfeifer's file (model + steady_state_model + shocks + stoch_simul), rename `lambda`, and assert '_compiled' in parse_mod(txt) so the symbolic path is guaranteed. Separately, the library should warn or raise instead of silently falling back at dynare.py:1768. Add a test that loads a .mod with verbatim plot code.

3. Drop the VFI comparison arm. Use frozen Dynare 8 outputs as the oracle: decision-rule tensors plus order-3 means and covariances (not autocorrelations). Compute Caldara-style Euler errors by Gauss-Hermite quadrature over (e, omega) on the unpruned perturbation rules. Freeze numbers only (GPL).

4. Build the Tallarini part as a hand-written unit-EIS .mod: log V = (1-beta) log u + beta/(1-gamma) log(s Vbar^(1-gamma)). Two pitfalls to state explicitly:
   - The realized SDF must be lag-dated: m = beta (c(-1)/c)(V/Vbar)^(1-gamma)/s(-1). A forward-dated m gives a gamma-invariant fake price of risk.
   - R_f must go through an auxiliary E_t[SDF] variable, as Pfeifer's E_t_SDF_plus_1 does.
   Use Tallarini's random-walk-with-drift detrended economy only after fetching the paper. Cite no Tallarini, Caldara or BB table value until a source has been read.

5. Keep BB as a stretch goal. It needs the steadystate.m port (parameter assignments in steady_state_model are ignored) and EMAS GIRFs (burn-in or three-component x0; pruning.py:1724).

6. Rate cost medium, not high.
vets.capabilities_check:
The listed symbols exist where the proposal says: solve_dynare_3rd_order (puremacro/dsge/dynare.py:1052), klein_solve (klein.py:285, KleinResidualError at klein.py:251) and EpsteinZinProblem (vfi/epstein_zin.py:37, psi==1 rejected at :55). The real entry point is load_mod (dynare.py:2134), and the moments come from Order3PrunedSolution.theoretical_moments (pruning.py:1989).

THE "VERIFIED BLOCKER" IS MISDIAGNOSED. Pfeifer's file sets `@#define extreme_calibration =1`, so gamma=40, sigma_bar=log(0.021) and eta=0.1 are active. The earlier gamma=2 and eta=0 variants (scratch repl-struct/try_cal2.py) edited the inactive @#else branch ('gamma = 5;', 'eta=0.06;'), so they changed nothing.

My runs:
(a) Benchmark (extreme_calibration=0, gamma=5): solves at orders 1, 2 and 3 (order 3 in 3.5 s). With the file cut down to model + steady_state_model + shocks + stoch_simul, it matches real Dynare 8 (MATLAB R2026a) to about 1e-13. That covers the means and variances of c, l, k, y, E_t_R_k, R_f, V and s, and every tensor from ghx to ghuuu plus ghs2, ghxss and ghuss.
(b) Extreme calibration: order 1 works for gamma<=25. It fails at gamma=30 (residual 1.9e-5) and gamma=40 (1.573e-3), and still fails at gamma=40 with eta=0. At gamma=40 the steady state is s=V^(1-gamma)=2.27e6, so this is a scaling problem.
(c) Replacing s with (V(+1)/Vbar)^(1-gamma) fixes orders 1 to 3. On the stripped file, ghs2 matches Dynare order 2 to 3e-13. Basu-Bundick's own steady-state file does the same thing (V=1 via V_normalization). Dynare's raw and rescaled solutions agree to 1e-9, so puremacro's refusal is a conditioning limit of its unscaled QZ and residual check, not a model property. A column-scaling pre-pass would be a small optional improvement.

Tallarini smoke test (0.7 s): a unit-EIS log-aggregator .mod solves at order 3 for gamma from 2 to 200. ghu[c] and ghu[l] are identical across gamma. sd(c) moves about 1e-3 relative. sd(m)/E(m) rises from 0.0034 to 0.100, and E[R_f] falls from 3.63% to 3.52% annualised. So no VFI is needed for psi=1.
vets.oracle_check:

Use only order-3 means and variances from Dynare. Its order-3 autocorrelations are known to be wrong (see memory note), so check those against closed forms or simulation.

Partial overlap, but the core is new:

ideas.title: Volatility shocks in emerging markets: Fernández-Villaverde et al. (2011) and the Born-Pfeifer (2014) comment
ideas.question: How much do shocks to the volatility of the country interest rate move output and investment in Argentina, and why does that effect exist only at third order?
ideas.description: A small-open-economy RBC with stochastic volatility in the interest-rate spread is solved at order 3 with pruning. The notebook computes the volatility-shock IRF, which is zero at orders 1 and 2, and Born-Pfeifer's variance decomposition and targeted moments. It connects to notebook 68 and to the Latin American data theme.

ideas.title: Capital-skill complementarity on the original data: Krusell-Ohanian-Ríos-Rull-Violante (2000)
ideas.question: Does the nested CES with equipment-skill complementarity reproduce the 1963-1992 US skill premium from factor quantities alone?
ideas.description: korv_gmm estimates elasticities with a panel GMM on EU-KLEMS log-differences, which is not KORV's two-step pseudo-ML on US 1963-1992 data. The course notebook quotes KORV's structural sigma and rho as references. A replication would rebuild KORV's data and estimator and compare the skill-premium path with the paper's figure.
ideas.paper: Krusell, Ohanian, Ríos-Rull and Violante (2000, Econometrica)
ideas.oracle_detail: KORV's estimates and skill-premium figure (to fetch). The Ohanian-Orak-Shen replication packages may supply updated data; unverified in this session.
ideas.data_detail: KORV's CPS-based labor quantities and wages and the equipment/structures capital series for 1963-1992. The source is not located.
ideas.library_gaps: KORV's pseudo-ML estimator with unobserved efficiency shocks is not implemented (korv_gmm is GMM).

vets.capabilities_check: The two listed symbols exist, but neither can do this replication. fit_korv_country is at puremacro/korv_gmm.py:168 and fit_korv_pooled at :221. Both run a two-step GMM on three self-instrumented log-difference first-order conditions (_moments, :99-127) with parameters (sigma_su, sigma_eu). That is not KORV's model. KORV estimate the nested-CES curvatures (sigma, rho, alpha, mu, lambda, psi_u0) from three equations: labor share, wage-bill ratio, and a structures/equipment no-arbitrage condition. They use two-step simulated pseudo-ML with latent labor-efficiency shocks (SR239 pp.15-19). In korv_gmm, sigma_es is a derived harmonic mean of sigma_su and sigma_eu (_allen_sigma_es, :136-148). In KORV it is the primitive 1/(1-rho). Smoke runs on KORV's own 1963-92 data (scratch smoke.py): fit_korv_country gives sigma_su=0.0003 and sigma_eu=0.81 (converged, 29 obs), against KORV's 1.67. fit_korv_pooled on one country has a single cluster, so the clustered Omega at :245 is rank 1 plus a 1e-8 ridge; the weight matrix is degenerate (it printed J=28.4, meaningless). The missing estimator is small to add. My scratch NumPy port of the Ohanian-Orak-Shen (OOS) GAUSS code (scratch spmle.py and spmle2.py, roughly 80 lines, numpy/scipy only) takes about 5 ms per likelihood evaluation with MCREP=500. On the original data it gives sigma=0.4119, rho=-0.5105, alpha=0.1107. With shocks switched off, the fitted skill premium (normalized to 1963=1) is 1.064/0.978/1.122 in 1970/1979/1992, against data 1.080/0.982/1.192 (log RMSE 0.043). It reproduces the rise in the 1960s, the fall in the 1970s and the rise after 1980. Caveat: starting from the GAUSS defaults (du0=-5, mu0=0.8, lambda0=0.2), my Nelder-Mead+BFGS run ended at a boundary (sigma=0.9994, mu=0.9999). A grid over (psi_u0, mu, lambda) found the correct basin.
vets.oracle_check: An independent oracle exists; I read the published numbers this session from these fetched sources. (1) The KORV working paper, Minneapolis Fed Staff Report 239 (Sept 1997), Table 2: sigma 0.401 (0.049), rho -0.495 (0.169), alpha 0.117 (0.003), eta_omega^2 0.043 (0.003), estimated on 1963-1992 with S=500. Table 3 gives elasticities 1.67 and 0.67. (2) Ohanian-Orak-Shen, FRB IFDP 1319 (May 2021), Table 5.1. Column I, "KORV(2000)": 0.401 (0.234), -0.495 (0.048), 0.117 (0.007), 0.043 (0.003). Column II, their replication on the original KORV data: 0.412 (0.015), -0.505 (0.056), 0.109 (0.003), 0.043 (0.004). Column III, updated data: 0.436, -0.517, 0.105, 0.083. Table 5.3 elasticities: KORV 1.67/0.67; updated 1963-92 1.77/0.66; updated 1963-2019 1.76/0.76. Column II is a strong oracle: a different code base (GAUSS, built on Violante's original code) run on the exact same data file. The point estimates agree across sources, but the standard errors do not: SR239 Table 2 and IFDP column I disagree for sigma, rho and alpha. The Econometrica 2000 table itself was not fetched; it is paywalled and web search was exhausted. The RED 2023 published numbers were also not checked against IFDP 2021. The proposal's plan to compare with the paper's figure is weak because it can only be done by eye. Parameter-level checks plus the three premium turning points are better.
vets.data_check: The proposal says the source "is not located". That is false. The Review of Economic Dynamics code archive, IDEAS entry red/ccodes 21-129 (https://red-files-public.s3.amazonaws.com/codes/21/21-129/Replic2.zip, about 1 MB), contains the original KORV series as OOS2022_SPMLE_CODES_AND_DATA/2SPMLE_data_korv_gross_original.csv. ideas.title: Time to build: Kydland-Prescott (1982)
ideas.question: Can a four-quarter time-to-build technology with non-separable leisure and a signal-extraction problem generate US business-cycle moments?
ideas.description: This would write KP's model with multi-quarter investment lags (the parser supports leads and lags of at least 2 through auxiliary variables) and compare its moment table with the paper. The agents' filtering problem (permanent versus transitory productivity) would need to be embedded.
ideas.paper: Kydland and Prescott (1982, Econometrica)
ideas.oracle_detail: KP moment table (to fetch). No independent Dynare replication was found in Pfeifer's DSGE_mod listing.
ideas.data_detail: Calibrated.
ideas.library_gaps: No solver for the agents' signal-extraction (partial-information) problem.

vets.capabilities_check:
The core machinery exists and works. I smoke-ran it in 0.08 s; scripts are in scratchpad/wf/kp82-review/ttb_smoke.py, ttb_sim.py, ttb_signal.py and ttb_edge*.py.
(1) Multi-period leads and lags: `_expand_multiperiod_leads_lags` (puremacro/dsge/dynare.py:1629, called from parse_mod at dynare.py:2066). A four-quarter time-to-build RBC, with FOC `phi*(lam+beta*lam(+1)+beta^2*lam(+2)+beta^3*lam(+3)) = beta^3*mu(+3)` and project states s1..s4, gives HP moments identical to a hand-expanded version with explicit L1/L2/M1/M2 (max diff 5.6e-14). BK holds (max |eig G| = 0.957).
(2) `LinearModel.theoretical_moments(hp_filter=1600)` (puremacro/dsge/build.py:674, class at build.py:199) agrees with a separate time-domain check (60 simulations x 1500 periods, dense HP matrix): sd(y) is 1.216+-0.005% vs 1.221% analytic, and sd(i) is 3.637+-0.016 vs 3.651. J=1 vs J=4 gives sd(y) 1.329 vs 1.221 and sd(i) 4.137 vs 3.651.
(3) The proposal overstates the signal-extraction gap. When information is exogenous (agents see only z = x + v), a steady-state Kalman filter from scipy.linalg.solve_discrete_are yields an ARMA(1,1) innovation representation that drops straight into the .mod. Its autocovariances match the true process to a relative 1.3e-15, and the model solves (sd(y) = 1.178%).
Gaps found:
(a) `load_mod(steady_state=...)` passes the override unchanged (dynare.py:2231), so the AUX_LEAD_* entries are missing and build_dynare raises "steady_state is missing values for ['AUX_LEAD_lam_1', ...]" (dynare.py:416). Passing the values through an initval block works.
(b) The auxiliary variable's root is taken as `aux.split("_")[2]` (dynare.py:1685, 1691). A variable such as lam_c resolves to 'lam', so AUX_LEAD_lam_c_* got a default guess of 1.0. That was harmless here because the solver converged, but it is latent.
(c) Lagged exogenous shocks such as e(-1) crash with an opaque "TypeError: 'numpy.float64' object is not callable" (dynare.py:409/441). Declaring an endogenous copy `ev = e` and using ev(-1) works. KP's timing re-dating would need this.
