ideas.title: Who controls inflation? Leeper (1991) regions, Sargent-Wallace arithmetic and the fiscal theory of the price level
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); fixed-regime prerequisite for the PLAN's Davig-Leeper notebook
ideas.question: Which pairs of monetary and fiscal rules give a unique equilibrium, and what pins down the price level when fiscal policy is active?
ideas.description: A flexible-price endowment economy with one-period nominal debt, a Taylor rule and a tax rule on lagged debt, written with dsge.build. Map the (phi_pi, gamma) plane into unique / indeterminate / no-stable-solution regions from the Blanchard-Kahn outcome. Under active fiscal and passive monetary policy, show that the price level jumps by nominal debt over the present value of surpluses (closed form). Add Sargent-Wallace unpleasant monetarist arithmetic (closed form), a Cagan seigniorage Laffer curve, and Sims (2011) 'stepping on a rake' with long-term debt in the sticky-price NK model. Extension: Davig-Leeper regime switching with solve_ms_dsge.
ideas.paper: Leeper (1991) JME; Sargent and Wallace (1981); Sims (2011) EER; Cochrane (2023) The Fiscal Theory of the Price Level; LS4 ch. 'Fiscal-monetary theories of inflation'; Walsh 4e ch. 4
ideas.oracle_detail: In this model the solution is unique iff (|phi_pi|>1 and |1/beta-gamma|<1) or (|phi_pi|<1 and |1/beta-gamma|>1), indeterminate for passive-passive and nonexistent for active-active. A scratch probe (scratchpad/wf/curr-theory/leeper_test.py, beta=0.99) classified 24 of 24 grid points correctly by catching dsge.build's BlanchardKahnError. The FTPL price-level jump and the Sargent-Wallace paths also have closed forms. Cite Leeper (1991) for the regions after reading the paper.
ideas.data_detail: Calibrations only. An optional empirical panel of US debt/GDP and primary surpluses can be fetched from FRED with puremacro.fetch.fred.fetch_series (puremacro/fetch/fred.py:46).
ideas.library_gaps: There is no structured determinacy result: regions must be classified by parsing BlanchardKahnError messages. Indeterminate models have no solution representation, because gensys returns zero G and Impact unless eu == (1,1) (puremacro/dsge/gensys.py:226). There is no Lubik-Schorfheide sunspot solution for the passive-passive region. gensys has 0 notebook call sites.
ideas.plan_overlap: PLAN (reviews/2026-09-23-notebook-catalog-plan/PLAN.md) lists Davig-Leeper (2007) with solve_ms_dsge. This notebook is its fixed-regime first half, and the two could be merged. Nothing in 00-68, course or curso covers FTPL. Only curso mentions Leeper, in reading lists.

ideas.title: Diamond (1965) OLG: dynamic inefficiency, social security, and the OLG solver checked against the closed form
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); extends 03, where OLG general equilibrium appears only in prose (notebooks/03_life_cycle_and_demographics.py:226)
ideas.question: When does a competitive economy accumulate too much capital, and how much capital does pay-as-you-go social security crowd out?
ideas.description: Two-period Diamond model with log utility, Cobb-Douglas technology and full depreciation. Covers the closed-form law of motion, the steady state versus the golden rule (dynamic inefficiency when r < n), PAYGO versus fully funded social security, and Samuelson/Tirole bubbles. Solve the same economy with vfi.olg at J=2 to validate the solver, then extend to J=40-60 Auerbach-Kotlikoff steady states with survival and population growth, comparing steady-state K, r and welfare across social-security regimes. Show J=2 transitions by iterating the closed-form map.
ideas.paper: Diamond (1965) AER; Samuelson (1958); Tirole (1985); Auerbach and Kotlikoff (1987)
ideas.oracle_detail: With log utility, k* = [beta(1-alpha)/((1+beta)(1+n))]^(1/(1-alpha)), plus closed-form r* and the golden rule and crowd-out formulas. Scratch probe (diamond_test.py: beta=0.4, n=0.3, alpha=0.33, delta=1, 4001-point grid): olg_stationary_equilibrium with FiniteHorizonProblem(horizon=2) and olg_aggregate reproduced k* to -2.1e-4 relative, a grid-limited error. Robustness: grid refinement plus random calibrations, per the 66 contract.
ideas.data_detail: Calibrations only. An optional dynamic-efficiency check (Abel et al. 1989 style) would need NIPA capital income versus investment from FRED/BEA (fetchable).
ideas.library_gaps: There is no OLG transition-path (Auerbach-Kotlikoff) solver. vfi.transition.transition_path (puremacro/vfi/transition.py:40) targets infinite-horizon households, and olg_stationary_equilibrium clears a single scalar price. olg_stationary_equilibrium and olg_aggregate have 0 notebook call sites. At J=2, the last period needs a penalty to force a' = 0.
ideas.plan_overlap: PLAN's 'OLG social security (steady states)' bigger bet; this notebook is its closed-form anchor and could absorb it. Related: QuantEcon 'Transitions in an OLG Model' and 'Two Computations to Fund Social Security', Acemoglu ch. 9, LS4 'Overlapping generations'. curso T02_A only asserts that the RCK steady state lies below the golden rule.

The closed form holds and is reproduced, but only to grid accuracy, not to rounding level:
- k* = [beta(1-alpha)/((1+beta)(1+n))]^(1/(1-alpha)), which I derived and checked numerically; no published number is used.
- PAYGO crowd-out, from the implicit scalar steady state s = beta/(1+beta)(w-d) - (1+n)d/((1+beta)R), k = s/(1+n): VFI matched it to 5.8e-5 relative at d=0.01 and 8.6e-4 at d=0.02.
- Eight random calibrations at n_a=2001: worst error 2.5e-3 relative.

Three caveats:
1. Grid refinement is not monotone. linspace grids nest, so n_a=2001 and 4001 picked the same savings point (identical +1.25e-4). A test of the kind notebook 66 uses (notebooks/66_optimal_policy_cgg1999_replication.py:353-380, rounding-level scorecard) would fail. The tolerance has to come from the grid: |k_num-k*| <= (Delta a/2)/((1+n)(1-alpha)), because the log-Cobb-Douglas map has slope alpha at the steady state.
2. If a_max is scaled by the closed-form w*, the grid can put a point exactly on s*. The dynamically inefficient calibration came out with an error of exactly 0, a coincidence that hides the real error. Use a grid that does not depend on the answer.
3. With log utility, Cobb-Douglas and delta=1, R* = alpha(1+beta)(1+n)/(beta(1-alpha)), so dynamic inefficiency needs alpha < beta/(1+2beta), which is below 1/3. The proposal's alpha=0.33, beta=0.4 economy is dynamically EFFICIENT (R about 2.24 > 1+n=1.3). The r<n section needs a low-alpha calibration: alpha=0.2, beta=0.6 gives R=0.867 < 1.3 and k*=0.160 > k_gold=0.0964, all verified.

The Tirole bubble steady state (R=1+n) is closed-form. It can also be checked with the solver by fixing K/L at the golden rule and reading the bubble off the market residual.

ideas.question: Can a Bewley-Aiyagari economy produce a Pareto wealth tail, and which ingredient does?
ideas.description: (1) A Kesten process a' = G a + y: the tail exponent solves E[G^zeta] = 1 (for lognormal G, zeta = -2mu/s^2), checked against simulation and against rank-size and Hill estimators. (2) puremacro's Aiyagari economy with bounded AR(1) income, with and without permanent beta types: the log-log CCDF slope keeps changing as a_max and the fitting window move, so there is no finite zeta, as the Stachurski-Toda theorem says. (3) Idiosyncratic return risk (Benhabib-Bisin-Luo) through combine_markov_chains and a log-spaced grid: the tail exponent matches the Kesten equation on the asymptotically linear saving rule. (4) Top shares against the Fed DFA, plus the Gabaix-Lasry-Lions-Moll convergence-speed argument.
ideas.paper: Kesten (1973); Stachurski and Toda (2019) JET; Benhabib, Bisin and Luo (2019) AER; Gabaix, Lasry, Lions and Moll (2016) Econometrica
ideas.oracle_detail: Kesten/Goldie tail equation (closed form); simulation truth for the estimators. The Stachurski-Toda (JET 182, 2019; corrigendum 2020, confirmed by search) theorem: with infinite lives, risk-free saving and constant discount factors, wealth inherits the income tail. Teaching issue to fix: T06_A fits a power law above the 80th percentile of light-tailed model distributions and prints zeta=3.499 (Aiyagari) and zeta=1.921 (beta mixture) with 95% CIs (lines 677-678). Its summary (line 965) calls the Aiyagari tail 'exponential (zeta~3.5)', a contradiction. The 'US empirical' zeta regresses five hard-coded thresholds of unstated source (line 773).
ideas.data_detail: The Fed DFA top-share series (WFRBST01134, WFRBSN09161, WFRBSN40188, WFRBSB50215) are frozen in the curso data folder that T06_A reads; FRED can refresh them.
ideas.library_gaps: There is no tail-exponent estimator (Hill, or Gabaix-Ibragimov rank-1/2). Discrete grids truncate the tail, so log-spaced grids with a very large a_max are needed. solve_hjb_achdou has no return risk or asset diffusion (puremacro/vfi/hjb_achdou.py:521 signature). combine_markov_chains has 0 notebook call sites.
ideas.plan_overlap: Not in PLAN. Notebook 01 covers Lorenz and Gini only. curso T06_A covers tails superficially and misleadingly (see oracle_detail). QuantEcon has 'Kesten Processes and Firm Dynamics', 'Wealth Distribution Dynamics' and 'IFP V: Stochastic Returns on Assets'.

vets.oracle_check:
(1) The Kesten/Goldie condition E[G^zeta]=1 and the lognormal formula zeta=-2mu/s^2 are correct, and simulation confirms them (above).
(2) Stachurski-Toda is confirmed from the arXiv API record 1807.08404 (JET 2019, doi 10.1016/j.jet.2019.04.001). Its conditions: infinite lives, risk-free saving and constant discount factors imply that wealth inherits the income tail. The 2020 corrigendum was not verified here because the search budget was exhausted.
(3) The oracle needs to be stated precisely:
- With iid returns and CRRA, the asymptotic saving rate out of cash-on-hand is s*=(beta E[R^(1-gamma)])^(1/gamma), G=s*R', and E[G^zeta]=1. With gamma=1 this gives s*=beta exactly.
- With Markov returns the correct oracle is the Beare-Toda spectral-radius equation (Econometrica 90(4):1811-1833, 2022; arXiv 1712.01431), not E[G^zeta]=1.
- Ma-Toda (JET 2021, arXiv 2005.02379) give necessary and sufficient conditions for the asymptotic MPC to be zero, which breaks the linear saving rule. Parameters must be checked against them.
- Calibration is fragile. gamma=2 with the same returns gives zeta=0.25 and never settles inside a grid capped at 1e5. For gamma=1 the Pareto regime starts only near a≈1e3-1e4 times mean wealth, where S≈1e-9; in the top-1% window the local slope is 2.4-2.6, not 1.5.
(4) The T06_A critique checks out and is stronger than stated. With a_max=60 and n_a=120, T06_A's run reproduces zeta=3.499 and 1.921 exactly, with 5.2e-4 and 2.1e-3 of the mass piled at the cap. At a_max=240 the same p80 OLS gives 7.13 and 5.58, while the mixture's Gini and top-10 share barely move (0.843 and 68.8%). The printed zetas are artifacts of the a_max cap (T06_A_wealth_inequality.ipynb:219, 677-678, 965). The 'US empirical' thresholds at :773-774 have no stated source.
The GLLM convergence-speed argument was not checked against the paper.

vets.oracle_check:
The oracle is real, independent of puremacro and obtainable.

(1) Kesten/Goldie: for lognormal G, E[G^zeta]=exp(zeta*mu+zeta^2*s^2/2)=1 gives zeta=-2mu/s^2. In my simulation (mu=-0.03, s=0.2, zeta=1.5, N=2e5, T=3000, 9 s), Hill gave 1.49 and Gabaix-Ibragimov gave 1.456 at k=1000. Hill drifted to 1.396 at k=20000, which shows the window sensitivity the notebook should teach.

(2) Stachurski-Toda: the arXiv 1807.08404 abstract, fetched this session (JET doi 10.1016/j.jet.2019.04.001), says: with infinite lives, risk-free saving and constant discount factors, wealth inherits the tail behavior of income shocks. With a bounded Tauchen income process the wealth support is bounded (zeta is infinite). My EGM runs at a_max 300 and 2000 gave the same distribution. The local slope rises across windows: 1.71 (80-95th percentile), 2.7, 5.9, 9.6.

(3) A stronger oracle for part (3) than 'Kesten on the saving rule': Ma and Toda (2021 JET, arXiv 2005.02379v5). I read the PDF text this session. Ex. 2.2 gives the asymptotic MPC c_bar = 1 - b^(1/gamma) with b = E[beta R^(1-gamma)]. Ex. 2.1 covers gamma=1, and Cor. 2.6 says income is irrelevant. So G = R'*b^(1/gamma) (G = beta*R' with log utility), and E[G^zeta]=1 in the iid case. For Markov returns, Beare-Toda (2022 Econometrica 90(4), arXiv 1712.01431, abstract fetched) gives the spectral-radius equation.

My check used beta=0.96, R in {0.85, 1.20} iid and 5-state income: zeta* = 2.1262. The EGM's top MPC is 0.0400, equal to 1-beta. The exact sparse stationary slope was 2.145 at CCDF 1e-8..1e-9, 2.128 at 1e-9..1e-10 and 2.121-2.127 at 1e-10..1e-11. At the top 1% to 0.01% the slope is still 2.7-2.8, so the assertions must use the far tail and the text must teach slow convergence. With two-point R, log G is nearly lattice, so the grid should use 3 or more lognormal nodes.

ideas.title: Endogenous growth, one model at a time: AK, Romer (1990), Aghion-Howitt and Jones (1995)
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); nothing in 00-68, the course or curso covers endogenous growth (curso T02_A covers only exogenous-growth RCK)
ideas.question: What pins down the long-run growth rate, and why did the scale effect predicted by first-generation R&D models fail in the data?
ideas.description: Closed-form balanced-growth rates and comparative statics for AK, Romer's expanding varieties (lab-equipment and knowledge-spillover versions), Aghion-Howitt quality ladders and Jones's semi-endogenous model. Compare the planner's and market growth rates (R&D underinvestment) and give the R&D subsidy that closes the gap. Solve transitional dynamics (Uzawa-Lucas or Jones) on the detrended system with dsge.build and solve_perfect_foresight. Run Jones's (1995) time-series test of scale effects on PWT growth against researcher counts.
ideas.paper: Romer (1990) JPE; Aghion and Howitt (1992) Econometrica; Jones (1995) JPE and QJE; Lucas (1988); Acemoglu (2009) chs. 11, 13, 14
ideas.oracle_detail: BGP growth rates: g_AK = (A - delta - rho)/theta, the Romer and Aghion-Howitt closed forms, and Jones g = lambda n/(1-phi). Numerical transitions must converge to the closed-form BGP, and their half-lives must equal the stable eigenvalue. Derive the formulas in the notebook (Acemoglu chs. 11, 13-14); do not quote them from memory.
ideas.data_detail: Theory part is synthetic. The empirical part needs PWT 10.01 and OECD MSTI researcher counts; puremacro has OECD SDMX fetchers (puremacro/fetch/sdmx.py, puremacro/fetch/_oecd_sdmx.py), but the MSTI dataflow code still has to be verified.
ideas.library_gaps: detrend_bgp and find_steady_state have 0 notebook call sites. There is no general PWT loader (see the development-accounting item). There is no growth-model module; everything is written with build.
ideas.plan_overlap: None. Syllabus source: Acemoglu (2009) Part IV (chs. 12-15) and ch. 11, verified from the TOC PDF fetched this session.

vets.oracle_check:
The self-derived closed-form BGP oracle is sound, and build reproduces it to machine precision. Two parts are wrong as stated.
(a) The listed formulas (g_AK=(A-delta-rho)/theta, g=lambda n/(1-phi)) are continuous-time (Acemoglu), but build and solve_perfect_foresight are discrete-time. The discrete Jones rate is (1+n)^(lambda/(1-phi))-1: 0.0150374 against 0.015 at n=0.01, lambda=0.75, phi=0.5. The discrete AK and Uzawa-Lucas rates are [beta(1+A-delta)]^(1/theta) and [beta(1-dh+B)]^(1/theta). Asserting the continuous-time formulas against the numerical output would fail.
(b) "Half-lives must equal the stable eigenvalue" is false for nonlinear paths. The nonlinear half-life is 2.60 periods from k0=0.5k* and 3.06 from 0.95k*, against a linear 3.10. ideas.title: Why hold money? MIU, cash-in-advance, Lagos-Wright and the welfare cost of inflation
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); monetary theory (Walsh 4e chs. 2-4, LS4 'Credit and currency') has no coverage anywhere in the catalog
ideas.question: What does 10% inflation cost, and why is the Friedman rule optimal in three different models of money?
ideas.description: Sidrauski money-in-utility: superneutrality, with steady-state capital independent of money growth. Cash-in-advance (Cooley-Hansen style): the inflation tax on consumption and labour, with dynamics solved through load_mod. Lagos-Wright: the closed-form decentralised-market quantity as a function of the nominal rate and bargaining power. Lucas (2000): the welfare cost of inflation from estimated money demand (log-log versus semi-log) on FRED data. Finally, the Friedman rule in all three models.
ideas.paper: Sidrauski (1967); Cooley and Hansen (1989) AER; Lucas (2000) Econometrica; Lagos and Wright (2005) JPE; Walsh 4e chs. 2-4
ideas.oracle_detail: Steady-state closed forms: MIU superneutrality, the CIA labour wedge and the Lagos-Wright first-order condition. The Lucas (2000) welfare-cost integral is closed form given the money-demand curve. Before citing, fetch and read the published welfare-cost numbers of Lucas (2000), Cooley-Hansen (1989) and Lagos-Wright (2005). Second route: Pfeifer's GPL McCandless_2008_Chapter_9.mod (MIU) run in Dynare, freezing numbers only.
ideas.data_detail: FRED M1/M2, nominal GDP and the 3-month T-bill rate through puremacro.fetch.fred.
ideas.library_gaps: None essential; there are no money-demand or welfare-cost helpers.
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

The external oracles exist and I reproduced them.

Costs match within 0.001; for example, Table 1 at θ=0.5 gives 0.032/0.041, and at θ=0.343 gives 0.046/0.068 (the 0.068 matched exactly). q matches within 0.006; the gap comes from rounded η and the unreported b.

It gives the closed forms w=A(η/(1-η))r^(1-η) and w=(B/ξ)[1-(1+ξr)e^(-ξr)], and Lucas's calibrations A=0.0488, η=0.5, B=0.3548, ξ=7. The sweep distortion from 1994 on matters as much as the 2020 break the proposal flags. M2 is not a valid substitute, because the own rate on M2 makes the T-bill rate the wrong opportunity cost. Lucas's own sample (1900-1994 annual, commercial paper rate) is built from historical sources (Census X-267, Anderson 2003, Friedman-Schwartz 1982), not from FRED. So the FRED fit cannot reproduce Lucas; at best it illustrates why measurement breaks matter. The data status is really "published calibrations plus illustrative FRED".

ideas.title: Menu costs versus Calvo: the selection effect and the kurtosis-over-frequency sufficient statistic
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); state-dependent pricing has no coverage (NK notebooks use Calvo or Rotemberg only)
ideas.question: Do state-dependent prices make money less powerful, and can two micro moments tell us by how much?
ideas.description: Solve a Golosov-Lucas steady state with VFIProblem: the log real price sits on a grid whose step equals inflation, so the drift is exactly one grid point, and idiosyncratic productivity follows a Rouwenhorst chain. Report the frequency, size and kurtosis of price changes against the Calvo counterpart, and show Caplin-Spulber neutrality. Compute the cumulative output effect of a small one-time nominal shock by pushing the distribution forward, and compare it with the Alvarez-Le Bihan-Lippi (ALL) statistic. A random free-adjustment probability raises kurtosis toward Calvo (CalvoPlus, Nakamura-Steinsson).
ideas.paper: Golosov and Lucas (2007) JPE; Alvarez, Le Bihan and Lippi (2016) AER; Caplin and Spulber (1987) QJE; Nakamura and Steinsson (2008) QJE
ideas.oracle_detail: The ALL (2016) cumulative output effect M = (delta/6 epsilon) Kur(dp)/N(dp) was obtained from search results citing NBER w20155; read the paper before freezing it. Calvo's exact cumulative response and Caplin-Spulber neutrality are the other closed forms; fetch the Golosov-Lucas (2007) published moments. Scratch probe (menucost_test.py; arbitrary monthly calibration): a 301-point price grid with 11 productivity states solved in about 8 s per menu cost kappa on numpy. kappa=0.01 gave a monthly frequency of 0.147 and kurtosis of 1.83; kappa=0.03 gave 0.080 and 1.94.
ideas.data_detail: Calibrated to published micro price moments (for example Nakamura-Steinsson 2008), which must be read from the paper; no data file is needed.
ideas.library_gaps: There is no general-equilibrium transition for a price-setting economy: vfi.transition.transition_path (puremacro/vfi/transition.py:40) is built around a price-path fixed point for savings models. There are no helpers for price-change moments. The grid-step-equals-inflation device restricts inflation to multiples of the grid step.
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

vets.required_changes:
1. Re-scope the oracles.
   - Use exact discrete-time checks: N*Var(dp) = sigma^2 (ALL Proposition 1, random-walk gaps, zero inflation), and Calvo delta(1-lambda)/lambda by push-forward, on a gap grid wide enough for the Laplace tails or with the truncated mass reported.
   - Present ALL eq. (1) as a continuous-time approximation. Show its ratio to the push-forward result and how it converges or fails, rather than asserting agreement.
   - Cite AER 106(10):2817-51 (doi 10.1257/aer.20140500) with w20155.
   - Name ALL's eps as the inverse labor-supply elasticity, separate from the demand elasticity.

2. Use random-walk gaps for the ALL section. Implement them as a post-decision state (last chosen gap) with z = rouwenhorst(n, 0.0, sigma) iid, spacing a multiple of h, and pre-decision gap = a - pi - s. The AR(1) rho=0.95 Golosov-Lucas design can stay for the moments and the Calvo comparison only.

3. Avoid the selection-lattice trap. Either keep a drift of one grid step, or make the shock lattice spacing equal to h. Explain that the grid device ties delta and pi to h.

4. Restate Caplin-Spulber. With sigma=0, output is constant and the price level rises by exactly pi each period, even though individual prices are sticky. Seed mu0 uniformly on the (s,S) cycle because stationary_distribution does not converge there. Do not claim that a one-time jump is neutral: it produces a permanent cycle on the grid.

5. Add push_distribution (distribution.py:17) and combine_markov_chains (discretize.py:136) to the capability list. Build CalvoPlus as an iid free-adjustment flag in z. Build Calvo with kappa=1e3 plus the flag, never -inf. Measure frequency as actual price changes.

6. Keep the runtime to about 8 solves, at 8-30 s each on numpy.

7. Read the calibration moments from fetched papers: ALL (AEA free PDF or w20155), NS08 (NBER working paper), and GL07 (NBER working paper, naming which version is cited).

vets.oracle_check:
I verified the formula in the NBER w20155 text: M = delta/(6 eps) * Kur(dp)/N(dp) (eq. 1). I read it this session in the PDF text that a parallel reviewer fetched to scratchpad/wf/menucost-adv/all.txt, lines ~91-95. The same text gives Kur = 1 (Golosov-Lucas), 3 (Taylor) and 6 (Calvo) at line 215. Crossref confirms the published version as AER 106(10):2817-2851, doi 10.1257/aer.20140500, and the AEA page offers a free PDF.

The formula rests on assumptions the proposed design breaks:
- continuous time
- zero steady-state inflation (small inflation is second order, line 237)
- Brownian (random-walk) price gaps (line 856)
- a quadratic loss and the steady-state decision rule (lines 1422-1430)
- eps in the formula is the inverse labor-supply elasticity, not the demand elasticity. The probe names its demand elasticity eps=7, so the two would be confused.

It fails as a closed-form oracle for the proposed design (monthly periods, AR(1) with rho=0.95, grid step equal to inflation). With a push-forward of a one-step shock (gl_ar1.py):
- kappa=0.01: M/delta = 2.215 against ALL 2.083 (ratio 1.06).
- kappa=0.03: M/delta = 1.841 against ALL 4.029 (ratio 0.46).
The cumulative effect falls as kappa rises, while ALL predicts it roughly doubles.

Random-walk gaps with a drift of one step (rw_gap3.py) give ratios of 0.36, 0.50 and 0.62 at monthly N = 0.17, 0.10 and 0.05. The formula is approached only slowly as the period shrinks.

Oracles that do hold exactly in discrete time:
- ALL Proposition 1, N*Var(dp) = sigma^2, for random-walk gaps at zero inflation. It came out at 0.000900 = sigma^2 for Calvo, menu cost and CalvoPlus.
- The discrete Calvo cumulative effect delta(1-lambda)/lambda. The push-forward path matches -delta(1-lambda)^(t+1) to about 1%. The total was 0.01712 against 0.01800 because a +/-0.6 grid truncates Calvo's Laplace tails (1.45e-5 mass at the edge), so the grid must be wider.

Caplin-Spulber neutrality for a one-time jump is false on the deterministic grid with the optimal reset-to-S rule (cs.py, L=8). Output/delta oscillates between -0.125 and +0.875 forever and never decays.

vets.oracle_check:
The formula is real and I read it in NBER w20155. That working paper is titled "Small and Large Price Changes and the Propagation of Monetary Shocks" (Alvarez, Le Bihan, Lippi 2014). I did not read the published AER 2016 version.
- Eq. (1) (PDF p.3) and Proposition 7, eq. (22) (PDF p.34): M ≈ (delta/eps)·Kur/(6N).
- eps is the inverse of the labor-supply elasticity: M = (1/eps)∫(delta − P)dt, eq. (15), PDF p.31.
- Eq. (21) is an exact n=1 closed form that runs from Calvo (1/(eps·N)) to GL (1/(6·eps·N)).
- The formula assumes zero inflation, random-walk (Brownian) price gaps and a first-order approximation in delta. Proposition 8 (PDF p.37) makes inflation only a second-order effect.

Refutation of the proposal's own setup: the formula fails badly there. With AR(1) Rouwenhorst productivity (rho=0.95, 11 states) and grid step = inflation (0.2%/month), my numerical eps·M/delta against ALL's Kur/(6N) was:
- kappa=0.03: 1.84 vs 4.03 (a factor of 2.2).
- kappa=0.03 with lam=0.05: 1.44 vs 3.14.
- kappa=0.01: 2.22 vs 2.08.
- Calvo lam=0.1: Kur is 5.0, not 6.
- With 3-point shocks and a drift of one grid step per period (still the ALL price-gap setup), the menu-cost model is nearly neutral: eps·M/delta = −0.37 against a prediction of 26.

The oracle holds in ALL's own environment, and VFIProblem can express it. Set the state to last period's post-decision gap, let z be an iid ±h shock times the free flag, and write keep as a'=a+s. With zero drift, h=0.002, 241 grid points and xbar/h≈20, the ratio of numerical M to δ·Kur/(6εN) was:
- GL (Kur=1.00): 0.993
- CalvoPlus (Kur=1.56): 0.993
- Calvo (Kur=5.59): 0.998
Each solve took about 24 s. A standalone numpy solver, independent of puremacro, gives the same numbers: 0.993/0.998/0.998/0.999 for Kur 1/1/1.47/3.22.

Exact discrete-time Calvo oracle: eps·M/delta = (1−lam)/lam, not 1/N. It matched to two decimals: 9.00 at lam=0.1 and 199.00 at lam=0.005.

Caplin-Spulber: neutrality is exact on the grid with no idiosyncratic shocks and a one-step shock, because the uniform cycle maps onto itself.

GL moments: I read Table 1 of NBER w10187 (PDF p.21, printed p.20), not the JPE 2007 version.
- Frequency of change: data .219, model .231.
- Mean price increase: data .095, model .075.
- S.d. of new prices: data .094, model .1.
- Quarterly inflation: data .009, model .01.
These are a loose calibration target, not a closed form.

ideas.title: Sovereign default: an Arellano (2008) replication
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); the only sovereign-debt content is notebook 36 (climate debt sustainability) and curso T04_C's TFP cost of a default
ideas.question: Why do emerging economies default in recessions and pay countercyclical spreads?
ideas.description: An Eaton-Gersovitz / Arellano endowment economy: output on a Tauchen or Rouwenhorst chain, one-period bonds, default with exclusion, stochastic re-entry and an output cost, and an equilibrium price schedule q(b', y) found by fixed point. Report business-cycle statistics, the default frequency, spreads, and the bond price schedule and default set figures. Show method sensitivity (grid size, discretizer, interpolation) as in Hatchondo, Martinez and Sapriza (2010).
ideas.paper: Arellano (2008) AER; Eaton and Gersovitz (1981); Hatchondo, Martinez and Sapriza (2010) RED; Chatterjee and Eyigungor (2012) AER
ideas.oracle_detail: Target: Arellano (2008) AER business-cycle statistics table, to be fetched and read before any number is cited. Second route: QuantEcon advanced lecture 14 'Default Risk and Income Fluctuations' (Python/Numba) run offline with its numbers frozen; check its code licence first. Internal checks: monotonicity of the default set and bond-price bounds.
ideas.data_detail: Model moments need only the calibration. A data comparison needs Argentine GDP (fetchable from IMF IFS/FRED) and EMBI spreads, which are not freely redistributable.
ideas.library_gaps: A new solver is required. VFIProblem continues with its own value function (puremacro/vfi/problem.py:213), so it cannot express E[max(V_repay, V_default)] with re-entry or an equilibrium price schedule. firm_value_with_exit covers only max(0, EV) (puremacro/vfi/firm_dynamics.py:30). A candidate is a vfi.default module (Arellano one-period; Chatterjee-Eyigungor long-term debt later).
ideas.plan_overlap: PLAN lists 'Arellano (2008) sovereign default' among the bigger bets ('needs a new model').

ideas.title: Should capital be taxed? Chamley-Judd, Straub-Werning and Aiyagari (1995)
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); 66 states that it 'does not validate nonlinear Ramsey policy' (notebooks/66_optimal_policy_cgg1999_replication.py:441)
ideas.question: Is the long-run optimal capital tax zero, and what overturns the result?
ideas.description: Representative agent: solve the Ramsey problem by the primal approach and show a zero capital tax at an interior Ramsey steady state (Chamley-Judd). Add the Chamley upper bound on the tax and solve the transition by perfect foresight. Show Straub-Werning's counterexample in Judd's worker-capitalist model with an intertemporal elasticity below one. Heterogeneous agents (Aiyagari 1995): the Ramsey steady state satisfies the modified golden rule f'(K) - delta = 1/beta - 1, which requires a positive capital tax; compute it with stationary_equilibrium and taxed returns. Appendix: Barro (1979) and Lucas-Stokey tax smoothing, with QuantEcon's code as a second route.
ideas.paper: Chamley (1986); Judd (1985); Straub and Werning (2020) AER; Aiyagari (1995) JPE; Lucas and Stokey (1983); LS4 'Optimal taxation with commitment'
ideas.oracle_detail: K at the modified golden rule is closed form, the heterogeneous-agent economy must support it with a positive capital tax, and the representative-agent interior Ramsey steady state has a zero capital tax. Straub and Werning (AER 110(1), 2020; confirmed by search) prove a positive long-run tax when the IES is below one; use it as a qualitative oracle. QuantEcon's Lucas-Stokey and AMSS lectures give independent numbers for the appendix.
ideas.data_detail: Calibrations only.
ideas.library_gaps: ramsey_model is a linear-quadratic approximation around the steady state the user supplies: Jacobians and the objective Hessian are evaluated at steady_state_dict (puremacro/dsge/ramsey.py:755-783). There is no nonlinear Ramsey steady-state solver (Dynare's ramsey_model steady state) and no primal-approach helper. derive_ramsey_focs (0 call sites) returns AST nodes that must be assembled into a model by hand. stationary_equilibrium has 0 notebook call sites.
ideas.plan_overlap: None. The PLAN notes that RamseyResult.focs prints raw AST reprs.

vets.required_changes:
1. Do not call ramsey_model anywhere. Say in the text why it does not apply: its LQ is valid only for a quadratic loss around an efficient steady state (ramsey.py:783, :850). Use derive_ramsey_focs at most to display the t>=1 FOCs of W(c,n;Phi), and render them with to_latex (PLAN.md:84).
2. Representative agent: hand-code the primal FOCs, including the time-0 terms -Phi*U_cc0*A0 and -Phi*U_c0*(1-tau0)*F_kn*k0. Pass them to solve_perfect_foresight (callable path, t=0 dummy via `shocks`) and find Phi by brentq over the implementability condition. Assert tau_k,t=0 for t>=2 to 1e-10, and show the huge tau_k,1 (about 319% in the smoke run) as the motivation for Chamley's bound.
3. Make the Chamley bound an optional stretch, or narrative only. If attempted, use the MCP complementarity of solve_perfect_foresight only for a finite binding spell (Chamley's T<infinity case). State that Straub-Werning's bound-binds-forever case (Props 8-9) has no interior steady state and cannot be shown by stacked Newton to a steady state.
4. Straub-Werning: in place of a Figure-1 replication, (a) solve the log case as a growth model with capital priced at 1/s and assert the wealth tax converges to 1-beta (Prop 1); (b) compute the sigma>1 limit in closed form and assert k_g ≈ 0.0126 and a limit tax of about 85%, citing NBER w20441 section 2.2 for the calibration and both numbers. Distinguish the gross-return wealth tax from the tax on net capital income. State that the positive long-run tax comes with workers' consumption going to 0. Leave out the full sigma≠1 transitions, which need a custom 2-D VFI.
5. Aiyagari: fix K_MGR in closed form. Solve for r_net with stationary_equilibrium (or reuse the solve_egm route from nb 67 as a second solver) and report tau_k=1-r_net/rho. Spell out that revenue funds non-transferred G, that labor is inelastic and that B=0. Better, plot tau_k against B, because the level is not pinned by the MGR alone. Frame Ramsey steady-state convergence as Aiyagari's assumption, and read the paper before citing the MGR proof.
6. Drop the Barro/Lucas-Stokey tax-smoothing appendix to its own notebook. QuantEcon code cannot run under Pyodide; if used at all, cite only fetched numbers.
7. The usual obligations: an _es twin, catalog rows in notebooks/README.md and docs/notebooks.md, and the _TEMPLATE conventions.
vets.capabilities_check:
All five symbols are at the stated lines: stationary_equilibrium at puremacro/vfi/equilibrium.py:35, VFIProblem at puremacro/vfi/problem.py:213, solve_perfect_foresight at puremacro/dsge/perfect_foresight.py:595, derive_ramsey_focs at puremacro/dsge/ramsey.py:202 and ramsey_model at puremacro/dsge/ramsey.py:540. Two of them are unfit for this notebook and two do the work.

Unfit: ramsey_model. It builds W from the Hessian of U alone (ramsey.py:783, used at :804), drops the gradient term, fixes every steady-state multiplier at 0 (ramsey.py:850) and, on the DAG path, sets the steady state to zeros (ramsey.py:633). That is correct only for a quadratic loss around an efficient steady state, as in CGG/nb 66. It is wrong for a distorted fiscal Ramsey steady state, even though the module docstring (ramsey.py:1) calls it a "Nonlinear Ramsey optimal policy engine".

Unfit: derive_ramsey_focs. It accepts only per-period constraints f(y+1,y,y-1). It cannot represent the implementability constraint (an infinite sum plus time-0 U_c0*A0 terms). At most it could print the t>=1 FOCs of W(c,n;Phi) under the resource constraint. Its only callers are ramsey_model (:770) and tests.

Work, confirmed by smoke runs in scratch wf/captax-review/:
(1) smoke_cj.py solves the primal Chamley-Judd transition. It hand-codes 4 FOCs, uses the callable path of solve_perfect_foresight with a t=0 dummy passed as `shocks`, and runs brentq on Phi over implementability. Result: converged in 0.7 s, Phi*=0.0406, tau_k,1=319%, max|tau_k,t>=2|=1e-13, tau_n=11.3%. The proposal's risk statement "the Chamley-Judd section cannot ship before a nonlinear Ramsey solver exists" is false: no new library piece is needed.
(2) smoke_aiyagari.py runs stationary_equilibrium with a VFIProblem (7-state Tauchen, 300-point grid, sigma=2, beta=0.96, alpha=0.36, delta=0.08). It solves for the after-tax r at K_MGR: r_net=0.0366 vs rho=0.0417, so tau_k=12.2%, in 10 s over 12 evaluations. Laissez-faire K=5.97 > K_MGR=5.60, showing overaccumulation.

Missing: nothing in the library can do the Straub-Werning sigma!=1 dynamics. The paper solves a 2-D Bellman equation over (k, C_-) with an endogenously computed feasible set, in Matlab on 64-128 workers (NBER w20441, Appendix B). VFIProblem cannot impose the equality constraint beta U'(C)(C+k')=U'(C_-)k on grid choices.
vets.oracle_check:
The closed-form oracles are stronger than the proposal claims.

(a) Representative agent with separable CRRA utility: W_c/U_c = 1+Phi(1-sigma) is constant for t>=1. So tau_k,t=0 exactly from period 2 on, not just in the steady state. This is the analytic oracle; the smoke run gives 1e-13. Ramsey steady state: beta(F_k+1-delta)=1.

(b) Straub-Werning, read in this session from the NBER w20441 PDF text:
- Prop 1 (log capitalists, gamma=0): the wealth tax converges to 1-R/R* = 1-beta. The planner's problem is a standard growth model with capital priced at 1/s, so solve_perfect_foresight can produce the transition.
- Prop 3 (sigma>1, gamma=0): c_t->0, k_t->k_g (low root of k/beta+g=f(k)+(1-delta)k), with a positive limit tax.
- Their calibration is beta=0.95, delta=0.1, alpha=0.3, g=20% of f(k) at the zero-tax steady state. The text reports k_g=0.0126 and a limit tax of about 85% (gross-return wealth tax). My smoke_sw.py computes k_g=0.01258 and 1-R/R*=0.8561, so these are reproducible closed forms.

(c) Aiyagari: K_MGR is closed form. tau_k>0 follows because household assets diverge as r->rho, so r_net<rho for any finite debt B. The tax level is not closed form; it depends on B and on whether revenue funds G or transfers. A second solver can cross-check it (solve_egm route from nb 67 vs VFIProblem).

Caveats: the Aiyagari (1995) abstract (IDEAS/RePEc, JPE 103(6):1158-1175) confirms only "positive even in the long run". I did not read the MGR statement or later critiques of Ramsey steady-state existence in this session; the author must read the paper before citing. QuantEcon numbers can be an appendix oracle only if fetched and cited.
vets.data_check: The proposal is correct: it needs calibrations only, with no data, fetch or licensing issue. The Straub-Werning calibration values are in the paper text (NBER w20441, section 2.2: beta=0.95, delta=0.1, alpha=0.3, g/f=20%). QuantEcon's code relies on quantecon/numba, which are outside the Pyodide-allowed set (numpy, scipy, pandas, matplotlib). So it can only be a cited external reference, not a runtime dependency or a second route inside the notebook.

The central risk in the proposal does not hold. The Chamley-Judd section can be built with the current library and does not need a nonlinear Ramsey solver. I tested each section with prototypes in scratch wf/capk-tax/.
(1) Representative agent, primal approach: hand-coded FOCs, solved with solve_perfect_foresight (puremacro/dsge/perfect_foresight.py:595) as a callable eq(yp,yc,yl,eps), with a t=0 indicator passed through `shocks`, plus an outer brentq on the implementability multiplier Phi (chamley_primal.py). (2) Chamley upper bound tau <= 1 (chamley_bound.py), written as an explicit Fischer-Burmeister complementarity. With sigma=2 and b0/Y=0.5 the bound binds for 6 periods, one period has an interior tax (0.3675), and the tax is zero afterwards (<= 1.9e-14). The binding spell lengthens with initial debt: 6, 8 and 11 periods for b0/Y = 0.5, 1.5 and 3.0. Run time about 9 s.
Caveat: the mcp_bounds auto-pairing (perfect_foresight.py:811-814) pairs a variable with the equation that loads most heavily on it. The multiplier eta does not appear in u_c(c_t) - beta*u_c(c_t+1), so it would be paired with the consumption FOC, the wrong equation. Write the complementarity by hand.
(3) Heterogeneous agents: solve_egm + continuous_stationary_distribution + brentq, the pattern at notebooks/67_bewley_classics_replication.py:103-117, handles taxed returns and endogenous labor directly (aiy95.py). Each table takes 3-8 s. stationary_equilibrium (puremacro/vfi/equilibrium.py:35) wraps a discrete-choice VFIProblem. It is usable, but it is less accurate when the after-tax return is within 0.5% of rho, which Table 2 requires.
(4) Library pieces the proposal lists but that do not fit:
- ramsey_model (ramsey.py:540) is a linear-quadratic approximation around the steady state the user supplies (confirmed at ramsey.py:755-783). It is wrong for this task and not needed.
- derive_ramsey_focs does have call sites, contrary to the proposal: ramsey.py:770 and tests/test_dsge_ramsey_bgp.py:99. At most it could serve as a cross-check.
- Straub-Werning transitions for sigma != 1 cannot be written as a VFIProblem (vfi/problem.py:213). Next-period states are chosen on grids, and the Judd constraint beta*U'(C)(C+k') = U'(C_-)k is an equality. The paper solves it with a custom Bellman equation on (k, C_-) with an endogenous feasible set (NBER w20441 p.12, eq. 4). For sigma > 1 the path goes to c_t -> 0 with mu_t -> infinity, which stacked Newton cannot target.

ideas.title: Job search from McCall to optimal unemployment insurance (Hopenhayn-Nicolini, Baily-Chetty)
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); complements 18 (Beveridge curve) and course 08, 11 and 24 (flows, DMP, Shimer)
ideas.question: How generous should unemployment benefits be, and should they decline with the duration of unemployment when search effort is hidden?
ideas.description: The McCall reservation wage as an optimal-stopping fixed point, and the lake model's closed-form stocks and flows. The Hopenhayn-Nicolini recursive contract (promised value as the state) produces benefits that decline with duration. Then the Baily-Chetty sufficient-statistic formula against a brute-force optimum inside a McCall model with savings.
ideas.paper: McCall (1970); Hopenhayn and Nicolini (1997) JPE; Shavell and Weiss (1979); Chetty (2008) JPE
ideas.oracle_detail: Closed-form McCall reservation-wage equation and lake-model steady state. Internal consistency: the Baily-Chetty formula must agree with the brute-force welfare optimum. Fetch and read the Hopenhayn-Nicolini (1997) table before citing it. QuantEcon advanced lecture 50 'Optimal Unemployment Insurance' is a second route.
ideas.data_detail: Lake-model flows can reuse the course's frozen CPS/JOLTS series (notebooks/course/data) or puremacro.fetch.jolts; the model part is synthetic.
ideas.library_gaps: There is no recursive-contract (promised-utility) solver and no optimal-stopping helper separate from firm exit.
ideas.plan_overlap: None. Syllabi: LS4 'Search and unemployment' and 'Optimal unemployment insurance', QuantEcon Job Search I-IX.

vets.required_changes:

vets.capabilities_check:
Three of the four cited symbols are poor fits.
- VFIProblem (puremacro/vfi/problem.py:213, P_z field at :225): the transition matrix is exogenous and beta is a constant. The Hopenhayn-Nicolini (HN) cost recursion C(V)=min c+beta(1-p(a))C(V^u) discounts by a choice-dependent factor, and the savings-plus-effort model needs job-finding probabilities that depend on effort, so VFIProblem cannot represent either. Case2Problem (vfi/case2.py:36,44) has the same exogenous P_z. VFIProblem can solve McCall only through a contrived encoding (a in {U, employed at w_k}, z = offer, infeasible choices set to -inf). I smoke-ran it: n=60 offers, beta=0.99. It matches the closed-form reservation wage to 1.3e-9 in 151 iterations and about 5 s (scratch/wf/mccall-ui-review/smoke_mccall.py). That makes it a good cross-check.
- firm_value_with_exit (vfi/firm_dynamics.py:30) solves V=profit+beta*max(0,E V'), with flow profit always received and exit worth 0. McCall's V=max(w/(1-beta), c+beta*E V) has a stopping value that depends on the state, so the function does not map onto McCall. Drop it.
- dmp_steady_state (models/dmp_regime_dependent.py:159) is a regime-dependent DMP free-entry solver and has nothing to do with McCall or UI. Drop it.
- labor_flows (transitions_from_cps_flows at labor_flows.py:76, transitions_from_shimer at :151) is useful only to calibrate the weekly job-finding hazard (HN assume p=0.1 a week).
- Nothing in the repo implements McCall, a reservation wage, HN, or Baily-Chetty. A grep of notebooks, course, curso, examples, replication and validation turned up none.
vets.oracle_check:
McCall: the closed-form reservation-wage fixed point wbar=(1-beta)c+beta*sum max(w,wbar)q is exact and independent, and the VFIProblem encoding hits it to 1e-9.

Baily-Chetty against the brute-force optimum: the formula is the planner's first-order condition after the envelope theorem, so agreement is internal consistency by construction, not independent evidence, and must be labelled that way (notebooks/_TEMPLATE.md:33-34).

ideas.title: Time inconsistency beyond LQ: Kydland-Prescott capital levy, Barro-Gordon reputation and sustainable plans
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); extends 45 (inflation bias, sign checks only) and 66 (stabilization bias against closed forms)
ideas.question: When can reputation substitute for commitment, and how large is the set of sustainable policies?
ideas.description: The one-shot Barro-Gordon game and its closed-form inflation bias, connected to discretionary_policy's inflation_bias field. The repeated game with trigger strategies: the lowest sustainable inflation as a closed-form function of beta. The Kydland-Prescott capital levy. The set of sustainable values for a small game, computed with the Abreu-Pearce-Stacchetti / Judd-Yeltekin-Conklin outer approximation (as in Chang 1998).
ideas.paper: Kydland and Prescott (1977); Barro and Gordon (1983); Chari and Kehoe (1990); Chang (1998) JET
ideas.oracle_detail: Closed forms for the Barro-Gordon discretionary equilibrium and the trigger-strategy bound. Second route: QuantEcon 'Credible Government Policies in a Model of Chang' and 'Sustainable Plans for a Calvo Model' (advanced lectures 54 and 60, listed on the TOC fetched this session), with their numbers frozen.
ideas.data_detail: Calibrations only.
ideas.library_gaps: There is no repeated-game or APS set-valued dynamic programming machinery.
ideas.plan_overlap: Partial overlap with 45 and 66. Syllabi: LS4 'Credible government policies I/II', Walsh 4e 'Discretionary policy and time inconsistency'.

vets.required_changes: 1) Drop "connected to discretionary_policy's inflation_bias field" as a check. Compute the discretionary bias with the solver: add c=c(-1) and put the loss on (y - y*·c). Assert pi_inf=a*lam*k exactly and show where the field departs from it: 0.016 vs 0.020 at beta=0.5 for Barro-Gordon. Either fix the library (derive inflation_bias from the solver with this augmentation; pure-forward tests keep their values) or document the field as valid only for the pure NKPC. In both cases correct the E[pi^disc]=+0.0248 claim in notebook 45 (lines 231 and 478, EN and ES), since the solver gives 0.0162 for its gamma_p=0.35 model, and adjust the example and docs/dsge_phase_c.md:68-70. 2) Replace the Chang (1998) 2-D JYC and 'frozen numbers' route with the QuantEcon lecture 53 (calvo.html) tables. Assert theta^MPE, theta_0^R and theta_inf^R from discretionary_policy and lq_commitment, and the closed forms for theta^MPE and theta^CR, with atol 1e-3. Keep Chang as a 'How comprehensive' pointer or an optional desktop stretch only. 3) Compute sustainable plans with a 1-D APS interval for a discretized Barro-Gordon game (Chari-Kehoe/Stokey), with the action bound explicit and varied. Compare three punishments: Nash reversion (closed-form bound above), Barro-Gordon one-period punishment (x>=(1-beta)/(1+beta) in the linear-surprise version) and APS worst punishment. The Abreu carrot-stick check from calvo_abreu can be a structural assert. 4) Keep the capital levy as a short closed-form two-period section or a 'Your turn' exercise. 5) Retitle, e.g. 'Commitment, discretion and reputation: Barro-Gordon, Calvo 1978 and sustainable plans'. Call the lambda_{-1}=0 path the time-0 Ramsey plan (theta_0^R to theta_inf^R), not a timeless-perspective plan. 6) Write all code from the equations. Do not copy QuantEcon code (CC BY-SA). Freeze only numbers that you re-read from the page when writing the notebook, and cite it.
vets.capabilities_check: The symbols exist: discretionary_policy is at puremacro/dsge/policy.py:397, lq_commitment at :894, optimal_policy at :1157 and ramsey_model at puremacro/dsge/ramsey.py:540. The core premise, linking Barro-Gordon to the inflation_bias field, is false as a validation. The field is set at policy.py:806-810 and returned at :878. It is a hard-coded formula for the purely forward-looking NKPC, kappa*lam/(lam(1-beta)+kappa^2)*y*. Its inputs are guessed heuristically: y_star at :706, a kappa fallback of 0.5 at :784-786, and an output weight of 0.25 at :802. y_star never enters the solved dynamics, as docs/dsge_phase_c.md:70 says. Checking it against a closed form therefore compares a formula with itself, and the formula is wrong outside the pure NKPC. Smoke runs (scratch .../wf/tc13-timeincons/smoke3.py, smoke6.py) show three things. (1) On a Barro-Gordon model written for the solver (y=a(pi-z(-1)), z=pi(+1)), the field gives 0.0160, 0.0190 and 0.0199 at beta 0.5, 0.9 and 0.99, against the closed form a*lam*k=0.0200. (2) The solver itself is right when the target is carried by a unit-root state c=c(-1) with loss on (y-y*c): long-run pi is exactly 0.020000 at every beta, and 0.10 on the pure-NKPC CGG model, matching the formula. (3) On notebook 45's hybrid NKPC (gamma_p=0.35, notebooks/45_...py:118-125), the field reports 0.02475 while the solver's long-run discretionary inflation is 0.01619. The field reads 0.02475 at every gamma_p; the solver gives 0.02475, 0.02157, 0.01619 and 0.01191 at gamma_p 0, 0.1, 0.35 and 0.7. So the value "E[pi^disc]=+0.0248" printed in notebook 45 (line 478) is inconsistent with that notebook's own model. Beyond the proposal, the library supports a stronger link. With the same target-state trick, discretionary_policy and lq_commitment solve the Calvo (1978) Ramsey-vs-MPE problem in under 0.2 s (smoke4.py, smoke5.py). There is no repeated-game, APS or capital-levy code. scipy.optimize.linprog(method='highs') is already used in the library (puremacro/did/sensitivity.py:581, puremacro/lp/quantile.py:42), so a small LP-based outer approximation stays Pyodide-compatible.
vets.oracle_check: The closed forms are derivable and independent. For the one-shot Barro-Gordon game, pi_d=a*lam*k. Under Nash reversion, with x=pi*/pi_d and L=1+lam*a^2, the lowest sustainable inflation is x>=[(1-beta)-beta*L]/[(1-beta)+beta*L], so zero is sustainable once beta>=1/(2+lam*a^2). I derived this in session, and a 1-D APS grid in aps.py matches it (0.00910 vs 0.00909 at beta=0.2; 0.00435 vs 0.00435 at beta=0.3). The best second route is QuantEcon lecture 53, 'Time Inconsistency of Ramsey Plans' (https://python-advanced.quantecon.org/calvo.html), not the Chang lecture. I read its tables and formulas this session through WebFetch. Parameters are alpha=1, u1=0.5, u2=3. For c=2 and beta 0.7/0.8/0.99: theta*=-0.167; theta_inf^R=-0.121/-0.111/-0.100; theta^CR=-0.100; theta_0^R=-0.083/-0.081/-0.079; theta^MPE=-0.071. For beta=0.85 and c=1/10/100: theta_inf^R=-0.131/-0.044/-0.006, theta_0^R=-0.107/-0.028/-0.003, theta^MPE=-0.100/-0.022/-0.003. Closed forms: theta^MPE=-alpha*u1/(alpha^2*u2+(1+alpha)c) and theta^CR=-alpha*u1/(alpha^2*u2+c). puremacro reproduced every entry to 3 dp. discretionary_policy gives MPE -0.0714 (all beta), -0.1000, -0.0217 and -0.0025. From the lq_commitment path (lambda_{-1}=0): theta_0 = -0.0827, -0.0813, -0.0793, -0.1066, -0.0283, -0.0035 and theta_inf = -0.1207, -0.1111, -0.1004, -0.1308, -0.0445, -0.0059. -0.0445 and -0.0035 sit on rounding boundaries, so freeze with atol 1e-3. This oracle is independent: QuantEcon uses the quantecon LQ solver, while puremacro uses Dennis iteration and Klein QZ. The other two proposed routes are weak. 'Credible Government Policies in a Model of Chang' publishes no numbers for the value set, only plots and convergence statistics: 16 iterations and 103.53 s at beta=0.3, 40 iterations and 276.16 s at beta=0.8, on 280 action points with N_g=10. It also depends on the polytope package, which is not in Pyodide. 'Sustainable Plans for a Calvo Model' (calvo_abreu) reports only booleans: the Abreu plan (mu=0.1 for T_A=10 periods) is self-enforcing (True) and the Ramsey plan is credible (True). Use it as a structural check, not a numeric oracle.
vets.data_check: Everything is synthetic: calibrations and grids only. No data acquisition or licensing issues. QuantEcon pages are CC BY-SA 4.0 (as stated on the pages fetched). Citing their printed numbers as oracle values is fine. Porting their code into the MIT-licensed repo (LICENSE) would bring share-alike obligations, so reimplement from the equations.

No notebook in 00-68, no course file in notebooks/course or curso/notebooks T00-T09, no example and no PLAN.md item covers repeated-game reputation, trigger strategies, sustainable plans (APS, Chari-Kehoe, Stokey), Calvo (1978) Ramsey vs MPE, or the capital levy. The only overlaps are thin. Notebook 45 asserts only the sign and monotonicity of the inflation_bias field (notebooks/45_...py:238, 521-525). Notebook 66 checks stabilization bias against CGG closed forms and never touches y*. curso T03_F cites Kydland-Prescott 1977 once in prose. puremacro/examples/dsge_optimal_discretion.py:11 mentions the Kydland-Prescott / Barro-Gordon bias only through the same field. A grep of PLAN.md and the 09-20 REVIEW.md finds no time-inconsistency item; PLAN's forward-guidance puzzle entry is a different topic.

ideas.title: Information frictions: Lucas islands, sticky information and rational inattention
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); no coverage (the 09-20 review's 'information-set lab' is about data vintages, not this)
ideas.question: How much monetary non-neutrality can information frictions alone produce?
ideas.description: Lucas islands: signal extraction with a closed-form Kalman gain, and the flattening of the Phillips curve as the variance of monetary shocks rises. The Mankiw-Reis sticky-information Phillips curve, written as a truncated sum in load_mod and checked against its closed-form IRF. Sims (2003) Gaussian rational inattention (posterior variance scales with 2^(-2 kappa)). A Blahut-Arimoto iteration that converges to the Matějka-McKay logit.
ideas.paper: Lucas (1972, 1973); Mankiw and Reis (2002) QJE; Sims (2003) JME; Matějka and McKay (2015) AER
ideas.oracle_detail: Closed-form Kalman gains, the sticky-information IRF, and the Gaussian rational-inattention and logit solutions. The truncation error of the sticky-information sum must fall geometrically with the truncation length.
ideas.data_detail: Calibrations only. The optional Lucas (1973) cross-country test needs output and inflation variances by country (IMF IFS or PWT, fetchable).
ideas.library_gaps: There is no rational-inattention solver (Blahut-Arimoto) and no sticky-information block; long lag sums have to be written into the .mod by hand.
ideas.plan_overlap: None. Syllabus: Walsh 4e 'Informational and portfolio rigidities'.

vets.required_changes:
1. Do not use EXPECTATION(k)(.) in the .mod. It raises NameError in load_mod (dynare.py path; the AST ignores k at _ast.py:763-767 and 878). Write sticky information as the forecast chain f1 = x(+1), fk = f{k-1}(+1), with E_{t-j}x_t = fj(-j), generated with @#for macros; this is verified to work. Optionally file a library issue to fix the operator, or reject it clearly, and correct docs/dsge_build.md:264.

2. Oracle for sticky information: use the price-level formulation with random-walk money.
- Closed form: p_t = L_t*a/(1-(1-a)L_t), with L_t = 1-(1-lam)^(t+1). The truncated model uses L_min(t,J) and must match to machine precision.
- Plot the gap to infinite J against J to show the (1-lam)^(J+1) decay.
- Cap J at 30 (468 variables, about 3 s natively). J=40 takes 15 s natively, which is risky under Pyodide.
- If the MR inflation Phillips curve with AR money growth is also shown, verify it against an exact MA-space solve rather than claiming a closed form.

3. Lucas islands: report the filtering gain P_pred Z'/F, or (a_filt - a_pred)/innov. kalman_filter's 'K' is T P Z' F^-1 and is 0 when T=0.

4. Rescope the rational-inattention section around the question:
- Keep Sims' Gaussian RI through kalman_filter (verified exact).
- Add RI price setting: the impact response 1-2^(-2k) to an i.i.d. nominal shock, and the AR(1)-tracking Kalman version.
- Demote Blahut-Arimoto/Matejka-McKay to a short appendix, or drop it. If kept, the oracle is the symmetric-case logit plus the MM optimality conditions (equal to 1 for chosen options, at most 1 otherwise), not "BA converges to the logit".

5. Add a Calvo NK comparison IRF (load_mod) so the non-neutrality answer is quantitative against a known benchmark.

6. The Lucas (1973) cross-country test stays optional. It needs a small cached WDI pull (no generic fetcher exists; see fetch/emissions.py:102 for the pattern), must be labelled a modern-sample rerun, and any values from the paper must be read from the fetched source.

7. Drop build (build.py:2348) from the capability list; it is unused.
vets.capabilities_check:
All three cited symbols exist at the cited lines: kalman_filter at puremacro/state_space.py:227, load_mod at puremacro/dsge/dynare.py:2134 and build at puremacro/dsge/build.py:2348. I smoke-ran each piece (scripts in scratchpad/wf/infofric-rev/smoke1-4.py).

(1) Sticky information through load_mod works when written as a hand-built forecast chain: f1 = x(+1), fk = f{k-1}(+1), p = lam*x + sum_j lam*(1-lam)^j*fj(-j). The chain can be generated with @#for macros (supported, puremacro/dsge/_macro.py:9). The price IRF matches the truncated-model closed form to about 2e-14 for J = 5, 10, 20, 30 and 40. Cost grows fast because every lag beyond one adds AUX_LAG variables (dynare.py:1656), so the model size grows roughly with J^2/2:
- J=20: 213 variables, 0.5 s
- J=30: 468 variables, 3 s
- J=40: 823 variables, 15 s natively, and likely more than a minute under Pyodide.

(2) The Dynare-native EXPECTATION(k)(x) operator does NOT work, although docs/dsge_build.md:264 and CHANGELOG.md:782 say it is supported. load_mod raises "NameError: name 'EXPECTATION' is not defined" even for EXPECTATION(0)(x(+1)). The AST drops the information-set index k: derivative at puremacro/dsge/_ast.py:763-767, evaluation at _ast.py:878, code generation at _symbolic.py:193. So EXPECTATION(-1)(x) would be treated as x_t on any path that got past the NameError.

(3) kalman_filter returns the prediction-form gain K = T P Z' F^-1 (state_space.py:196). For a static Lucas signal-extraction problem (T=0) it prints K=0, even though a_filt is correct (0.175 = theta*0.7 with theta = 0.25). The notebook must compute the filtering gain as P_pred Z'/F.

(4) Sims Gaussian RI through kalman_filter is exact. With signal noise chosen to match kappa, the steady-state posterior variance equals sigma_e^2*2^(-2k)/(1-rho^2*2^(-2k)) to 10 digits, and the ratio of posterior to prior variance equals 2^(-2k) for k = 0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2.

(5) The library has no rational-inattention or Blahut-Arimoto code, but an inline NumPy version is about 15 lines and runs in 2 ms.

build is not needed.
vets.oracle_check:
Obtainable and mostly independent, with two caveats.

Sticky information: for a permanent unit shock to money (m a random walk, desired price x = (1-a)p + a*m), the exact IRF is p_t = L_t*a/(1-(1-a)*L_t) with L_t = 1-(1-lam)^(t+1). Truncating at J replaces L_t with L_min(t,J). I verified both. The gap to the infinite-J model falls geometrically, like (1-lam)^(J+1). With lam=0.25 and a=0.1 (my test calibration, not the paper's) it was 0.306, 2.33e-2, 1.34e-3 and 7.5e-5 at J = 10, 20, 30 and 40. The proposal's "geometric truncation error" claim holds.

Caveat 1: the closed form exists for this price-level formulation with random-walk money. MR's inflation Phillips curve with AR money growth has no closed form here; check it with an exact MA-space (lower-triangular) solve.

Lucas islands: theta = s_z^2/(s_z^2+s_p^2), and the scalar steady-state Riccati equation has a closed form. Both are independent of the library.

Caveat 2: Blahut-Arimoto iterates the Matejka-McKay fixed point itself, so "converges to the MM logit" is circular as an oracle. Real independent checks are:
- the symmetric case equals the plain logit (verified exactly);
- MM's optimality conditions (verified at a corner solution: the left-hand side equals 1 for the two chosen options and is 0.907 and 0.366 for the two unchosen ones);
- the concavity of the objective. A softmax-BFGS direct optimizer stalls near corners (objective 0.45928 against BA's 0.45964), so it is a weak cross-check.

No published table values are needed. I state none.
vets.data_check:
The core notebook needs no data, only calibrations. The optional Lucas (1973) cross-country test is harder than "fetchable" suggests:
- There is no generic World Bank WDI indicator fetcher. The only World Bank code is fetch_wdi_emissions (puremacro/fetch/emissions.py:102) and raw API calls in fetch/energy_transition.py:225.

ideas.title: Lumpy investment: (S,s) plants and whether lumpiness survives aggregation
ideas.anchor_notebook: new showcase notebook (69+); course 10_b1_capital_ajuste_es.py covers only convex adjustment costs and q theory
ideas.question: Do fixed adjustment costs at the plant level change aggregate investment dynamics once prices adjust?
ideas.description: A plant-level (S,s) investment problem with a fixed cost and an adjust decision on the VFIProblem d_grid. Report the steady-state distribution of capital gaps, the hazard of adjusting (Caballero-Engel) and the spike share. Contrast partial-equilibrium with general-equilibrium responses to an aggregate shock, the Thomas (2002) / Khan-Thomas (2008) smoothing result, with a Krusell-Smith-style forecast rule.
ideas.paper: Khan and Thomas (2008) Econometrica; Thomas (2002) JPE; Caballero and Engel (1999) Econometrica
ideas.oracle_detail: In the frictionless limit (fixed cost to zero) the model must converge to the closed-form frictionless investment rule. The simulated panel must reproduce the distribution-implied hazard. Fetch and read the Khan-Thomas (2008) published moments before citing them.
ideas.data_detail: Calibrations only; plant-level spike moments come from published papers.
ideas.library_gaps: krusell_smith is written for households. General equilibrium with a firm distribution over (k, z) and aggregate shocks needs a new firm-side approximate-aggregation loop. Case2Problem has 0 call sites.
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

vets.required_changes:
1. Replace the d_grid design:
   - Use VFIProblem without d_grid on a geometric capital grid with log step -log(1-delta)/m, so not adjusting means moving down m indices (KT trend growth folds into (1-delta)/gamma).
   - Fold iid xi nodes into the exogenous state using a flat-index z_grid.
   - Or, preferably, write a small solver with a continuous target and a closed-form uniform-xi hazard.
2. Remove Case2Problem and krusell_smith from capabilities, and drop the KS forecast rule.
3. Do GE as a perfect-foresight response to a one-time unanticipated TFP shock. This needs a new library piece:
   - a KT plant block (continuous k*(z), hazard G(xi*), forward step via lottery_push);
   - a Newton/Broyden price-path solver with finite-difference sequence-space Jacobian and price bounds, e.g. transition_path(method="broyden").
   - Add tests before writing the notebook.
4. Oracles:
   - frictionless closed-form target;
   - KT lemma 2: frictionless heterogeneous-plant GE equals the representative-firm RBC path from dsge.solve_perfect_foresight;
   - closed-form uniform vintage distribution and spike share 1/N for a deterministic fixed cost with no idiosyncratic shock;
   - KT Table 2 plant moments and Table 3 PE-vs-GE investment volatility, cited to NBER w12845 PDF p.41-42 (that version, unless the Econometrica 2008 text is fetched);
   - label the panel-vs-distribution check as internal consistency.
5. Reframe the question as PE-vs-GE and lumpy-vs-frictionless impulse responses (a 2x2). State that Table 3's skewness and kurtosis need aggregate risk and are out of scope.
6. Show KT's traditional-vs-extended rows (inaction 0.789 vs 0.073) as the plant-level teaching point. Define the hazard on the gap log k*(z) - log((1-delta)k), and say it is a step function if xi is discretised.
7. Mention the literature after KT only after fetching it.
8. Runtime budget: steady-state brentq about 40 s; keep T around 40 and nk at 200 or less.
9. Treat it as a new 69+ bilingual notebook, not an addition to course 10_b1.
vets.capabilities_check:
The partial-equilibrium (PE) half works with the library as it stands. The general-equilibrium (GE) half has no working capability.

(1) VFIProblem (puremacro/vfi/problem.py:213; d_grid at :229) fits, but d_grid is the wrong tool. The adjust decision already follows from whether k' equals (1-delta)k, and a d axis would double the return tensor (returnfn.py builds (n_d,n_a',n_a,n_z)). Undepreciated capital is off-grid unless the grid is geometric with log step -log(1-delta)/m, so that not adjusting means moving down m indices. There is no closed-form expectation over a continuous fixed cost xi~U[0,xibar], so xi nodes must be folded into the exogenous state (kron(P_z, ones/n_xi)), and the hazard then comes out as a step function.
- Smoke run (scratchpad/wf/lumpy-inv-rev/smoke_pe.py): nk=141, 5 z states x 8 xi states, lumpy solve 1.7 s. The frictionless solve matches the closed-form target with log errors of -0.008 to +0.012, within the half grid step of 0.0132. simulate_panel (simulate.py:22) with 20k plants reproduces the stationary adjust share (0.1254 vs 0.1253, L1 distance 0.010).

(2) Case2Problem (case2.py:36) is numpy-only and uses integer a' indices (:95), so it needs the same geometric grid and adds nothing. It has no call sites outside tests/test_vfi/test_vfi_case2.py. Drop it.

(3) krusell_smith (krusell_smith.py:192) is hard-wired to households: _solve_household at :124 builds a consumption-savings rf, and _firm_prices at :112 is a representative firm. None of it can be reused for a distribution of plants, and it has no step that clears the market for p each period, which the KT algorithm needs.

(4) The best existing GE vehicle is transition_path (transition.py:40), a perfect-foresight response to a one-time unanticipated (MIT) shock with one price, p=1/C and w=eta/p. It failed in my smoke runs (smoke_ge3.py, smoke_ge4.py):
- Frictionless case: the price path went to NaN within 200-400 iterations (the implied C went negative).
- Lumpy case: the gap stalled at 1.28e-2 after 400 iterations with damping 0.05 (103 s).
- The cause is its fixed-damping update (:81), which has no Newton step or price bounds, combined with piecewise-constant aggregates on a discrete k' grid.
- The grid also makes impulse responses jagged: frictionless PE investment for a 1% TFP shock went +56.5%, -12.7%, -11.7% (m=6).
- It calls np.asarray(prob.z_grid) at :65, so list-valued z_grid is not supported; a flat-index workaround is needed.
- The Broyden solver in continuous_transition.py:593 is private and hard-coded to household capital demand (r_max=0.041), so it cannot be reused.

(5) Pieces that can be reused: lottery_push (distribution.py:36), stationary_distribution, tauchen, and solve_perfect_foresight (dsge/perfect_foresight.py:595), which can serve as the representative-firm oracle.
vets.oracle_check:
The proposed oracles only partly hold up.

(a) Frictionless limit vs the closed-form target: independent and verified (see capabilities).

(b) "Simulated panel reproduces the distribution-implied hazard" is internal consistency only, since it runs the same policy through Monte Carlo. _TEMPLATE.md says such checks do not establish validity, so label it that way.

Stronger independent oracles are available:
- (c) KT Appendix B lemma 2, read in NBER w12845 p.12 of the PDF: without adjustment costs, aggregates do not depend on idiosyncratic productivity differences. So the frictionless heterogeneous-plant GE response to an MIT shock must equal a representative-firm RBC path from solve_perfect_foresight.
- (d) Deterministic fixed cost with no idiosyncratic shock: the stationary vintage distribution is uniform over N periods and the spike share is 1/N, both in closed form.
- (e) Published values, fetched this session from nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w12845/w12845.pdf. The Econometrica 2008 text was not obtained, so cite the working-paper version.
  - Table 2 (PDF p.41), LRD data: inaction 0.081, positive spike 0.186, negative spike 0.018, positive investment 0.815, negative investment 0.104. Traditional lumpy model: inaction 0.789. Extended lumpy model: 0.073, 0.185, 0.010, 0.752, 0.175.
  - Table 3 (PDF p.42), standard deviation of aggregate I/K: PE frictionless 0.128, PE lumpy 0.085, GE frictionless 0.010, GE lumpy 0.010. Persistence: 0.210 for PE lumpy, 0.662 for GE lumpy.
  - Table 3 comes from a 10,000-period simulation with aggregate risk, so MIT-shock impulse responses can only be compared with it qualitatively. That covers the PE/GE amplitude ratio; the skewness and kurtosis columns are out of reach.
vets.data_check:
The model is fully synthetic, so there are no licensing issues. The plant data behind the moments is the Census LRD, which is restricted-access (RDC), so only the moments published in KT Table 2 (credited there as "DATA: Cooper and Haltiwanger (2005)") can be used.

KT Table 1 parameters, read from w12845 PDF p.41: gamma 1.016, beta 0.977, delta 0.069, alpha 0.256, nu 0.640, phi 2.400, rho_z 0.859, sigma_z 0.014, rho_eps 0.859, sigma_eps 0.022, b 0.011, xibar 0.0083.

Reproducing KT's no-cost band b=0.011 on a geometric grid needs a log step of about 0.011 (m around 6 once delta and gamma are folded into (1-delta)/gamma). That gives nk around 200 with 15 eps states and about 8 xi states, and a return tensor of roughly 4.8M entries per period. Numpy handles this, but it fixes the runtime budget.

Measured runtimes: a steady state found by brentq over p takes 35-42 s; one transition iteration takes about 0.25 s at nk=215.
vets.novelty_check:
The topic is novel.
- Nothing on lumpy investment, (S,s) rules or Khan-Thomas appears in notebooks 00-68, puremacro/examples, replication, validation, PLAN.md, REVIEW.md or docs/replication.md.
- Course notebook notebooks/course/10_b1_capital_ajuste_es.py mentions lumpy/non-convex adjustment only in exercise prompts (lines 353, 377-378, 405).
- 04_firm_dynamics covers Hopenhayn entry and exit with a fixed operating cost, not investment.
- docs/models.md:344 covers a non-convex hiring cost (labour, not capital).
- PLAN.md's Krusell-Smith/Den Haan item is household-side, so it does not overlap.

ideas.title: Lag-augmented LP against Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2021) Table 1
ideas.question: Do lag-augmented LPs with Eicker-Huber-White SEs keep 90% coverage across persistence (rho in {0,.5,.95,1}) and horizons up to 60, and does puremacro's la_lp, as the catalog calls it?
ideas.description: Re-run MOPM's AR(1) design (T=240, 90% nominal) for LP-LA, non-augmented LP with HAR SEs and AR delta-method intervals, and score each cell against Table 1. Then run la_lp in a bivariate VAR design with extra_lags=1 against the library default (p+max h), which every catalog call uses. Plot coverage and median length by horizon; the exercise varies rho and h. The 2,000-rep pilot takes about 1.5 s for 12 cells; use longrun.chunked for the 5,000-rep version.
ideas.paper: Montiel Olea & Plagborg-Møller (2021, Econometrica), 'Local Projection Inference is Simpler and More Robust Than You Think'
ideas.oracle_detail: MOPM Table 1, read this session from arXiv 2007.13888 (pypdf text, scratch mopm2021.txt:416-442). LP-LA coverage: rho=.95 gives .878/.838/.806/.814 and rho=1 gives .874/.777/.676/.428 at h=1/6/12/36. Non-augmented LP with EWC HAR at rho=.95, h=12: .752. AR delta at rho=1, h=36: .348. A hand-coded LA-LP pilot (R=2000, scratch lalp_check.py) gave .889/.841/.804/.800 and .866/.748/.662/.428, within Monte Carlo error (s.e. about .007). Second oracle: the simulation truth rho^h.
ideas.data_detail: AR(1) and bivariate VAR(1) simulations; no data needed.
ideas.library_gaps: (1) la_lp defaults to extra_lags=max(horizons) (puremacro/lp/la_lp.py:164). Its docstring says 'PMW recommend p_aug >= p + h' (la_lp.py:131) and attributes the method to Plagborg-Møller-Wolf 2021 (la_lp.py:1; the same attribution is in notebooks/07_local_projections.py:287-288 and examples/la_lp_pmw_demo.py:1). MOPM Section 4, read this session, says 'we are including one additional lag'. Pilot (scratch lalp_check2.py; T=240, VAR(1), rho_y=.95, R=300): the default p+H gives coverage .82/.79/.76/.75 at h=1/6/12/24 with wider bands; extra_lags=1 gives .887/.85/.847/.83. Every catalog call uses the default: 14:262, 50:114, course/06:323, T05_B, T04_A. (2) la_lp cannot estimate a variable's response to its own innovation: with x==y the lags are collinear and it raises LinAlgError. (3) The library has no EWC HAR estimator for the non-augmented comparator, no wild recursive bootstrap (LP-LA_b), and no la_lp validation case.
ideas.plan_overlap: Not in PLAN.md. Complements the 09-20 review's 'uncertainty lab'.
