ideas.title: Regional multipliers and the missing intercept
ideas.question: What does a cross-regional panel regression with time fixed effects identify, and how far is it from the aggregate multiplier?
ideas.description: Synthetic regions receive Bartik-style spending shocks (a national shock times regional shares), plus a common general-equilibrium response (monetary policy or taxes) that time fixed effects absorb. panel_lp and panel_lp_iv recover the relative multiplier exactly, not the aggregate one. Show how the gap depends on the policy rule, and use spatial_lp for spillovers.
ideas.paper: Nakamura & Steinsson (2014 AER; 2018 JEP 'Identification in Macroeconomics'); Chodorow-Reich (2019); Wolf (2023) 'The missing intercept'
ideas.oracle_detail: The DGP defines the relative and aggregate effects analytically, and estimates are checked against them by simulation.
ideas.data_detail: Synthetic. State unemployment series are bundled in curso/notebooks/data_curso if an application is wanted.
ideas.library_gaps: No two-region NK model to generate the offset structurally. panel_lp_iv and spatial_lp have no notebook calls.
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

vets.required_changes:
1. Change "recover the relative multiplier exactly". The exact result is invariance to kappa: panel_lp at 1e-15, spatial_lp at 4e-16, shift_share_iv identical. Recovery of m_rel holds only up to sampling error and O(h/T) fixed-effects bias. Show Monte Carlo means, and use n_lags=0 with lagged-growth controls instead of level lags.
2. Derive kappa from the policy rule with a closed-form toy, and label it as a toy: the static monetary-union Keynesian cross, m_rel = 1/(1-(1-w)mpc) and m_agg = 1/(1-mpc+sigma*phi). Show that the panel estimate is flat in phi while an aggregate time-series IV tracks m_agg. Add a common demand shock and a national G that is partly endogenous, so the aggregate estimate is imprecise or biased and the precision trade-off is visible.
3. Define the multiplier as cumulative dy over cumulative dg. Use a per-horizon forward-sum spending column with panel_lp_iv(n_lags=0), or the ratio of panel_lp responses of y and of cumsum(g) to z. Warn that beta_h with persistent Bartik shocks is not a multiplier.
4. Before showing panel_lp_iv bands, fix it in puremacro/lp/panel_iv.py:45-59: put all second-stage exogenous regressors in the first stage, use lags of x, compute cluster/DK standard errors from 2SLS residuals, add an optional cumulative mode, and add a test against manual 2SLS. Otherwise show point estimates only and state that its se is unreliable.
5. Remove shift_share_iv from the core design. Keep it at most as a side cell on a cross-section with K spending categories, to show that its partialled-out constant is the same missing intercept.
6. Run spatial_lp on the exogenous or reduced-form shock, and state that aggregate = m_rel + c*gamma + kappa while 'total' is still a relative contrast.
7. Make it a bilingual showcase notebook (EN and ES twins, catalog and learning-guide entries) and link it from course notebook 09 §4. Do not edit 09 itself unless that is intended.
8. Cite no published multipliers unless they are fetched in-session, and verify the Wolf (2023) reference.
vets.capabilities_check:
All five symbols exist and are exported. I ran smoke tests in scratch/wf/regmult-rev (smoke.py, mc2.py, mc3.py, cummult.py), with N=48 regions and T=160.
(1) panel_lp, puremacro/lp/panel.py:26. Adding a common term kappa*gbar_t to the data-generating process (DGP) leaves beta unchanged to 1.1e-15 and se to 2.8e-17, so the core claim holds. It is not exact beyond h=0. The panel_lp_horizon_loop lag builder (_panel_helpers.py:276-277) adds LEVEL lags of a random-walk y. The Monte Carlo mean of beta_4 is 1.383 with n_lags=1 and 1.452 with n_lags=0, against a truth of 1.5 (MC s.e. about 0.011). That is an O(h/T) within-estimator bias.
(2) panel_lp_iv, puremacro/lp/panel_iv.py:14. It is manual 2SLS with three defects. (a) The first stage (lines 45-46) uses only z plus `controls`, not the second stage's n_lags lags. (b) The second stage (lines 54-55) controls for lags of xhat=pi*z rather than lags of x. (c) Its se comes from second-stage residuals computed with xhat. In the MC (200 reps, rho_G=0.9, endogenous local spending, n_lags=1) the mean is 1.480 with sd 0.049. Proper 2SLS gives sd 0.026 with the same controls and 0.017 with lags of g. The 90% band covers 0.85. With n_lags=0 the point estimate is correct (1.4995), but the reported se is 0.0235 against a sampling sd of 0.012, so coverage is 0.995. Tests check only row-order invariance and F>5 (tests/test_lp/test_panel_parity.py:101; tests/test_dgp_adversarial.py:92). With a persistent Bartik shock, beta_h is an impulse response per unit of impact spending (5.86 at h=4), not a multiplier. A per-horizon cumulative-spending column with n_lags=0 recovers the cumulative multiplier (1.251 against 1.25).
(3) panel_lp_dk, panel_dk.py:19: fine.
(4) spatial_lp, spatial/lp.py:983. Direct 1.48 against 1.5; indirect 0.287 against 0.3; kappa-invariance holds to 4.4e-16. It has no IV path (docstring line 98), so x must be exogenous.
(5) shift_share_iv, bartik/akm.py:146. It is a CROSS-SECTIONAL estimator that needs K>=2 sector shocks (line 211), so it cannot take the proposed one-national-shock panel. In a K=25 long-difference cross-section, beta is identical for kappa=0 and kappa=4 because the constant is partialled out (line 224), so it only works as a side example. Everything runs in about 7 s and needs only numpy, scipy and pandas, so it is Pyodide-safe.
vets.oracle_check:
The DGP oracle is partly tautological. The relative multiplier is simply the coefficient you plant. What can be verified exactly is invariance to the aggregate component kappa, and the library already asserts it: the spatial/lp.py:40 docstring, docs/spatial.md:434, and tests/test_spatial/test_lp.py:268-284. As proposed, "the gap depends on the policy rule" would be imposed by hand, because no structural model links kappa to the rule.
A closed-form structural toy works and I verified it. It is a static monetary-union Keynesian cross of my own construction, not taken from a paper: m_rel = 1/(1-(1-w)mpc) and m_agg(phi) = 1/(1-mpc+sigma*phi), which gives kappa = m_agg - m_rel. With mpc=0.4, w=0.5, sigma=1 and 60 reps, the panel cumulative multiplier is 1.251 (truth 1.25) at h=0 and h=4 for every phi in {0, 0.5, 1.5}. An aggregate time-series IV recovers m_agg: 1.666, 0.909 and 0.476, against 1.667, 0.909 and 0.476.
A dynamic two-region New Keynesian model in the style of Nakamura-Steinsson could be written with dsge.build_dynare (used in notebook 66). No such model exists in the repo, and it has no reference solution. No published numbers are needed. The Chodorow-Reich (2019) citation is confirmed in docs/spatial.md:486. The Wolf (2023) citation was not verified in this session because the web-search budget was exhausted.
vets.data_check: The lab is synthetic and needs no data. The state unemployment series exist as 51 *UR.csv files in notebooks/course/data (tracked in git) and in curso/notebooks/data_curso. They are FRED/BLS LAUS data, public domain, running from 1976-01 to 2026-05. They cannot support a real multiplier application, because the repo has no regional spending or military-procurement data or fetcher. A Bartik employment application (not a fiscal one) is possible from STATE_INDUSTRY_SHARES_2005, which is hard-coded in puremacro/fetch/state_industry_panel.py (BEA SAEMP25N 2005), combined with FRED national supersector employment (needs network). Keep the lab synthetic and drop the unemployment-data suggestion or mark it optional.
vets.novelty_check: This does not duplicate existing material. No notebook calls spatial_lp, panel_lp_iv or shift_share_iv; the only mention is in the text of notebooks/07_local_projections.py:292 and its Spanish twin. Notebooks 14 and 50 cover AGGREGATE multipliers only. Notebook 30a (a state-sectoral Bartik notebook) was planned in docs/plans/2026-05-10-notebook-30a-state-sectoral-bartik.md but never shipped. The topic is not in PLAN.md or in the 09-20 review. The anchor notebook, notebooks/course/09_a5_panel_narrativa_es.py §4, says time effects absorb common shocks but never says that this also removes the general-equilibrium response. The lab is the natural follow-up.

vets.required_changes: 1) Fix panel_lp_iv (puremacro/lp/panel_iv.py:45-58), or have the notebook compute reduced form over first stage by hand. Proper within-2SLS: same sample in both stages, residuals from actual x, lags of x as controls, cluster/DK SE. Add a regression test against manual 2SLS. Right now the SE is about 2.3x too wide (coverage 1.00 at nominal 0.90). 2) Make the offset structural. Minimum: a closed-form two-region currency-union Keynesian-cross/NK toy in which the relative multiplier is policy-invariant and the aggregate multiplier is a function of the Taylor coefficient phi, so "gap vs policy rule" is derived, not assumed. Stretch: a Nakamura-Steinsson two-region .mod solved with load_mod, run through the paper's own regressions (time-FE panel vs aggregate), with NBER WP 17391 Table VI/VII as the published target. The anchors are relative 0.83 across rules, aggregate 0.20 / 1.00, and 1.00 as the Woodford constant-real-rate closed form. Cross-check against MATLAB Dynare. Make the stretch optional, because exact 0.83 needs their full calibration, annual time aggregation and CPI deflation. 3) Re-cite Wolf (2023): use Prop. 2 / eq. 9 for the term, flag footnote 12 (cross-regional regressions differ), and use demand equivalence only as a coda on recovering the intercept from aggregate fiscal time-series evidence. Lead with NS 2014, NS 2018 JEP 32(3):59-86 ("identified moments": separable 0.83 vs GHH 1.42 vs roughly 1.5 in the data discriminates between models) and Chodorow-Reich 2019. 4) Drop shift_share_iv, or confine it to a side cross-section of long differences with 2 or more spending categories. 5) Use spatial_lp only on the exogenous Bartik reduced form, and show that `total` is still a relative contrast. 6) Ship it as a standalone lab (notebook 69, bilingual) linked from course module 09, not inside it. 7) Cite tests/test_spatial/test_lp.py:268 as the existing invariance check.
vets.capabilities_check: All five symbols exist, but two of them don't fit the proposal as written. panel_lp (puremacro/lp/panel.py:26) and panel_lp_dk (puremacro/lp/panel_dk.py:19) do the two-way-FE LP on y_{t+h}-y_{t-1}. In my scratch simulation (N=50, T=60, Bartik z=s_i*G_t, endogenous regional spending), adding kappa*gbar_t for kappa in {-1,0,+1} left panel_lp and panel_lp_iv estimates identical to 6 decimals. So the missing-intercept mechanics hold. Problems: (1) panel_lp_iv (puremacro/lp/panel_iv.py:45-58) is not true within-2SLS. It builds x_hat = pi*z with pi estimated on a different sample (the first stage keeps t=0, which the second stage drops). It controls for lags of x_hat instead of lags of x (lags are built at _panel_helpers.py:275-287). Its SE is panel_lp's generated-regressor SE. Over 200 Monte Carlo draws that SE was a median 2.34x the correct cluster-robust 2SLS SE, and nominal-90% coverage was 1.00 (0.87 with the correct SE). The point estimate is close but not exact (1.4967 vs 1.4934 from a manual 2SLS on one draw). With n_lags=2 the mean was 1.467 against a true 1.5. No test compares it with 2SLS (tests/test_lp/test_panel_parity.py:101 only checks that first_stage_f is returned). (2) spatial_lp (puremacro/spatial/lp.py:983) has no IV path (docs/spatial.md:463), so it can only take the exogenous Bartik reduced form. (3) shift_share_iv (puremacro/bartik/akm.py:146) is a cross-sectional AKM estimator that needs K>=2 sectors (akm.py:212). It cannot handle the Nakamura-Steinsson design of one national shock times a regional sensitivity. For a structural offset, puremacro.dsge.load_mod (dsge/dynare.py:2134) can solve a linear two-region NK .mod, and MATLAB Dynare can serve as a cross-check. No two-region model ships today.
vets.oracle_check: The proposed closed form is real but tautological. When the DGP sets a relative effect beta and an aggregate effect beta+kappa, invariance to kappa is plain within-transform algebra. It is already a unit test (tests/test_spatial/test_lp.py:268, test_total_is_a_relative_contrast_not_an_aggregate_multiplier) and a documented claim (docs/spatial.md:434). "The gap depends on the policy rule" means nothing unless kappa comes from a rule. There is an independent published oracle, read this session from the fetched NBER WP 17391 (Nakamura-Steinsson, revised June 2013). Table VI (separable preferences, sticky prices), closed-economy aggregate multiplier vs open-economy relative multiplier: Volcker-Greenspan 0.20 / 0.83; constant real rate 1.00 / 0.83; constant nominal rate infinite / 0.83; constant nominal rate with rho_g=0.85 1.70 / 0.90. Flexible prices: 0.39 / 0.43 and 0.32 / 0.43. Table VII (GHH): 0.12 / 1.42, 7.00 / 1.42, infinite / 1.42, and 8.73 / 2.04 with rho_g=0.50. The text gives the empirical relative multiplier as roughly 1.5 and calls the constant-real-rate value of 1 a Woodford (2011) result. Table numbering in the AER 104(3) version is unconfirmed. Chodorow-Reich (2019, AEJ:Policy 11(2):1-34; abstract read on aeaweb) gives a preferred cross-sectional multiplier of 1.8, calls it a rough lower bound for the national no-monetary-response multiplier, and puts that multiplier at 1.7 or above. The Wolf citation is misapplied. Wolf (2023, AER 113(8):2232-69; the fetched MIT PDF is the March 2023 version) defines the missing intercept for household-level regressions (Prop. 2, eq. 9). Its footnote 12 says cross-regional regressions contain local GE effects and do not identify his direct effects, and points to Wolf (2019) for the regional case.
vets.data_check: Synthetic is the right choice. notebooks/course/data and curso/notebooks/data_curso hold state unemployment CSVs (AKUR.csv, ALUR.csv, ...) but no state military procurement or state GDP, so an empirical Nakamura-Steinsson application is impossible. Unemployment alone gives no multiplier. Drop the "application" option or label it a placebo or illustration.
vets.novelty_check: Novel as teaching material. No notebook (00-68, notebooks/course, curso/notebooks) or example teaches relative vs aggregate multipliers. Grep for "missing intercept", "relative multiplier", "regional multiplier" and "Chodorow" hits only puremacro/spatial/lp.py and docs/spatial.md / docs/es/spatial.md. PLAN.md cites Nakamura only for the forward-guidance puzzle (PLAN.md:118). The 09-20 REVIEW.md has no regional item. panel_lp_iv appears only in prose (notebooks/07_local_projections.py:292), and spatial_lp has no notebook or example call. Notebooks 14 and 50 cover aggregate tax multipliers and notebook 55 covers Allen-Arkolakis spatial GE, so none overlaps. The invariance fact itself is already tested and documented, so the novelty lies in teaching it with a structural reason, not in the fact.

ideas.title: Low-frequency econometrics: cosine transforms and long-run covariability (Müller-Watson)
ideas.question: What can 70 years of data say about long-run relations, and how many low-frequency observations does that amount to?
ideas.description: Project series onto q low-frequency cosine weights and derive the exact covariance of those weights under I(0), I(1) and local-to-unity. Estimate long-run correlations and regressions (consumption and income, inflation and unemployment) with Müller-Watson-style inference. Link to EWC HAR, which uses the same projections.
ideas.paper: Müller & Watson (2008 Econometrica; 2018 Econometrica 'Long-run covariability'; 2020 'Low-frequency econometrics')
ideas.oracle_detail: The covariance matrix of the cosine weights follows from the autocovariances and is checked by simulation. Müller-Watson published estimates must be fetched.
ideas.data_detail: GDPC1 and PCECC96 in curso/notebooks/data_curso, and CPI and UNRATE in puremacro/datasets/data.
ideas.library_gaps: No low-frequency or cosine-transform module; new code is needed and can be shared with EWC.
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

vets.required_changes: 1) Bundle a frozen FRED snapshot under the package, e.g. puremacro/replication/data/mw2018.csv with GDP, PCEC, PCECTPI and CNP16OV, plus a source note. Build MW's definition: PCE-deflated per-capita growth, 1948Q1-2015Q4, q=12. Assert against NBER WP 23186 Table 1a I(0) and I(1) rho and beta within ±0.03, and cite the WP table explicitly. Treat GDPC1 and PCECC96 as a robustness row only. 2) Limit inference to the I(0) and I(1) exact formulas plus a one-parameter local-to-unity Omega(c) GLS sensitivity sweep. State plainly that MW's robust (A,B,c,d) sets and the Table 5 numbers are not reproduced. Add a Table 2-style Monte Carlo in which I(0) intervals are applied to I(1) data and the reverse. 3) Add a small shared module, e.g. puremacro/inference/lowfreq.py, with cosine_basis, cosine_transform, exact lowfreq_cov(T, q, c), lr_covariability(x, y, q, model) and ewc_hac. Unit-test it on Psi orthonormality, on the I(1) limit diag((pi*j)^-2), and against a Monte Carlo. Coordinate with any EWC proposal so there is one implementation. 4) Correct the capability list: use hac_fixed_b and llsw_critical_value for the HAR link, and use welch_psd only as the 'cannot see periods above 16 years' contrast. 5) For the Phillips pair, read CPIAUCSL and UNRATE directly, not load_macro_monthly. Label CPI as a proxy for PCE inflation and compare to MW Table 5 row 6 only qualitatively. 6) Fix the citations: 2008 Econometrica 76(5):979-1016; 2018 Econometrica 86(3):775-804 (numbers from WP 23186); 'Low-Frequency Econometrics' as NBER WP 21564 (2015), not 2020. 7) If the sample is extended to 2026, raise q to about 14 to keep the 11-year cutoff. Match MW's sigma_{y|x} normalization before comparing it. 8) Deliver the notebook as number 69 with a bilingual twin plus catalog and docs entries, following notebooks/_TEMPLATE.md with asserts on headline numbers. Scratch evidence is in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-jalonso-Documents-RESEARCH-puremacro/25d917e9-42e4-445b-993d-b9f78c13ca41/scratchpad/wf/lowfreq-mw/ (smoke.py, mwdef.py, phillips.py, mw2017_w23186.pdf).
vets.capabilities_check: The three listed symbols exist and ran in about 1.3 s (smoke.py in scratch wf/lowfreq-mw/). They are dfgls_test (puremacro/tests/unit_root.py:465), welch_psd (puremacro/spectral.py:71) and newey_west_se (puremacro/inference/hac.py:10). None of them does the core work, though; all three are side material. welch_psd defaults to n_seg=64, so its lowest nonzero frequency is a 64-quarter period (16 years), and the Hann window leaks into it. It cannot resolve the MW band, which is periods above 2T/q, about 11 years for T=271 and q=12. Use it only as a contrast. The HAR link should call hac_fixed_b (puremacro/inference/hac_fixed_b.py:75) and llsw_critical_value (:51), which the proposal leaves out. The library has no cosine basis, no low-frequency covariance, no long-run regression inference and no EWC. A grep for cosine, EWC, Muller and long-run covariability over puremacro/ returns nothing beyond Bartlett fixed-b. My prototype of the missing core was about 60 lines of numpy/scipy, so it is Pyodide-safe. The checks passed: Psi'Psi/T=I to 7e-16, Psi'1=0 to 7e-14, and the I(0) and I(1) inference ran.
vets.oracle_check: The oracle is strong and I verified it on two levels. (1) Closed form. Under I(0) the cosine weights are iid with covariance proportional to I. Under I(1) they are independent with variance proportional to (pi*j)^-2, which I derived by integration by parts and which MW state (NBER WP 23186, PDF p.15). The exact finite-T matrix Psi' Sigma_T Psi/T^3 matched diag((pi*j)^-2) to 0.16% at T=272, and a 20,000-draw Monte Carlo matched the exact matrix to 1.8e-3 on diagonal entries of about 0.10. Under local-to-unity (c=-10) the covariance is clearly non-diagonal (largest off-diagonal is 2.1 times the smallest diagonal), which is a good teaching point. (2) Published numbers. I fetched MW 'Long-Run Covariability' NBER WP 23186 (Feb 2017) and read Table 1a (PDF p.16) for GDP and consumption with q=12: I(0) rho 0.93, beta 0.76, 90% CI (0.60, 0.92); I(1) rho 0.93, beta 0.84, 90% CI (0.66, 1.01). I rebuilt their data definition from current-vintage FRED: nominal GDP and PCE deflated by PCECTPI, per capita using CNP16OV, 1948Q1-2015Q4, T=271. That gave I(0) rho 0.918, beta 0.756, CI (0.58, 0.93) and I(1) rho 0.928, beta 0.822, CI (0.64, 1.00), within 0.02, which fits vintage revisions. With the chained GDPC1 and PCECC96 series named in the proposal, I(1) gives rho 0.85 and beta 0.71, which misses the table. The (A,B,c,d) rows of Table 1, and every Table 5 entry (including the Phillips row), come from the 11-parameter robust least-favorable or Bayes machinery. They cannot be reproduced cheaply. The published Econometrica 86(3):775-804 version is paywalled and may differ from the WP.
vets.data_check: GDPC1, CPIAUCSL and UNRATE are in puremacro/datasets/data. PCECC96 and CNP16OV exist only in curso/notebooks/data_curso (bundle_2026A manifest), and showcase notebooks never read from there. They load puremacro.replication._data.load_csv (_data.py:14, as used in notebooks/20_unit_roots_with_power.py:77-80) or puremacro.datasets. Quarterly cnp16ov is available in puremacro/replication/data/gali1999.csv. MW's definition also needs nominal GDP, PCEC and PCECTPI, none of which is bundled. All are BEA/BLS series via FRED, public domain; I pulled them through Python fredgraph.csv without a key. load_macro_monthly (puremacro/datasets/loaders.py:159) cuts the sample to 1971 because its dropna at :195 joins NFCI, so the Phillips section must read CPIAUCSL.csv and UNRATE.csv directly. MW's Phillips pair uses PCE inflation; the bundled series is CPI. With bundled CPI and UNRATE, 1948-2015, q=12, u on pi gives I(0) rho 0.36, beta 0.21, 90% CI (-0.08, 0.51) and I(1) rho 0.09, beta 0.07. MW WP Table 5 row 6 reports rho 0.26 and beta 0.21 with beta 90% CI (-0.24, 0.76), but those are (A,B,c,d) estimates, so the comparison can only be qualitative.
vets.novelty_check: Novel. Notebooks 00-68 contain nothing on low-frequency or cosine-transform econometrics. Notebook 25 does frequency-domain connectedness, 26 does bandpass filters and 20 does DF-GLS power. The curso T00-T09 and notebooks/course cells only mention 'cosine' as TF-IDF similarity. I found no hits in examples/, PLAN.md (reviews/2026-09-23-notebook-catalog-plan) or REVIEW.md, and no EWC anywhere. Anchoring on notebook 20 fits, since both are about persistence. It pairs naturally with the 09-20 review's proposed uncertainty/coverage lab, and with any EWC HAR proposal, which should share the same Psi code.

ideas.title: DML on the real 401(k) data
ideas.question: Do dml_plr, dml_irm and dml_iv reproduce the paper's 401(k) estimates on the actual SIPP 1991 data?
ideas.description: Replace notebook 60's simulated data (60:82: 'Generate canonical 401(k) benchmark dataset matching Chernozhukov et al. (2018) moments') with the public SIPP extract. Compare PLR, IRM and IV with lasso and ridge learners against the paper's tables and against frozen DoubleML output. Show sensitivity to seeds and fold splits.
ideas.paper: Chernozhukov et al. (2018, Econometrics Journal)
ideas.oracle_detail: The paper's 401(k) tables (to fetch; not read this session), plus DoubleML (Python) run offline and frozen as an independent-software fixture.
ideas.data_detail: The SIPP 1991 401(k) extract distributed with the DoubleML package.
ideas.library_gaps: The learners are limited to lasso, ridge and logistic regression, so the paper's tree and forest rows cannot be matched. Check that repeated cross-fitting with median aggregation is exposed.
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

vets.required_changes:
1. Add a bundled dataset: puremacro/datasets/data/sipp1991_401k.csv plus load_401k() in puremacro/datasets/loaders.py, with the MIT notice, source URL and sha256 1123d5f0...b4b2. No runtime fetch.
2. For Table 3 (LATE), add a small dml_iivm/DoubleMLIIVM to puremacro/causal/dml.py (interactive IV score, paper sec. 5.2, with a no-always-takers option), or implement the verified IRM-ratio construction with its delta-method SE in the notebook. Do not compare dml_iv (partially linear IV) with Table 3. Instead, show dml_iv next to the paper's linear-IV figure of $13,102 and explain the estimand difference.
3. Implement the median method (100 splits in the paper) as a notebook helper, or as an n_rep option on the three estimators. Use 100 splits only for ridge. Use at most 5-10 splits for lasso/logistic with n_alphas=20, tol=1e-4, max_iter=200 passed through learner_kwargs. Budget about 5 minutes for the build.
4. Oracle: compare with the paper's Tables 2-3 as a tolerance band (the range across the paper's learners plus or minus one median-method SE), not a match to the Lasso cell. State in the prose that the paper's Lasso uses rlasso on the 401K.R:67 dictionary. Cite the page and table for every number.
5. Build the DoubleML fixture offline: DoubleML 0.11.4 run on puremacro-reconstructed folds (set_sample_splitting) with deterministic OLS/unpenalized-logit learners. Freeze theta and se for PLR, IRM-ATE, IRM-ATT, PLIV and IIVM into tests/fixtures, and assert at 1e-8 in tests/test_dml_irm_iv.py.
6. Rebuild notebook 60 on the real data, but keep the simulated weak-IV counterfactual (60:209-230) and replace the simulation-specific asserts (60:161-165, 60:192-195, 60:291-293). Alternatively, keep 60 and add a new notebook 69. Update the _es twin, notebooks/README.md, docs/notebooks.md and docs/es/notebooks.md.
7. Fix the stale line at docs/causal_dml.md:393.
vets.capabilities_check:
All three symbols exist in puremacro/causal/dml.py: dml_plr at :2077 (class DoubleMLPLR :1840), dml_irm at :2420 (class DoubleMLIRM :2132) and dml_iv at :2776 (class DoubleMLIV :2487). I smoke-ran them on the real SIPP extract (N=9915, scratch wf/dml401k-feas/smoke.py). Single split, controls = 9 raw covariates + 4 squares + 36 pairwise interactions = 49 columns:
- PLR lasso K=5: 9604 (se 1296)
- PLR ridge K=5: 9994 (se 1326)
- IRM lasso/logistic K=5: 7744 (se 1178), 0 trimmed
- PLIV K=5: 13810 (se 1858), F_eff about 7550
On raw covariates only, IRM is unstable: lasso 1558 (se 3797), OLS 777 (se 4506). The dictionary is therefore essential.

Four gaps the proposal misses or understates:
1. dml_iv is a partially linear IV model (dml.py:2491-2494). The paper's Table 3 is the LATE from the interactive IV model (paper sec. 5.2, pp.37-38), a different estimand. PLIV gives about 13.8k against the Lasso LATE of 8,944. There is no dml_iivm. I verified a workaround: the ratio of two dml_irm fits (Y on e401 and p401 on e401, same random_state, sharing folds and propensity) reproduces DoubleMLIIVM exactly (1128.553857 in both, OLS/logit learners). Its SE has to be rebuilt from the DMLIRMResult fields g0_pred, g1_pred and propensity_scores.
2. There is no repeated cross-fitting or median aggregation: no n_rep anywhere in dml.py, and docs/causal_dml.md:57 says the split is a single seeded permutation. The paper uses 100 splits with the median method (Table 2 note, p.42; authors' 401K.R:81 and :120).
3. The lasso chooses its penalty by BIC, not the Belloni et al. (2012) rule the paper uses (docs/causal_dml.md:77 and :396). No rlasso exists anywhere in puremacro.
4. Runtime. The coordinate loop is Python-level. With default settings, one split of IRM K=5 takes 295 s, PLR 93 s and PLIV 106 s. With n_alphas=20, tol=1e-4, max_iter=200, a lasso fit takes 1.8 s, a logit fit 6.6 s and PLR K=5 13 s, with nearly the same estimate. Ridge takes 0.3 s.
vets.oracle_check:
Both oracles are obtainable. I read the paper's values this session from the text of arXiv 1608.00060v6 (pypdf), pp.42-43. Lasso column, point [median SE] (median-method SE):
- Table 2, IRM ATE: 2-fold 6830 [1282] (1530); 5-fold 7170 [1201] (1398).
- Table 2, PLR: 2-fold 7717 [1346] (1749); 5-fold 8187 [1298] (1558).
- Table 3, LATE: 2-fold 8978 [2192] (3014); 5-fold 8944 [2259] (3307).
- Text: no-controls estimate $19,559 (se 1413); Poterba-style linear IV $13,102 (se 1922).
The data's naive difference in means is 19559.34, an exact match, which confirms the dataset.

Caveat on matching the Lasso cells. The authors' 401K.R:67 builds the lasso dictionary as (poly(age,6)+poly(inc,8)+poly(educ,4)+poly(fsize,2)+5 dummies)^2, several hundred terms, with the rlasso penalty (c=1.1). Even DoubleML 0.11.4 with sklearn LassoCV on the 49-column dictionary, K=2 and 10 reps misses them: PLR 10100 (1335) vs 7717, IRM 7927 (1206) vs 6830, IIVM 11765 (1726) vs 8978. So the published comparison must be a tolerance band, not a cell match. For example, "within the paper's range across learners plus or minus one median-method SE", where PLR 5-fold spans 8187 to 9247 and LATE 5-fold spans 8944 to 11764. The puremacro median-method results already fall close: ridge PLR K=5 over 20 splits gives 9923 [1330] (1340), and tuned-lasso PLR K=5 over 5 splits gives 9543 (1307).

The DoubleML oracle is strong for exact algebra. With folds shared through set_sample_splitting (rebuilt from puremacro's rng code) and deterministic OLS/unpenalized-logit learners, puremacro matches DoubleML to at most 2e-12 relative error on PLR, IRM-ATE, IRM-ATT (DoubleML calls it 'ATTE'), PLIV and the IRM-ratio LATE (scratch parity.py, late.py). DoubleML is not in the work env. It installs into a scratch pip --target together with optuna, colorlog, alembic, sqlalchemy and tqdm, so it can only serve as an offline-generated frozen fixture.

ideas.title: The main business-cycle shock: max-share over a frequency band (Angeletos-Collard-Dellas 2020)
ideas.question: Is there a single shock that drives most business-cycle-frequency variation in unemployment, output and hours, and is it inflationary?
ideas.description: Max-share identification targeting the 6-32 quarter band, compared with horizon-based max-share and news shocks. A DSGE with several shocks shows that the max-share shock is a mixture of them.
ideas.paper: Angeletos, Collard & Dellas (2020, AER) 'Business-Cycle Anatomy'; Barsky & Sims (2011)
ideas.oracle_detail: A DSGE DGP with known shocks and variance shares. ACD's published variance shares must be fetched.
ideas.data_detail: ACD's 10 US quarterly series from FRED, and Fernald TFP (a copy is in curso/notebooks/data_curso/fernald_tfp.csv).
ideas.library_gaps: maxshare targets forecast-error variance at a horizon (maxshare.py:35), not a spectral band, so a frequency-domain objective is needed. news_maxshare has no notebook calls.
ideas.plan_overlap: None.

vets.required_changes:
1. Add band_maxshare/identify_maxshare_band(Y or A_list, Sigma, target, band=(6,32), nq) to puremacro/var/identify/maxshare.py. It should take the top eigenvector of Re∫band C_k^* C_k dw by Gauss-Legendre and return q, the band share, IRFs and optional draws (minnesota_gibbs gives HPD bands). Test it against a state-space population factor.
2. Build the oracle from solve_sw07 (G, Impact): population band matrix, factor weights, and per-shock band shares. Do not list theoretical_moments as the oracle tool. Set the eb std explicitly to 0.24, citing sw07_pfeifer.mod:10-17. Ideally show that the default 1.8513 turns the "mixture" into a single risk-premium shock. Target y or lab, since there is no u.
3. Either implement a true Barsky-Sims routine (zero impact on TFP, sum of FEV shares over h=0..H) or drop the news comparison. In both cases fix the news_maxshare docstring and docs/var.md:260-261, and note the maxshare/identify_maxshare horizon off-by-one.
4. Empirical part: freeze ACD's panel with Table 11/12 transforms, 1955Q1-2017Q4, using a tools/gen_notebook_data_acd.py generator and a CSV in puremacro/replication/data. Run p=2 with the Minnesota BVAR. Check against NBER w24875 rev1 Table 1 with loose tolerances, e.g. the u share inside [66.80, 79.94] and the inflation share below about 15%. State that the data vintage differs. Fetch the AER Table 1 before citing it as the published value.
5. Keep the scope to the 6-32q band, horizon max-share and the SW07 mixture. Drop the long-run 80-inf band.
vets.capabilities_check:
Partly present. The listed symbols exist, but none of them does what the notebook needs.
(1) identify_maxshare (puremacro/var/identify/maxshare.py:272) is time-domain only. Its objective sums squared IRFs over h=0..max_fev_at-1 (maxshare.py:132-177, 350-361). It exposes .q, which is enough for a horizon-based comparison.
(2) news_maxshare (maxshare.py:98-100) is the same engine at H=40, and it is NOT Barsky-Sims. It has no zero-impact restriction on TFP, and its objective is the unweighted sum of squared IRFs (the FEV share at H), not BS's sum of FEV shares over h=0..H. The docstring and docs/var.md:260-261 still call it "the Barsky-Sims news shock". tests/test_var/test_news_maxshare.py:8-62 only checks that FEVD at H exceeds FEVD at h=0. There is also an off-by-one between the two helpers: maxshare(horizon=H) sums 0..H (maxshare.py:71) but identify_maxshare(max_fev_at=h*) sums 0..h*-1. No notebook calls either helper; only notebooks/17:217 uses identify_maxshare(max_fev_at=12).
(3) theoretical_moments (puremacro/dsge/build.py:674) is the wrong tool for the oracle. It lives on the build/load_mod Model, not on the SWResult from solve_sw07. It returns per-variable band variances and time-domain FEVD, not the cross-shock band matrix Omega whose top eigenvector is the population factor. Its bandpass is an ideal band [2pi/high, 2pi/low] computed by Gauss-Legendre quadrature (dsge/_moments.py:94-210), and the transfer function H_j is computed inline there but never returned.
Smoke run: I wrote a 25-line band max-share and ran it (scratch smoke.py and mc.py, under 1 s). It builds the Hermitian band matrix Re∫C_k(e^-iw)^* C_k(e^-iw) dw from VAR A_list and Sigma, as in ACD eq. (1). I used solve_sw07 (smets_wouters.py:680) with 7 observables (y, c, inve, lab, pinf, r, w). Over 100 Monte Carlo replications with T=250 and a VAR(4), the identified shock matched the population mixture: median cosine 0.955 (p10 0.907) and median R2 on the true shocks 0.895. Its median correlation with identify_maxshare(max_fev_at=16) was 0.897. Everything runs in NumPy and fits within Pyodide. puremacro/var/bvar.py:266 minnesota_gibbs can supply posterior draws for HPD bands as in ACD.
vets.oracle_check:
Obtainable and independent, but it has to be built on solve_sw07, not theoretical_moments.
Population oracle: Omega = ∫band Re(H_k^* H_k) over the true shocks, with H = (I - G e^-iw)^-1 Impact diag(sd). Its top eigenvector gives the exact mixture weights, and the VAR estimate is scored by correlating the identified shock with the true shocks.
HAZARD: the default puremacro/dsge/smets_wouters.py:769-771 sets SW07_SHOCK_STDS eb=1.8513. This matches Pfeifer's shocks block (sw07_pfeifer.mod:347; I fetched the upstream file and it has the same value). With it, risk_premium_shock_irf(unit_sd=True) gives +6.2% output on impact, and eb takes 97% of y's 6-32q variance (factor q ≈ 0.99 on eb). The "mixture" lesson then disappears. The mod header (sw07_pfeifer.mod:10-17) says the mode-file std is 0.24 for code-units b. With eb=0.24 the output factor is a real mixture: eb 0.61, eqs 0.58, em -0.34, ea 0.30, eg 0.25, with a factor share of 0.88. The facets are also not interchangeable: cosine y-lab 0.91, y-inve 0.77, y-c 0.68. That matches ACD's JPT finding in spirit, since ACD fn 40 says JPT is essentially SW07; ACD's JPT numbers must not be claimed.
Published empirical targets: read this session from NBER w24875 rev1 (Aug-2019 revision) PDF, Table 1, short run 6-32q, posterior median with 68% HPDI. u 73.71 [66.80,79.94], Y 58.51, h 47.72, I 62.09, C 20.38, TFP 5.86, Y/h 23.91, wh/Y 27.02, inflation 6.96, R 22.27. The spec, from the same PDF: a 10-variable levels VAR with p=2, a Minnesota prior and 50,000 Gibbs draws, 1955-2017, band [2pi/32, 2pi/6]. The AER 110(10) version was not fetched, so its values may differ. Treat these as approximate targets only.
vets.data_check:
Available as public data.
ACD Table 11 (read from the WP PDF) lists FRED mnemonics: A939RX0Q048SBEA, GDP, GDPDEF, PCND, PCESV, PCDG, GPDI, OPHNFB, PRS85006173, PRS85006023, CNP16OV, UNRATE and FEDFUNDS. Hours also use CE16OV. Table 12 gives the transforms. TFP is Fernald's utilization-adjusted DTFPu, cumulated.
Repo assets: puremacro/fetch/fernald.py, and curso/notebooks/data_curso/fernald_tfp.csv (dtfp and dtfp_util, 1947Q2-2026Q1, 316 lines). FUENTES.md:135-141 gives Fernald's terms only as "consult the publisher's terms". The other series are public-domain BEA, BLS and Fed data.
Caveats: the curso copy is outside the package and not reachable in Pyodide, so the notebook needs a frozen panel in puremacro/replication/data plus a tools/gen_notebook_data_*.py generator, following the speccurve17 pattern. Fernald's series and the NIPA data have been revised since ACD's 2016 download, so an exact Table 1 match is impossible.
vets.novelty_check:
Novel.
- No notebook, course file, curso notebook, example or docs page mentions Angeletos-Collard-Dellas or frequency-band max-share. The curso T04_C grep hit was a false positive on max(SHARE...).
- Notebook 17 uses horizon max-share as one of six schemes for an uncertainty shock.
- Notebook 25 does Barunik-Krehlik band FEVD for Cholesky and generalized shocks, not an optimised rotation.
- Notebook 26 covers bandpass filters.
- Notebook 45 covers DSGE news_irf, not VAR news identification.
- PLAN.md has BKK moments (line 101) and a notebook-35 rebuild around Gali 1999 (line 78). They touch technology and hours but use different methods.
- No PLAN.md duplicate.

vets.oracle_check: The proposed oracle is right in spirit but imprecise, and a stronger closed form exists; I verified it in scratch. (a) At psi=0 the debt coefficient is 1+r*=1.01, which is explosive, not 1. The exact 1 comes from the consumption Euler equation. The pencil (B,A) has generalized eigenvalues exactly {rho_y, 1, 1+r*}; the check against {0.85, 1, 1.01} has max error 0.0, because the characteristic factor is (lam-1)(lam-(1+r*)). The solved G shows the unit root only with the default div, and only to about 1e-16; with div=1.0 the result is eu=(0,0) and G=0. So assert |lam-1|<1e-12 and name the div setting; do not rely on the warning. (b) For psi>0 the debt root has a closed form: lam=[(1+a+ks)-sqrt((1+a+ks)^2-4a)]/2, where a=1+r*+(d/y)psi, s=c/y and k=psi/(gamma(1+r*)). It matches klein's G within 1.3e-14 for psi in {1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 5e-2}, and all eigenvalues are below 1. That is a real closed-form oracle for any psi, not just the psi=0 knife edge. (c) The data asserts 0.968 and 0.852 (10b:226-227) are course regression pins from the bundled OECD QNA edition of 2026-08-01 (10b:165). They are not published values and should be labelled as pins. (d) 10b:1036-1051 quotes García-Cicco, Pancrazi and Uribe (2010): 0.60 vs 1.50, sigma_g 0.030/0.0071, rho_g 0.83/0.35, and log marginal likelihoods 547.6 vs 600.6. ideas.description:
One cell per feature, each with an assertion.

§0 Provenance (4.0.0/4.0.1 and the Unreleased advisory): load_icio_data() -> MRIOTable.from_trade_calibration(..., negative_investment='to_inventory').accounting_report().world_reported_value_added gives 7.046e11, against 81,589,615.1 in tests/fixtures/trade/oecd_2023/manifest.json (8,636x). Print the SOURCES.md attribution. check_oecd_source on a temp CSV: a planted corrupted= digest raises MRIOIntegrityError; an unknown digest returns 'unknown_edition' with a RuntimeWarning.

§1 4.0: load_dynare_dr and verify_dynare_parity from a dict.

§2 4.1 fixes:
(a) theoretical_moments(hp_filter=1600) of an AR(1) with rho=0.9 against the time-domain HP-weights oracle of tests/test_hp_spectral_gain.py (the old code overstated by 22%).
(b) A 100-draw coverage Monte Carlo of the lp_iv 90% band, with the design of tests/test_lp_iv_tsls_se.py:88 (cov_uv=0.8).
(c) markov_stationary on a nearly decomposable chain (a valid vector) and on a chain with two closed classes (ValueError).
(d) Pointers to notebooks 59/60/61.

§3 4.2: solve_flexible_trade_equilibrium on notebook 62's 2x2 table with a 25% tariff. rho_va=0.5 routes to quasi_condensed with flexible_settings_applied=True. rho_va=1+1e-9 equals method='quasi_condensed' to 7.3e-14, but differs from the inactive (legacy) route by 2.27 (see notes).

§4 4.3: accounting='consistent' plus compute_hicksian_welfare on the two-country consumption benchmark (inlined from tools/reference_validation/validate_trade_welfare.py:22), with the country order swapped. The default closure gives A's EV -27.55% vs -45.99%; foreign_saving_units='world_income' makes it order-invariant. solve_policy_equilibrium on a prohibitive Leontief schedule raises PolicyEquilibriumError with .viability.

§5 Unreleased DSGE:
- Claim to x^2 at order 2: the default Var(y)=0; pruning=True gives 2A^2v^2 (0.0100428 at beta=.95, rho=.8, s=.1) and autocorrelations rho^(2k).
- Order-3 ergodic_moments with the Gaussian AR(1) 'a' as the shape oracle (skewness 0, kurtosis 3).
- discretionary_policy(loss_criterion='conditional'), pointing to notebook 66.
- solve_ms_dsge on a model with one row scaled by 1e9 is certified with relative_residual (rtol=0.0 reproduces the 4.3 failure).
- CollocationProblem at sigma=2: 'sigma' vs 'gamma', and Euler vs Bellman.
- solve_aiyagari_continuous(r_bracket=(-0.06, 0.04)), pointing to notebook 67.

§6 Unreleased trade engines, one tiny demo each (all under 3 s here):
- reduced_stability: root 2/9.

ideas.title: Is this input-output table safe to use?
ideas.question: How do you tell a corrupted or unbalanced MRIO table from a usable one before it drives a tariff counterfactual?
ideas.description:
1. Case study, the bundled 77x11 table. accounting_report() gives world VA 7.046e11 vs 81,589,615.1 for the clean 2019 release (fixture manifest), 8,636x. CHANGELOG.md:77 records 35.5% of intermediate cells equal.

2. Registries: OECD_ICIO_MD5 (years 2019, 2020) and OECD_KNOWN_CORRUPTED_MD5, whose registered explanation reads 'lost decimal points'. check_oecd_source's three outcomes, shown on temp files: whitelisted, unknown_edition with a warning, refused. identify_source(expected_sha256=), and verify_zip_member on a zip built in the notebook.

3. Native readers on the repo mini fixtures (tests/fixtures/trade/mrio/figaro_2c2s_26ed.csv and exiobase_2r3s_ixi, 'not run' in the browser): regularize_table gates all pass. Then plant faults (negative VA, a broken row identity, a sub-1e-6 phantom, a trade-balance gap) and watch the named gates fail. regularized=False and the downstream warnings from aggregate_mrio and to_calibration_matrix follow.

4. Productivity certificates. compute_spectral_radius Collatz-Wielandt bounds; check_hawkins_simon_viability sweeping tariff rates, with a certified violation from about 3.7 ([1.6978224, 1.6978224] at 9 per CHANGELOG.md:54, labelled a regression). The list/array schedule fix: a list read as the zero-tariff baseline in 4.3.0 (rho 0.3379685 vs 0.3762996).

5. Concordance/aggregate_mrio conservation (exact P M P^T) with USA/CHN/REST blocs; coarse_tariff_rates 11o vs 11b with benchmark revenue preserved (3.17148e9 both in the docs run).

6. Final-use semantics: cx_category and the FIGARO/WIOD/Eora rule that Cx is inventories, and why an empty Cx forces accounting='consistent'.

7. regularize_mrio_table's capped VA floor and balance_ras(return_info=True) on an infeasible target.
ideas.oracle_detail: Planted faults whose location is known must be named by the gates. Conservation identities of P M P^T are exact. The manifest's clean world VA (repo file) against the bundled table. Collatz-Wielandt bounds bracket rho computed by numpy.linalg.eigvals on small tables
ideas.data_detail: Bundled npz; inline synthetic and temp files; repo-only mini fixtures in tests/fixtures/trade/mrio and the oecd_2023 manifest (guarded 'not run' fallback)
ideas.library_gaps: The mini native fixtures and the clean-release world totals live in tests/ and are not in the wheel. Consider shipping a small public-domain native sample or the manifest totals so the browser version runs every section
ideas.plan_overlap: Refines PLAN.md:128-129 'Is this input-output table safe to use?' with concrete sections, oracles and numbers checked in this session

ideas.title: Three trade models, one tariff
ideas.question: When the same tariff runs through consistent accounting, nested-CES block Newton, the condensed Leontief model and the flexible CGE, which numbers must agree, which differ by construction, and why?
ideas.description:
One small table: the 2-country x 2-sector analytic table of docs/trade_household.md and notebook 62, plus the OECD 3x3 fixture where present. HOME imposes a 15% tariff.

(a) solve_trade_equilibrium(accounting='consistent') plus compute_hicksian_welfare.
(b) solve_ces_block_newton at flat technology reproduces (a) row by row (CHANGELOG.md:18). Then NestedCESTechnology(0.3, 0.5, 1.5, rho_va=0.8) with continue_tariff_homotopy and certify_ces_equilibrium, and compute_hicksian_welfare on the result.
(c) BalancedIOTable.from_trade_calibration -> calibrate_condensed -> solve_condensed -> compute_measures: the exact EV split, Fisher terms of trade, PE bound and GE-minus-PE term. It is a one-factor model, so its numbers differ by design; the notebook says which measures are comparable.
(d) solve_flexible_trade_equilibrium with rho_va, sigma_y and variable_markups. Show metadata routing, effective_method and flexible_settings_applied, the 4.2/4.3 advisory (settings silently ignored), and the discontinuity between the inactive legacy route and quasi_condensed (2.27 on this table under a 25% tariff, see notes).
(e) Household welfare under four demand systems. Fixed baskets reproduce Hicksian to 1e-10 (0.6305 in both, docs run). Cobb-Douglas 0.6311, LES 0.6309, CES 0.6308. Show Slutsky symmetry and negativity, and fit_supernumerary_share's identification caveat.
(f) foreign_saving_units: order invariance under 'world_income'.
ideas.oracle_detail: Flat-technology CES equals consistent accounting row by row. Fixed-basket household EV equals compute_hicksian_welfare to 1e-10. Slutsky symmetry. The independent primal expenditure minimization in tools/reference_validation/validate_trade_welfare.py:45 (SLSQP) checks EV. Condensed raw-flow certificate at 1e-10
ideas.data_detail: Hand-balanced tables inline; optional repo fixture tests/fixtures/trade/oecd_2023/2019_3regions_3sectors.npz
ideas.library_gaps: Decide and document the intended behaviour at the flexible routing switch (inactive-legacy vs active-quasi_condensed discontinuity) before teaching (d). The primal expenditure oracle lives in tools/, not the package
ideas.plan_overlap: Refines PLAN.md:130-131 'Three trade models, one tariff': adds the flexible route (d), the foreign-saving closure (f) and concrete agreement targets

- The SLSQP primal oracle does exist (tools/reference_validation/validate_trade_welfare.py:45). It is built on scalar_reference (validate_trade_accounting.py:32), a Brent solver for a 2-country x 1-sector table only, so it cannot check the 2x2 or 3x3 tables. tools/ is also not in the package or the Pyodide build, so the notebook must inline a compact version (about 60 lines of NumPy/SciPy) for a 2x1 warm-up table.
- The condensed 1e-10 certificate is an internal block of the same package.

Stronger oracle found this session: the condensed engine (ported from the IO rebuild) and consistent accounting (4.3.0) are separately developed, and they must agree exactly under three conditions: balanced benchmark trade, uniform factor shares within each country, and residents' purchases abroad (Cx/X) exempt from tariffs. The condensed model never tariffs X (tariffs.py:41). On a symmetric balanced 2x2 table the relative producer prices agreed to 3.3e-12 with 5%/2% taxes and to 3.3e-12 without taxes, under both foreign-saving closures. If Cx is tariffed the gap is 4e-4. On the unbalanced docs table the gap is 5e-4 (world_income) or 2.4e-3 (numeraire), because the condensed model spreads the deficit across C/G/X while consistent accounting takes it from I.
A second independent check: the PE unit-cost bound is a closed-form Leontief price solve that the notebook can reproduce with numpy.linalg.solve.
No paper or published table is involved, and I used no published numbers.

ideas.title: Where equilibria stop existing
ideas.question: How does puremacro tell 'no equilibrium', 'solver failed' and 'unstable or indeterminate equilibrium' apart, and what evidence does each verdict carry?
ideas.description:
1. Productivity boundary. check_hawkins_simon_viability over a tariff grid, and solve_policy_equilibrium's pre-screen raising PolicyEquilibriumError with .viability (about 1 ms vs 0.3 s, CHANGELOG.md:55).

2. Existence boundary of the condensed model on its synthetic economy. A 500% USA duty passes existence_gate, but the positive-wage equilibrium ends near 259% (lambda*=0.51773). Natural continuation stalls at lambda=0.515625; pseudo-arclength raises FoldDetected with sigma_min/sigma_max 3e-11; solve_condensed ends in EquilibriumNotFound. Plot the U.S. wage along the branch going to zero. All of this is pinned in tests/test_trade_condensed.py:1101-1120.

3. Solver-stack failure, not nonexistence. sigma_path on the OECD 3x3 fixture near unit elasticity: the docs (docs/trade_continuation.md:255-266) report a stop at fraction 0.450 (sigma 0.900), and 0.479 (sigma 1.041) on the reverse path. Keller finds roots with negative final expenditure, which the audit rejects. The notebook would make this claim reproducible; today's slow test accepts either outcome.

4. Local stability. reduced_stability gives the 2/9 closed-form root on the toy; the OECD 3x3 fixture is unstable at intermediate sigma 0.5 and stable at 1 (tests/test_trade_stability.py:502-514).

5. Determinacy. stability_report on the analytic two-country dynamic accounts (determinate) vs the bundled table (846 stable roots for 847 stocks, unstable root 1.00185 concentrated in IRL; regression only, corrupted-derived), and DynamicDeterminacyError gating solve_dynamic_transition.
ideas.oracle_detail: Root 2/9 of the toy reduced Jacobian. Spectral radius of the tariff-inflated A (numpy eigvals) against the Collatz-Wielandt bounds. The condensed boundary is characterised by the wage going to zero and the Jacobian becoming singular (test-pinned lambda values). Blanchard-Kahn root count vs number of predetermined stocks
ideas.data_detail: Condensed synthetic economy (test fixture synth_calib; needs a public constructor or inline copy), inline toy tables, analytic_two_country_accounts (puremacro/trade/dynamic/accounts.py:662); OECD 3x3 fixture repo-only; bundled table for the regression-only determinacy cell (15 s)
ideas.library_gaps: existence_gate, continuation, arclength and CondensedLeontiefModel are used by the tests. Check that they are public and documented before the notebook imports them. The synthetic condensed economy of the tests has no public constructor
ideas.plan_overlap: Refines PLAN.md:132-134 'Where equilibria stop existing (a sequel to 64)' with the Hawkins-Simon pre-screen and concrete test-pinned targets

ideas.title: Long-Plosser multisector RBC on the stacked Newton-Krylov
ideas.question: How does a stacked-time Newton-Krylov with block-tridiagonal preconditioning scale with the number of sectors, and does it recover a closed-form multisector policy?
ideas.description:
- Long-Plosser: log utility, Cobb-Douglas, full depreciation. The policy is closed form (constant input and consumption shares), so the stacked transition from a capital shortfall can be checked date by date.
- StackedProblem with an analytic JVP, complex step and central differences.
- solve_stacked_newton_krylov with BlockTridiagonalPreconditioner (Thomas vs SuperLU) and StructuredBlockTridiagonalPreconditioner, against no preconditioner: preconditioned_lgmres iteration counts as N sectors go 2 -> 50.
- compare_horizons horizon doubling.
- Agreement with solve_perfect_foresight (the docs RBC case gives 4.6e-11; CHANGELOG.md:24 reports 3.5e-11 on a 4,000-unknown 20-sector transition).
- Hulten's theorem for the first-order GDP response to sector shocks.
ideas.paper: Long and Plosser (1983), Real Business Cycles, JPE
ideas.oracle_detail: Closed-form Long-Plosser policy (derivable, no table needed). Hulten's theorem (Domar weights). Cross-check with solve_perfect_foresight
ideas.data_detail: Model-generated; no data
ideas.library_gaps: None. Naming: CHANGELOG lists compare_stacked_horizons, docs use compare_horizons (both exported, stacked_newton.py:134-135)
ideas.plan_overlap: Already in PLAN.md:122-124 (Long-Plosser on stacked Newton); this entry adds a concrete scaling and oracle design

vets.required_changes:
1. Reframe the question from "scaling with N" to "What makes a stacked transition hard: the number of sectors or the persistence of the input-output network?" Sweep N (2, 10, 50) to show that matvec counts do not change with N, and show the O(T n^3) setup and memory_bytes. Sweep the input share, rho(A) about 0.5 to 0.94, where None degrades from about 150 to about 2300 matvecs and time_block_jacobi and SGS fail while the exact steady inverse stays at about 22.
2. Report matvec counts through a counting jvp_fn wrapper, not krylov_outer_iterations.
3. Recast Hulten. The impact GDP response is theta_j, the long-run response is [(I-A)^{-1} theta]_j, and consumption-equivalent welfare is beta*gamma_j, the Domar weight. Assert all three against the stacked solve (observed agreement 1e-13 to 4e-14).
4. Specify the formulation: n_vars=2N, logs, block s=(log lam_s, log Y_{s+1}) so that y_init supplies only predetermined output, X_ij eliminated analytically, log Z normalized so that Y*=1. Either keep fixed labor and say so, or add the labor FOC.
5. Run compare_stacked_horizons (import from puremacro.dsge, or compare_horizons from puremacro.dsge.stacked_newton) on the high-input-share calibration, where 30/60 fails (0.032) and 60/120 gives 1.6e-4. At Long-Plosser shares every horizon passes at 1e-13.
6. Label the input-output matrix as synthetic, and never use the bundled 77x11 table.
7. Anchor on notebook 41 or make it a new notebook 69, not 52.
8. Hold the notebook until the release that ships stacked_newton.
9. Keep the solve_perfect_foresight parity at N<=20 (7.7 s locally at N=50), and cap max_iter and krylov_maxiter on the failing preconditioner demos so the Pyodide build stays short.
10. Fix the citations: the CHANGELOG 3.5e-11 figure is for decoupled Ramsey sectors, the Ramsey docs figure is "about 5e-11" (docs/dsge_stacked_newton.md:126), not 4.6e-11, and state that this notebook qualifies the docs claim at docs/dsge_stacked_newton.md:90.

- A StructuredBlockTridiagonalPreconditioner built from the steady-state blocks with LU factors converges with Jacobi and symmetric sweeps at low input shares (140 and 49 matvecs/T). At high input shares (rho(A) about 0.94) both fail: symmetric SGS ends in line_search_failure with a true linear residual of 1.03 against 0.10 requested.

Scaling with N:
- Low input shares (labor share 0.35-0.6, rho(A) about 0.5), T=150: the exact steady inverse needs 20-23 matvecs for N=2, 10 and 50. With no preconditioner it needs 141-185 and still converges, in 0.55 s at N=50 (15,000 unknowns). time_block_jacobi needs 122-142.
- High input shares (labor share 0.03-0.08, rho(A) about 0.94): exact still needs 21-23. None needs 942-2327. time_block_jacobi FAILS at every N (17-35 s wasted).
- Iteration counts do not depend on N. What drives them is persistence (rho(A)) and T.
- Memory of the Thomas factors is 24 MB at N=50, T=150.

solve_perfect_foresight parity: 5.0e-12 at N=5 and at N=50. At N=50 it takes 7.7 s against 0.16 s for the stacked solver.
vets.oracle_check:
The closed form is independent of the solver and can be derived by hand. The value of output V_i=lam_i Y_i solves V=theta+beta A V_{+1}, so V=gamma=(I-beta A)^{-1} theta. Then C_i=(theta_i/gamma_i)Y_i and X_ij=beta a_ij gamma_j Y_i/gamma_i, which gives log Y_{t+1}=kappa+A' log Y_t. The stacked path matches it date by date to 1e-13, and the oracle catches timing errors: putting lam_{t-1} in y_init fixes lam_0 at its steady-state value and gives the wrong path.

The Hulten claim as proposed is FALSE. The first-order GDP response is not the Domar weight. Measured in lp_hulten.py (N=10, sector j=3, permanent 1% shock):
- Impact response of real consumption GDP: 0.076832 = theta_j, the consumption share.
- Long-run response: 0.172304 = [(I-A)^{-1} theta]_j, the undiscounted Leontief inverse.
- Consumption-equivalent welfare: 0.154487 = beta*gamma_j, the Domar weight gamma_j=[(I-beta A)^{-1} theta]_j=sales/GDP, discounted one period by the timing. This holds exactly (4e-14) because the model is log-linear.

So Hulten holds for welfare, not for GDP at any horizon.

compare_horizons tells you nothing at Long-Plosser-like shares: the gap is 1.6e-13 at 30/60 dates and 1e-15 at 60/120. It becomes informative at high input shares: 0.032 at 30/60 and 1.6e-4 at 60/120.

No published number is needed. The "4.6e-11 docs RBC" figure in the proposal is not in any doc I grepped. docs/dsge_stacked_newton.md:126 says "about 5e-11" for the Ramsey case.

ideas.title: Filter-induced cycles on random walks: HP, BK, CF, Hamilton and Beveridge-Nelson
ideas.question: What cycles do HP, Baxter-King, Christiano-Fitzgerald, Hamilton and Beveridge-Nelson filters manufacture from a series with no cycle at all?
ideas.description: DGP 1: Gaussian random walk, T=400, R=300. DGP 2 (control): a trend plus a stationary AR(2) with a planted 20-quarter cycle. Apply hp_filter(1600), baxter_king_filter(6,32,12), christiano_fitzgerald_filter, hamilton_filter(h=8,p=4) and beveridge_nelson_filter. Measure cycle ACFs, welch_psd spectra and business_cycle_band_power. An end-point part compares the revision of the last HP cycle value as 1-8 new observations arrive: two-sided hp_filter vs dsge.one_sided_hp_filter. A cross-check compares LinearModel.theoretical_moments(hp_filter=1600) with simulated HP moments of a stationary build() model. Runtime: 6.3 s native for R=300 x 5 filters. In real Pyodide hp_filter costs 41 ms per call at T=400, against 2.7 ms natively, so budget about 20 s. Figure: (a) average cycle spectrum of each filter on the random walk against the closed-form curve; (b) ACF of each filter's cycle against theory; (c) end-point revision fan for HP. Exercise: change lambda or the BK band. Assert that the simulated HP ACF is within 0.05 of the closed form at lags 1-8. Prompts: why is the Hamilton cycle of a random walk an 8-quarter difference, and why is the BN cycle nonzero in samples?
ideas.paper: Nelson and Kang (1981); Harvey and Jaeger (1993); Cogley and Nason (1995); Baxter and King (1999); Christiano and Fitzgerald (2003); Hamilton (2018)
ideas.oracle_detail: The HP cycle gain 4*lambda*(1-cos w)^2/(1+4*lambda*(1-cos w)^2), applied to the random-walk spectrum, gives the cycle's spectrum and ACF. Computed here: spectral peak at 30.1 quarters for lambda=1600; ACF at lags 0-6 of 1, 0.72, 0.48, 0.29, 0.13, 0.00, -0.10. The simulation (R=300, T=400) matched within 0.02. The Hamilton cycle of a random walk is approximately y_{t+8}-y_t with ACF 1-k/8 (simulated 0.87, 0.74, 0.61, 0.49 against 0.875, 0.75, 0.625, 0.5). The BN cycle of a random walk is identically 0; the simulated s.d. of 0.139 is AR(4) sampling error.
ideas.data_detail: Simulated random walks and AR(2) cycles.
ideas.library_gaps: None blocking. hp_filter is about 15x slower in Pyodide than natively (41 ms vs 2.7 ms at T=400), which matters for Monte Carlo on tablets. There is no helper that returns a filter's theoretical gain, so the lab computes the HP and BK gains inline.
ideas.plan_overlap: 26 filters one synthetic series with no Monte Carlo and no closed form. PLAN.md's 'Business-cycle moments done right' (BKK / King-Rebelo) uses the HP/bandpass theoretical moments; this lab is its methodological prelude. The end-point part links to lab 69-info-set.

Do the same for bandpass_filter=(6, 32) as CF's target. Explain the klein_solve warning: filtered moments exist even though unconditional ones do not.
2. Reframe the end-point part. one_sided_hp_filter equals the two-sided real-time endpoint (assert max|diff| < 1e-4 for t >= 20) and never revises. The fan should show hp(y[:T0+j])[T0-1] minus the real-time value, for j = 1-8, against the exact revision variance from the linear weights. Link course/01 §3 (real-GDP 2019Q4 revision) instead of repeating it.
3. Vectorize the HP Monte Carlo and the fan: one solve with R right-hand sides, plus 8 solves for the fan. Assert equality with hp_filter on one series. Budget about 5 s in Pyodide instead of 20 s, which currently leaves out the roughly 118 s fan.
4. Panel (a): call welch_psd with n_seg=128 or more, not the default 64. Plot the closed form in welch_psd units (2π·S(ω)) and state the 30.1-q peak from the closed form, not the Welch grid. Say that the lowest bin is biased by leakage.

ideas.title: Discretization error in heterogeneous-agent inputs: Tauchen, Rouwenhorst, Farmer-Toda
ideas.question: How much does replacing an AR(1) by a finite Markov chain change an answer that is known exactly, and which discretizer should a Bewley model use at high persistence?
ideas.description: Oracle A: a Lucas tree with log-dividend growth x'=(1-rho)mu+rho x+eps and CRRA gamma, with c=d. Its price-dividend ratio is a closed-form series in the Gaussian moments of sums of x; on a chain it is v=(I-beta P D)^{-1} beta P D 1 with D=diag(exp((1-gamma)x)). Calibration: beta=0.95, gamma=2, mu=0.02, rho in {0.5,0.9,0.95,0.99,0.995}, sigma scaled so the series converges. Oracle B: chain moments (markov_stationary; unconditional sd ratio, autocorrelation) against the AR(1). Consequence C: the Aiyagari equilibrium rate at rho=0.9 under each discretizer, reusing notebook 67's EGM helper. Grid: n in {3,5,9,15,25}. Prototype (max log error over states within 2 sd), rho=0.95, sigma=0.01. At n=5: Tauchen 4.0 (sd ratio 1.31, autocorrelation 0.988; the discretized model nearly diverges), Rouwenhorst 0.016, Farmer-Toda 0.011. At n=15: 0.013, 0.0037 and 0.00098. Tauchen n=3 at rho=0.99 collapses (sd ratio 0). Farmer-Toda is worse than Rouwenhorst at n<=5. Runtime: farmer_toda takes 1.2-2.4 s per chain natively at n=3-5 and 0.41 s in Pyodide at n=9, rho=0.99; the grid takes about 20-30 s and the Aiyagari solves dominate. Figure: log error vs n (log scale) for each method at three rho; a table of chain sd ratio and autocorrelation; Aiyagari r by method. Exercise: choose rho and n. Assert that the Rouwenhorst sd ratio is 1 and its autocorrelation equals rho to 1e-10, and that the Rouwenhorst error falls from n=5 to n=15.
ideas.paper: Tauchen (1986); Rouwenhorst (1995); Burnside (1998); Kopecky and Suen (2010); Farmer and Toda (2017)
ideas.oracle_detail: The exact price-dividend ratio is sum_n beta^n exp((1-gamma) m_n(x) + 0.5(1-gamma)^2 V_n), with m_n and V_n the conditional mean and variance of sum_{j<=n} x_{t+j} for a Gaussian AR(1). It was derived in this session and truncation-checked (N=4000 against 20000). The AR(1) moments are closed form.
ideas.data_detail: No data; calibrations are set in the notebook.
ideas.library_gaps: (1) aiyagari_steady_state and the other steady-state helpers in puremacro/vfi/examples.py hardcode tauchen (lines 47, 122, 180, 240, 305, 357) and take no discretizer argument. (2) farmer_toda is slow at small n (BFGS with edge-row fallbacks, discretize.py:104-133; 1-2.4 s natively) and less accurate than Rouwenhorst at n<=5 in the prototype; document or speed it up.
ideas.plan_overlap: 67 already swaps Tauchen-7 for Rouwenhorst-7 at rho=0.9 in Aiyagari's Table II. This lab generalises that with a closed-form oracle and adds Farmer-Toda, which has 0 notebook call sites. PLAN.md's Bewley row mentions a Kopecky-Suen comparison.

2) Replace "max log error within 2 sd" with the centre-node (x=mu) log error and the log error of the stationary-mean P/D against its closed form. Keep every n odd.
3) Fix the calibration as sigma = 0.2(1-rho), holding long-run growth volatility fixed. State that at rho >= 0.99 this makes the process tiny, so the Bewley recommendation rests on Consequence C.
4) Show farmer_toda twice: the library default m=3, and the authors' rule m = sqrt(2(n-1)) if rho <= 1-2/(n-1) else sqrt(n-1), cited to alexisakira/discretization discreteAR.m. Drop the claim that "FT is worse than Rouwenhorst at n<=5".

vets.oracle_check: Oracle A is independent of discretize.py, and I rederived and checked it. The chain P/D is v=(I-beta P D)^{-1} beta P D 1 with D=diag(exp((1-gamma)(mu+grid))). The exact P/D is sum_n beta^n exp((1-gamma)m_n + 0.5(1-gamma)^2 V_n) with m_n = n mu + (x-mu) rho(1-rho^n)/(1-rho) and V_n = (sigma/(1-rho))^2 sum_{k<=n}(1-rho^k)^2. Checks: truncation N=4000 vs 20000 differs by 1.8e-15; the iid limit matches q/(1-q) to all printed digits. Two flaws: (1) Linear solve without a spectral-radius guard. Tauchen n=3 has rho(beta P D)=1.0251 at rho=0.95 and 1.0655 at rho=0.9, so the chain price is infinite. np.linalg.solve still returns [-40.9, 13.5, 5.5], and the proposal's "within 2 sd" metric reads only the finite middle node, giving a bogus error of 0.089. Tauchen n=5 at rho=0.95 has radius 0.9999, which explains the knife-edge 4.0. (2) The "states within 2 sd" metric is not like for like. Tauchen and Farmer-Toda span +/-3 sd while Rouwenhorst spans +/-sqrt(n-1) sd, so at n=3 Tauchen and FT are scored on one node and Rouwenhorst on three. Every n in the grid is odd, so use (a) the error at the centre node x=mu and (b) the stationary-mean P/D against the exact unconditional mean, which is also closed form: add 0.5(1-gamma)^2 b_n^2 sd_u^2 to each term, with b_n = rho(1-rho^n)/(1-rho). Oracle B (chain moments) is closed form but not new (see novelty). The Burnside (1998) attribution was not checked against the paper in this session; the formula was checked numerically as above.

ideas.title: Weak identification in a DSGE: Calvo, labour elasticity and the Taylor rule
ideas.question: Which structural parameters can data on output, inflation and the interest rate pin down, and how does weak identification show up in finite samples?
ideas.description: DGP: a three-equation NK model written as a .mod string and built with build_dynare. kappa=(1-theta)(1-beta theta)/theta*(sigma+varphi), with Calvo theta=0.75 and labour elasticity varphi=1. AR(1) demand, cost-push and monetary shocks (rho 0.9/0.5/0.5); observables x, pi and i. Population part: identification(varobs=['x','pi','i'], params, lags=2) under several parameter sets, iid vs persistent shocks, and observable subsets. Computed here: with {calvo, varphi, phi_pi, phi_x, rho_r, rho_u, rho_v}, J2 rank was 6/7 with null combination '0.0544 * calvo + 0.9985 * varphi = 0'. Dropping varphi gave full rank, condition number 326, and phi_pi collinearity R^2 of 0.973. Sample part: profile log-likelihoods of calvo and phi_pi at T in {100,400,1600} via make_state_space_from_varobs + kalman_filter. Then a Monte Carlo of posterior modes (LinearModel.estimate with UniformPrior on calvo, phi_pi, phi_x, rho_r, n_draws=10), R=30 at T=200, run in longrun.chunked. The mode run takes 1.2 s native and 1.7 s in Pyodide per replication (measured), so about 50 s in Pyodide; identification takes 41/77 ms. Figure: Ratto strength bars; profile likelihood curves by T; violins of mode estimates against the truth. Exercise: add varphi to the estimated set. Assert that j2_rank < j2_n_params and that the null vector loads on calvo and varphi.
ideas.paper: Canova and Sala (2009); Iskrev (2010); Komunjer and Ng (2011); Ratto (2011)
ideas.oracle_detail: Parameters are planted. The rank deficiency is exact by construction (kappa depends on theta and varphi only through one composite), so the reported null space must match it. Estimation dispersion is measured against the known truth.
ideas.data_detail: Simulated from the NK .mod string.
ideas.library_gaps: (1) LinearModel.estimate raises for build() models ('needs a model built with build_dynare or load_mod', build.py:1918) and is Bayesian only; there is no ML route, so a Monte Carlo of estimators is slow. (2) There is no public loglik(model, params, data) helper; profiles compose make_state_space_from_varobs and kalman_filter by hand. (3) Shock s.d.s cannot be estimated from a plain prior dict on a build() model unless they are model parameters.
ideas.plan_overlap: PLAN.md: 'Three samplers, one posterior' lists identification strength, and this lab could precede it. 45 calls identification once on another model, with a summary only.

vets.capabilities_check:
All eight symbols exist at the cited lines: build_dynare (dynare.py:244), identification (identification.py:630), LinearModel.identification (build.py:392), LinearModel.estimate (build.py:886), make_state_space_from_varobs (observation.py:92), kalman_filter (state_space.py:227), UniformPrior (priors.py:753) and longrun.chunked (longrun/_job.py:321). (1) The claim is true: estimate() is Bayesian only and raises for build() models (build.py:1916-1920). It is irrelevant here because the lab uses build_dynare.
(2) The claim is partly false. LinearModel.smoother(data, varobs=...).loglik (build.py:1067 -> smoother.py:108-150) returns the log-likelihood with the stationary Lyapunov initialisation. It matched a hand-built kalman_filter to 2 decimals. A bare kalman_filter call uses the diffuse P0=1e6*I (state_space.py:227), which shifted loglik by about 22 at T=400. Hand-composed code must pass P0.
(3) This does not apply to build_dynare models. The public puremacro.dsge.EstimatedParams/EstimatedParamSpec (_estimated_params.py:130-177, exported in dsge/__init__.py:126-127) can be passed as priors=, and it takes kind='stderr_shock' and an explicit init.

(a) Setting rho=0 for the iid variant makes build_dynare raise 'no predetermined state variables detected' (dynare.py:498). Passing states=['r','u','v'] fixes it (verified: J2 6/6, cond 91.5).
(b) Every mode search starts at the prior mean (_estimated_params.py:169-177), which matters on a ridge (see gaps).
(c) The null-combination string is written as an equation, '... = 0' (identification.py:328), but it is a null DIRECTION. The iso-kappa curve has calvo and varphi rising together, while the equation reading suggests they move in opposite directions.

The oracle is real and independent of puremacro. On a moment-based ridge, the null direction must be proportional to (dkappa/dvarphi, -dkappa/dtheta) = (lambda(theta), -(sigma+varphi)*lambda'(theta)), where lambda = (1-theta)(1-beta*theta)/theta and lambda' = beta - 1/theta^2. I also verified a likelihood-level oracle. From 6 random starts (via EstimatedParamSpec init), the ML modes spread along the ridge: calvo 0.759-0.824, varphi 1.12-3.22. The implied kappa was 0.1668 every time (true 0.1717), and phi_pi was identical at 1.5079 (t6_ridge.py). The ridge is therefore exactly the analytic iso-kappa curve.

Paper anchor, read this session in Canova-Sala ECB WP 583 (Jan 2006; published JME 56(4):431-449 per the IDEAS page):
- p.21, eq. (5): the Phillips-curve slope (phi+nu)(1-zeta*beta)(1-zeta)/((1+omega*beta)zeta) nests this lab's kappa.
- p.25: 'Figure 6 shows that ridges are present ... little information about the correct combination of lambda_y and lambda_pi or nu and zeta'.
- p.28-29: 'parameter estimates and standard errors of weakly identified and under-identified parameters are independent of the sample size'.
Their Table 1 uses impulse-response matching, not likelihood, so it is a qualitative anchor only and not a numeric target. I could not check the Iskrev (2010), Komunjer-Ng (2011) and 'Ratto (2011)' citations because the web-search budget was used up. 'Ratto (2011)' needs a precise reference.

ideas.title: Policy accounting lab: one fiscal shock from identification to a stated multiplier
ideas.question: When the true government-spending multiplier is known, which reported number (impact, cumulative, peak, or converted from logs) answers which question, and which identification recovers it?
ideas.description: DGP: solve_sw07() at the module's SW07_POSTERIOR_MODE calibration (not re-estimated), simulated by hand as z_t = G z_{t-1} + Impact e_t with SW07_SHOCK_STDS (T=240, burn-in 200). SW07's g enters the resource constraint in units of steady-state output (smets_wouters.py:613-615), and its process loads on the technology innovation (cgy*ea, line 492). Truth, from model IRFs to eg (computed here): impact multiplier 0.974; cumulative sum(y)/sum(g) 0.791, 0.708 and 0.616 at h=4, 8 and 20. Estimators: (a) a Blanchard-Perotti recursive VAR with g first (fit_var + Cholesky); (b) Ramey-Zubairy one-step LP-IV, one lp_iv call per horizon with n_lags=0 and explicit predetermined lags, as in examples/ramey_zubairy_2018_multipliers.py:173-186, using a noisy narrative instrument z = eg + 0.5*eta; (c) the two-step ratio of cumulated LP coefficients; (d) a units pitfall that converts log responses with a sample Y/G ratio. Prototype (R=200, T=240) for the cumulative multiplier at h=8: recursive VAR mean 0.983 (sd 1.15) against truth 0.708, contaminated by technology; LP-IV mean 0.646 (sd 1.84). Deliverable: an accounting table defining each reported number's estimand, numeraire (units of steady-state output), horizon aggregation (impact, cumulative, present value with beta), shock definition (eg vs g innovation) and uncertainty (MC s.d., AR set). An optional trade contrast gives the same table for a tariff using trade.compute_hicksian_welfare. Runtime: solve 5 ms; about 1 s native per 200 replications per horizon; about 10 s native and 30 s or less in Pyodide for five horizons. Figure: true vs estimated multiplier paths with MC percentiles; bars of one shock's multiplier under four definitions. Exercise: change the instrument noise or the VAR ordering. Assert that the truth equals the IRF-ratio identity to 1e-12 and that the LP-IV median is within MC tolerance.
ideas.paper: Blanchard and Perotti (2002); Smets and Wouters (2007); Ramey (2011); Ramey and Zubairy (2018)
ideas.oracle_detail: True multipliers are exact ratios of solve_sw07 IRFs, i.e. the model's own numbers, not published ones. Accounting identities (cumulative = ratio of cumulated IRFs, units) are checked to rounding.
ideas.data_detail: Simulated from the SW07 calibration bundled in code; no SW07 data fixture needed.
ideas.library_gaps: (1) SWResult (smets_wouters.py:168) has no simulate or irf method, so the lab writes the recursion. (2) There is no multiplier helper (cumulative or present-value multiplier with unit conversion). (3) lp_iv lags x automatically, and with x a forward window sum those lags contain future values; hence n_lags=0 plus explicit controls. Document this pitfall.

ideas.title: Compact starter: simulate first, then replace the data
ideas.question: What is the smallest reproducible path from data to fit, diagnostics, figure and exported table, and how do you know the pipeline works before trusting it on real data?
ideas.description: Step 1: simulate a bivariate VAR(2) with planted coefficients and a known Cholesky IRF. Run lag_select, then fit_var, is_stable, cholesky_svar(n_boot=200) and lp_hac, and assert that the true IRF lies inside the 90% band at most horizons (one seed plus a 50-replication check, under 5 s). Step 2: run the same function on bundled monthly okun.csv (industrial production growth and the unemployment rate, 1948 on; load_csv('okun')). Step 3: export the table with LPResult.to_markdown or to_latex and save the figure, then invite the reader to point the loader at their own CSV. Runtime: seconds. Figure: one IRF panel with bands, the simulated truth overlaid in step 1. Exercise: replace the CSV path or ordering. Assert that the pipeline returns finite bands and is_stable is True.
ideas.oracle_detail: Step 1 recovers a planted VAR IRF; it is a pipeline check, not evidence about Okun's law.
ideas.data_detail: puremacro/replication/data/okun.csv (939 monthly rows: date, indpro, unrate), already used by notebook 20.
ideas.library_gaps: None.
ideas.plan_overlap: 09-20 REVIEW brainstorm item 5. PLAN.md calls 'DSGE from a Python function' 'the starter the 09-20 review asked for'. Decide whether this data-side starter and that model-side starter both ship or merge into one.

As proposed, the assertion is fragile:
- (a) With small second-lag coefficients (A2=[[.1,0],[.05,.1]], T=300), BIC picks p=1 in 50/50 reps. VAR 90% pointwise coverage then falls to 0.59, and at seed 0 one response lies 0/13 inside. The '1 seed + 50-rep' assert would fail.

ideas.title: Nowcast density calibration done on the nowcasts themselves (rebuild 59)
ideas.question: Are the DFM's own recursive out-of-sample nowcast densities calibrated on the simulated panel, and does the Berkowitz test detect a deliberately under-dispersed density?
ideas.description: Replace the independent rng draws (59.py:223-226) with recursive out-of-sample DFM nowcasts on the simulated Mexico panel. Compute PITs from the model's mean and s.d. Run Berkowitz LR and KS tests, then repeat with an under-dispersed variant (parameter uncertainty ignored, or sd scaled by 0.6) to show rejection. Relabel the fan chart as illustrative (no 'official Banxico'). Keep the exact news identity.
ideas.oracle_detail: Under the DGP's true conditional density the PITs are exactly U(0,1), so Berkowitz rejection rates over replications must be near nominal size. The mis-scaled variant has a known direction of failure.
ideas.data_detail: The existing seeded panel on real INEGI/Banxico/BCB identifiers, flagged SIMULATED (59.py:18, :168).
ideas.library_gaps: None known; recursive refitting may be slow, so cap the number of evaluation quarters.
ideas.plan_overlap: REVIEW.md:119-122 (59 prose) and the information-set lab; the guide caveat already exists (docs/notebooks.md:78-82).

All four symbols exist and run, and the recursive loop is cheap. realtime_nowcast is at puremacro/nowcast/realtime_nowcast.py:246, banbura_modugno_news at news.py:300, pit_uniformity_test and fan_chart at evaluation.py:213 and :486.
